agroforestry__drought__agro_pastoral.mechanism: Live fences carry livestock through drought as a fodder reserve: live fences of Gliricidia sepium, Leucaena leucocephala and similar species supply high-quality fodder when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. During drought, understorey crop yield can be higher than in an open system even under intense shade, silvopastures are credited with better water infiltration rates, and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1].
agroforestry__drought__agro_pastoral.conditionality: The US and Sahelian parkland units come from agro-pastoral systems; the US silvopasture unit is high-income evidence that names infiltration rather than a drought outcome, and the Sahelian parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. The understorey yield benefit holds in drought years only, as tree shade can lower understorey yields under normal rainfall [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. The Kenyan FMNR unit is a compiler rating on a technology sheet, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size, and few units say how large the drought benefit is [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. No unit in this row measures the benefit in a severe or extreme drought.

agroforestry__drought__agro_pastoral__in.mechanism: A US silvopasture study lists better water infiltration among silvopasture's services, used here as a soil-water component of drought [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. Against this, earlier work cited in a temperate alley-cropping study found greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years because of tree–crop competition [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3].
agroforestry__drought__agro_pastoral__in.conditionality: This is a high-income scope row resting on two second-hand statements that point in opposite directions, so no clear effect can be drawn [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3]. The silvopasture statement does not mention drought, and the shelterbelt finding concerns crop yield rather than an agro-pastoral outcome, applied here by default; neither transfers directly to LIC/LMIC agro-pastoral systems [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3].

agroforestry__drought__all.mechanism: Most of the evidence finds that agroforestry reduces drought losses, but the finding splits by sub-practice and some measured results show no benefit or harm. On the benefit side: in Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, farmers said deep-rooted trees reach water from deep down and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind; the study concludes that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought, citing deep root systems that use a greater soil volume for water [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10, ev_t3_drought_roots_quandt17_2, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. Trees also share deep water: hydraulic redistribution in Sahelian parklands lets crop roots use deep soil moisture reached only by tree roots [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3]. In an induced drought in eastern Canada only the monocrop lost yield, and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Nyando District, Kenya, households in an agroforestry project typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods, and many farmers reported selling fuel wood and timber from their trees to buy food during the drought [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25% [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. Live fences of species such as Gliricidia sepium and Leucaena leucocephala supply livestock fodder in the dry season, when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. For shaded coffee and cocoa: in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest, the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly raised coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; and reviews cite a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season and low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11]. In a 25-year-old walnut-based alley-cropping system in southern France, winter pea still yielded less under the trees than in the full-sun control under both rainfall regimes, but the yield drop caused specifically by an imposed spring drought was smaller under the trees: full-sun yield fell 22% under drought while the alley-cropped yield rose by 12 to 20% relative to its own rainfed baseline, which the authors attribute to drought shifting yield formation from the shade-sensitive pod-set stage to grain filling [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3]. In a multi-site Argentine study of tree-covered pasture (silvopastoral systems) against treeless grassland, the normal-year forage benefit reversed under severe drought at some sites: at the semi-arid Santiago del Estero site the relative response swung from +2% in normal years to -89% in a dry year, while at the humid Chaco site it swung the other way, from -15% to +26%, and in the semi-arid aridity category overall there was no significant difference between systems in either normal or dry years — a result the authors attribute to tree-forage competition for water overtaking facilitation once drought intensity passes about 35% rainfall reduction [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_6].
agroforestry__drought__all.conditionality: The class is moderate because it is set by a vote across sub-practices: the regeneration-on-farmland, planted silvoarable and silvopastoral cells read as clear benefits, the linear-boundary and cross-family cells as small benefits, and the shaded perennial-crop cell is conflicting. Few of the benefit units say how large the effect is, which also holds the class at moderate. The clearest harm finding is a direct field measurement in Ghana: during the extreme drought of 2015/16 all cocoa plants under Albizia ferruginea shade trees died and cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality, while cocoa in full sun kept higher sap flux and soil water content was higher in full sun, pointing to competition for water between shade trees and cocoa [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. What separates the sides is mainly system and severity: deep-rooted trees in dryland fields and fodder trees in pastures read as buffers, while in shaded tree crops under extreme drought the trees compete with the crop for scarce soil water. Trade-offs pull the other way, now with more direct field evidence: in a semi-arid Kenyan growing season that received only 317 mm of rain, maize under dispersed Grevillea robusta trees yielded 0.02 t/ha against 1.53 t/ha in unshaded sole maize, a near-total loss under the trees in a dry season [ev_crop_yield_lott09_4]. In semi-arid Brazil, in a low-rainfall year, maize yielded very little whether or not it was grown among alley-cropped trees, with no significant difference between the two systems — the drought year erased the tree benefit rather than reversing it [ev_crop_yield_martins13_2]. A Senegal review finds no clear consensus on windbreak hedges in drought, with some studies reporting higher yields in drier years and others harm to rainfed crops [ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17]. The understorey yield benefit holds in drought years only, since tree shade can lower understorey yields under normal rainfall, and the Kenyan household link to perceived drought held in Burat but not in Kinna [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5]. Several units are proxies or ratings rather than measurements: the Canadian and US units are high-income evidence, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The German soil-water difference was not significant everywhere and is high-income evidence, and the Nyando timber-sales finding is farmer-reported [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. The parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. The Latin American silvopastoral units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees, and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The Ethiopian Faidherbia result is a drought-year comparison reported as an 'up to' figure; the same study reports its normal-season gain separately, so this hazard-year gain is not the usual yield effect [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In shaded cocoa and coffee the evidence is split: a review cites that under warmer, water-limited conditions competition between trees and cacao for scarce soil water can reduce soil moisture and cacao yields below those of open-sun farms [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8]; and in the Ghana experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced yield decline and only partly compensated for it [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the Ethiopian study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in the extreme climate shocks [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]; and across cabruca cocoa farms in southern Bahia, Brazil, drought yield loss was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2]. Apart from the Ghana field study, these harm findings are second-hand readings in reviews. The cocoa and coffee units are crop-specific and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; the Ghana shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. The Argentine multi-site study is the clearest statement of why severity matters: it explicitly frames the switch from facilitation to competition as a function of drought intensity, and shows the sign of the effect also depends on site aridity and on whether the stocking system is native-forest or planted silvopastoral, so it cannot be read as a single transferable number [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_6, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1]. The French walnut-pea result is a cushioned loss, not an absolute gain: agroforestry pea yield remained below the full-sun yield in both rainfall regimes, and the smaller drought-specific loss is a relative measure against each system's own rainfed baseline, from a single season and site with the two conditions not randomised within the parcel [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3]. Both of these are upper-middle-income Argentina and high-income France, sitting at a different distance from the LIC/LMIC target than the Kenyan and Ethiopian evidence already in this row. A multi-species silvopasture trial on degraded rangeland in arid India adds a further measured harm result on the pastoral side: understorey herbage yield fell further under drought beneath every tree and shrub species than in the treeless control, which the authors attribute to shading and competition for soil moisture; the same trial measured the trees also supplying extra dry-season browse fodder, a trade-off this register keeps separate rather than netting off against the herbage loss [ev_drought_hazard_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_2]. This Indian evidence is lower-middle income, inside the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__drought__all__income_group.mechanism: In an induced-drought experiment in an eastern Canadian soybean-intercropping agroforestry system, crop losses occurred only in the monocropping system [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. A US silvopasture study lists better water infiltration among silvopasture's services, used here as a soil-water component of drought [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. In a French walnut-based alley-cropping system, imposed spring drought cut full-sun pea yield by 22% while the alley-cropped yield rose 12 to 20% relative to its own rainfed baseline, though alley-cropped pea still yielded less overall than the full-sun control in both rainfall regimes [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3].
agroforestry__drought__all__income_group.conditionality: This is a high-income scope row: all units come from Canada, Germany, the USA or temperate settings, outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. The Canadian result is reported second-hand in an IPCC chapter, which also notes N-fixation declined in both systems, the German soil-water result is a component measure that was not significant at all positions, and the US unit is a background statement that does not mention drought [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. No unit says how large the effect is, and none measures it in a severe or extreme drought. The French result adds a fourth high-income unit to this scope row: a single season and site, drought imposed experimentally with rainout shelters, and the two conditions not randomised within the parcel; the benefit is a smaller drought-specific loss, not a yield advantage over full sun [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3].

agroforestry__drought__all__income_group.mechanism: In two Isiolo County communities in Kenya, a household survey and interviews conclude that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought: households listed agroforestry as important for their livelihood during drought, in Burat households practising it mostly said droughts were less frequent while most households without it said the opposite, 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind, and farmers explained that deep roots let trees get water from deep down so they keep producing fruit when there is no rain [ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10, ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_roots_quandt17_2, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. Trees also act as a fodder and cash reserve: in southern Zambia trees were the most important source of animal food and milk production during drought, in Senegal's sylvopastoral zone tree leaves, fruits and pods make up about 40 per cent of cattle diet and 80 per cent of small-ruminant diet before the rains, and in Nyando District, Kenya, agroforestry-project households typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods while many farmers sold fuel wood and timber to buy food during the drought [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21, ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. The Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts, and in Ethiopia's sustainable land management programme stakeholders rated 14 of 22 cases as having a substantial or high effect on drought vulnerability, naming income from commercial agroforestry as one route that reduced vulnerability in some communities [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In a throughfall-exclusion experiment in Ghana, cocoa dry bean yield was 12 to 45% higher under shade than in full sun at every level of rainwater suppression, and in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly positive for coffee yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1].
agroforestry__drought__all__income_group.conditionality: Tree–crop competition can reverse the effect: a review cites Kenyan trials in which competition with Grevillea robusta for limited soil water delayed maize flowering and could lead to crop failure, an FAO review for Senegal finds no clear consensus on windbreak hedges in drought (some studies report higher yields near hedges in drier years, others harm to non-irrigated crops), and a model cited in a review found no significant effect on Nigerian agroforestry household net revenues under 1°C warming and a 7% fall in annual rainfall [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. In Kinna, drought perceptions did not differ between households with and without agroforestry [ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5], and the severe-drought evidence is a cited Honduran observation with no measured size [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3]. The Kenyan resilience findings come from a single survey and are perception-based, the Zambian, Senegalese and competition findings are secondary citations in reviews, the Ethiopian rating credits a bundled programme rather than agroforestry alone, the FMNR unit is a compiler rating, and the Nyando timber-sales finding is farmer-reported [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. The Honduran point is an earlier finding cited in an ICRAF working paper, and the parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3, ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In the Ghana cocoa experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced decline, and the Ethiopian coffee study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in extreme climate shocks; both are among the no-benefit results in this row [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]. The Ghana shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so its transfer to agroforestry is borderline, and the cocoa and coffee units are crop-specific, entering because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]. The Ethiopian Faidherbia result is a drought-year comparison reported as an 'up to' figure, not the usual yield effect [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2].

agroforestry__drought__cropping_irrigate.mechanism: Agroforestry raised soil moisture over controls (RR 1.6) in a sub-Saharan African meta-analysis, and a cited synthesis reports perennial trees added to cropland raise rainfall infiltration by 59% [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_10]. Live fences supply fodder in the dry season when pasture is scarce, and shaded understorey crops can yield more than open systems under drought [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. In Ethiopia, income growth through commercial agroforestry is named as one option that reduced drought vulnerability [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4].
agroforestry__drought__cropping_irrigate.conditionality: The quantified evidence is soil water, a component proxy for drought impact; the Ethiopian result is for a bundled land-management programme based on stakeholder responses, and the other units are reviews citing other studies [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_10, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. Only the Ethiopian unit names a country (low income); the rest are regional or pantropical reviews [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. No unit is from an irrigated cropping system; the evidence is applied to irrigated cropping systems by default [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_10, ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1].

agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed.mechanism: On rainfed cropland the evidence divides on whether trees add water the crop can use or compete with the crop for it. Hydraulic redistribution in Sahelian parklands lets crop roots use deep soil moisture reached only by tree roots [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3]. In an experimentally induced drought in eastern Canada, crop losses occurred in the monocrop only, not in the soybean intercropping agroforestry system, and during drought understorey crop yield can be higher than in an open system even under intense shade [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]; the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In a French walnut-based alley-cropping system, imposed spring drought cut full-sun pea yield by 22% while the alley-cropped yield rose 12 to 20% relative to its own rainfed baseline, even though alley-cropped yield stayed below the full-sun yield in both rainfall regimes [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3].
agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed.conditionality: The sub-practices disagree, so the roll-up states conflicting evidence. On the gain side, regeneration-based farmland holds the stronger result and reads as a benefit throughout: Sahelian parkland trees make deep soil moisture available to crop roots, the FMNR compiler rates drought impacts as mitigated, Quesungual farmers reported no total maize loss in the 1997 El Niño dry period, and Ethiopian wheat under Faidherbia albida out-yielded open-field wheat in the El Niño year, a hazard-year result kept apart from the study's normal-season gain [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. On the conflicting side, planted silvoarable systems pair gains (the Canadian induced drought, German alley-cropping soil water) with reversals measured directly: in a Kenyan growing season that received only 317 mm of rain, maize under dispersed Grevillea robusta trees yielded 0.02 t/ha against 1.53 t/ha in unshaded sole maize, a near-total loss [ev_crop_yield_lott09_4], and in semi-arid Brazil, in a low-rainfall year, maize yielded very little whether or not it was grown among alley-cropped trees, with no significant difference between the two systems [ev_crop_yield_martins13_2] [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. Boundary plantings read as a small, unquantified benefit: a live-fence fodder role in drought, set against a Senegal review that finds no consensus on windbreak hedges in drought [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17]. What separates the sides in the units' own words is whether tree roots reach moisture the crop cannot, or compete with the crop for limited soil water close to the trees. The understorey drought-year result sits outside the voting sub-practices, and that benefit reverses under normal rainfall [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. The Canadian result is high-income temperate evidence, the live-fence fodder unit is a pantropical review, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating rather than a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The German soil-water difference was not significant at all positions and is high-income evidence [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. This French result belongs to the planted-silvoarable cluster already described as pairing gains with a reversal: it is a cushioned loss relative to the system's own rainfed baseline, not a yield advantage over full sun, from a single season and site, and is high-income evidence outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3].

agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed_.mechanism: In an experimentally induced drought in eastern Canada, crop losses occurred in the monocrop only, not in the soybean intercropping agroforestry system [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In a French walnut-based alley-cropping system, imposed spring drought cut full-sun pea yield by 22% while the alley-cropped yield rose 12 to 20% relative to its own rainfed baseline [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3].
agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed_.conditionality: Both units point to a benefit, but neither says how large it is, and neither measures a severe or extreme drought [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. This is a high-income temperate scope row (Canada, Germany) outside the LIC/LMIC target; the Canadian result is reported second-hand in an IPCC chapter, and the German soil-water result is a component measure that was not significant at all positions [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. This is a cushioned loss, not an absolute gain: alley-cropped pea still yielded less than the full-sun control in both rainfall regimes, from a single season and site with the two conditions not randomised within the parcel, and is high-income temperate evidence outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3].

agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed_.mechanism: The evidence for rainfed cropping points both ways. A review cites Kenyan trials in which maize grown with Grevillea robusta competed with the trees for limited soil water, which delayed maize flowering and development and could lead to crop failure [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10]. Against this, the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts, and in Ethiopia's sustainable land management programme income growth through commercial agroforestry was named as one option that reduced drought vulnerability in some communities [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].
agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed_.conditionality: An FAO review for Senegal reports no clear consensus on windbreak hedges in drought: some studies find higher yields near hedges in drier years, while others judge the hedges could harm non-irrigated crops; and a model cited in a review found no significant effect on Nigerian agroforestry household net revenues under 1°C warming and a 7% fall in annual rainfall [ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. Whether trees help or hurt the crop in drought turns on how strongly they compete for limited soil water [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10]. Much of the pool is second-hand: the competition result and both review findings are secondary citations, the Ethiopian rating belongs to a bundled programme (terracing, bunds, area closure, small-scale irrigation and agroforestry) rather than agroforestry alone, the FMNR unit is a compiler rating, and the source of the Nigerian model notes its weak fit may understate impacts [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. The Honduran point is an earlier finding cited in an ICRAF working paper [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].

agroforestry__drought__mixed_crop_livest.mechanism: In mixed crop–livestock settings the evidence points the same way, though few units say how large the effect is, so the class is a slight reduction in drought impact. In two Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, farmers said deep-rooted trees reach water from deep down and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14]. In the Brazilian semi-arid, live fences of Gliricidia sepium, Leucaena leucocephala and similar species carry livestock through dry periods with high-quality fodder when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. The Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Nyando District, Kenya, households in an agroforestry project typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods, and many farmers reported selling fuel wood and timber from their trees to buy food during the drought [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1].
agroforestry__drought__mixed_crop_livest.conditionality: The Kenyan household units are a single study of survey and farmer-interview evidence, and the link between agroforestry and perceived drought held in Burat but not in Kinna [ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5]. The understorey yield benefit holds in drought years only, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The Nyando units rest on income and coping strategies as proxies for drought impact, and the timber-sales finding is farmer-reported rather than measured [ev_household_income_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_2]. No unit measures the effect in a severe or extreme drought.

agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.mechanism: On pastoral land the benefit runs through fodder and herd condition. Live fences of Gliricidia sepium, Leucaena leucocephala and similar species are used to feed livestock in the dry season and supply high-quality fodder when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. In Colombia, a review citing Altieri and Nicholls 2013 reports that forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25% [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year (Murgueitio et al. 2011) [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. During drought, understorey crop yield can be higher than in an open system, and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. A multi-site Argentine study adds further detail on pastoral drought: forage production under trees exceeded treeless grassland or pasture at drought intensities at or below the authors' dry-year threshold, and held up in very humid areas in both normal and dry years, a result corroborated by a companion reading of the same sites [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1].
agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.conditionality: The evidence on pastoral rangeland splits rather than agreeing on one direction. On the benefit side, Colombian and Argentine forage and milk gains hold up to around the authors' dry-year threshold, and the Kenyan FMNR rating and understorey-yield citation point the same way [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. On the harm side, the same Argentine study found the benefit reverses under severe drought at some sites: at semi-arid Santiago del Estero the relative forage response swung from +2% in normal years to -89% in a dry year, at the humid Chaco site it swung the other way (-15% to +26%), and in the semi-arid aridity category overall there was no significant difference between systems in either normal or dry years, the authors attributing the reversal to tree-forage competition for water overtaking facilitation above about 35% rainfall reduction [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_6]. A multi-species silvopasture trial on degraded rangeland in arid India measured the same kind of reversal directly: understorey herbage yield fell further under drought beneath every tree and shrub species than in the treeless control, attributed by the authors to shading and competition for soil moisture, though the trees also supplied extra dry-season browse fodder not counted in that herbage comparison [ev_drought_hazard_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_2]. What separates the sides is drought severity and which forage layer is counted: below a site-specific dry-year threshold, or once browse is added to grass, pastoral agroforestry holds or gains; past that threshold, or counting herbage alone, tree-grass competition for scarce water dominates. The evidence base is thin and mostly second-hand: the silvopastoral units are earlier studies cited in a Spanish-language review and a CATIE edited volume, the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees, and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. Only the Latin American silvopastoral and Indian units come from pastoral rangeland systems; the live-fence review, the understorey statement and the Kenyan FMNR rating are applied here by default [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The FMNR unit is a compiler rating, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The Colombian and Argentine sources are upper-middle income and the Indian source lower-middle income, so the row transfers as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.mechanism: In Cañas, Costa Rica, cattle on pasture with high tree density gained 2 to 5% more weight in the dry season than those on low-cover pasture, attributed partly to longer grazing and rumination under reduced heat stress [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. Against this, earlier work cited in a temperate alley-cropping study found greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years because of tree–crop competition [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3].
agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.conditionality: The units point in opposite directions and neither measures drought losses in a pastoral system: the shelterbelt result is a temperate cropping finding applied to pastoral rangeland by default, and the Costa Rican result is dry-season liveweight gain [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. Both are earlier findings cited second-hand, from high-income or temperate settings outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3].

agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.mechanism: In this lower-middle-income context, the evidence splits between one favourable rating and one measured harm. The Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that the technology improves the micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates the impact of droughts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. Against that, a multi-species silvopasture trial on degraded rangeland in arid India measured the opposite: understorey herbage yield fell further under drought beneath every tree and shrub species than in the treeless control pasture, which the authors attribute to shading and tree-grass competition for soil moisture; the same trees did supply extra dry-season browse fodder for sheep, goats and camels, a trade-off kept separate from the herbage finding rather than netted against it [ev_drought_hazard_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_2].
agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.conditionality: What separates both sides is what is measured and how: the Kenyan unit is a practitioner's compiler rating on a technology sheet, not a measurement, while the Indian unit is a direct field measurement of herbage yield under an established silvopasture trial. Counting herbage alone, trees made the Indian system's drought loss worse than the treeless control; counting the browse fodder the trees also supplied, the system offered a different kind of drought benefit that the herbage figure does not capture. All units are from lower-middle-income countries (Kenya, India), inside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_singhrao08_1]. Neither source directly names a pastoral or rangeland crop system as such: the Kenyan unit names no farming system, and the Indian trial is on rangeland proper, so this row is in context by farming system as well as income group.

agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.mechanism: In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant through intense drought while grass monoculture biomass fell to a quarter [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1], and milk production in the El Niño year with the lowest rainfall in several decades still rose 10% on the previous year after a switch to intensive silvopasture that also let irrigation be dropped [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. In a multi-site Argentine study, forage production under trees exceeded treeless grassland or pasture at drought intensities at or below the authors' dry-year threshold, and held up in very humid areas in both normal and dry years, a result corroborated by a companion reading of the same sites [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1].
agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.conditionality: The same Argentine study is the source of this row's measured harm: it found the benefit reverses under severe drought at some sites — at semi-arid Santiago del Estero the relative forage response swung from +2% in normal years to -89% in a dry year, at the humid Chaco site it swung the other way (-15% to +26%), and in the semi-arid aridity category overall there was no significant difference between systems in either normal or dry years, which the authors attribute to tree-forage competition for water overtaking facilitation above about 35% rainfall reduction [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_6]. The Colombian units are earlier studies cited in a Spanish-language review and a CATIE edited volume rather than new primary measurements, and the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. All units in this scope row are upper-middle income (Argentina, Colombia), which is why it transfers in_context to its own scope.

agroforestry__drought__tree_perennial.mechanism: Under drought, trees in tree-crop systems have been found to protect the crop, to compete with it for water, and to make no difference. On the protective side, in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly raised coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; reviews cite a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season (Lin) and low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11]; and a review adds that under normal rainfall tree shade can lower understorey crop yields while during drought those yields can be higher than in an open system, even in intense shade [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. General agroforestry reports point the same way: live fences supply livestock fodder in the dry season, when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]; and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. On the competing side, a review cites that under warmer, water-limited conditions competition between trees and cacao for scarce soil water can reduce soil moisture and cacao yields below those of open-sun farms (Blaser et al.) [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8]; the field study by Abdulai et al. in Ghana measured this directly: during the extreme drought of 2015/16 all cocoa plants under Albizia ferruginea shade trees died, cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality with sap flux density cut to 115 against 170 in full sun (grams per square centimetre per day), sap flux recovered to 163 in full sun but only 37 under A. toxicaria, and soil water was higher in full sun, which the authors link to strong competition for soil water [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. Between them sit no-effect findings: in a Ghanaian throughfall-exclusion experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on cocoa yield was not significant, so shade may not prevent the yield decline under drought [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the Ethiopian coffee study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in extreme climate shocks [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]; and on Bahia cocoa farms drought yield loss was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2].
agroforestry__drought__tree_perennial.conditionality: The studies disagree, so the row states no direction. What separates the sides, as far as the evidence says, is whether the trees draw on the same scarce soil water as the crop: the losses are attributed to that competition, measured in the Ghanaian shade-tree study (Abdulai et al.) as lower soil water under the shade trees than in full sun, while the gains come with a named companion tree (Gliricidia), a shade-management setting (canopy openness) or a drought year in which shade relieved the understorey [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. A second separator is what is measured: the Ghanaian throughfall-exclusion experiment found the overall better performance of cocoa under shade can only partly compensate for the reduced yield during drought, so a higher yield under shade is not the same as protection from drought [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. Shade-tree species is a third: in the Abdulai study every cocoa plant under Albizia ferruginea died against 77% under Antiaris toxicaria [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. Tree species, density and canopy management are therefore the design questions for drought-exposed tree-crop systems. The cocoa and coffee units are crop-specific and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; the throughfall-exclusion experiment's shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. Many units on both sides are second-hand readings in reviews [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_crop_yield_watts22_8]; the Abdulai shade-tree study, measured on a single farm, is the field anchor of the harm side [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. Only the cocoa and coffee units record a tree-perennial system; the live-fence, FMNR and understorey units record none and are applied here by default, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating rather than a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. The field units are from low-income Ethiopia, lower-middle-income Ghana and upper-middle-income Brazil [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1, ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2].

agroforestry__drought__tree_perennial__i.mechanism: Studies disagree on what trees do to tree crops in drought in low- and lower-middle-income settings. On the benefit side, in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade trees strongly raised coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1], and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. On the harm side, a field study in Ghana found that during the extreme drought of 2015/16 all cocoa plants under Albizia ferruginea shade trees died and cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality, while cocoa in full sun kept higher sap flux; soil water content was higher in full sun, which the authors link to stronger competition for water in the shaded systems [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1].
agroforestry__drought__tree_perennial__i.conditionality: Several units find no effect either way. In a Ghana rainwater-suppression experiment on cocoa, the shade-by-drought interaction on yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced yield decline and only partly compensated for it; the shade there came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. The same Ethiopian coffee study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in the extreme climate shocks [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]. What separates gains from losses is shade management and how severe the shock is: the Ethiopian gain appears at high canopy openness, while the Ghana deaths came under dense shade trees in an extreme drought [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. The harm finding is a direct measurement while the benefit units are a yield model and a compiler rating, which is why the harm side carries real weight despite resting on a single study [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. Only the cocoa and coffee units are measured in tree-crop systems; they are crop-specific and enter under the shaded perennial-crop scope ruling, while the Kenyan FMNR rating is applied to tree-crop systems by default [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts].

agroforestry__drought_hazard.mechanism: Trees on farms slightly reduce the damage drought does to farm households. In Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, a farmer said deep-rooted mango trees get water from deep down, others said trees do not dry up fast and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind; the study concludes that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10]. Reviews report that under drought understorey crop yields could be higher than in an open system even in intense shade, and that live fences supply livestock fodder when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. In an eastern Canadian soybean intercrop, experimentally induced drought caused crop losses in the monocrop only (Nasielski et al. 2015) [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet rates drought impacts as reduced, its compiler judging that FMNR improves micro-climate and soil moisture and therefore mitigates the impact of droughts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. In a French walnut-based alley-cropping system, an imposed spring drought cut full-sun pea yield by 22% while the alley-cropped yield was relatively improved by 12 to 20% against its own rainfed baseline [ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3].
agroforestry__drought_hazard.conditionality: Effects are not uniform, and for some adopters the trees made drought losses worse. During the extreme drought of 2015/16 in Ghana, a field study found that all cocoa plants under Albizia ferruginea shade trees died and cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality, while cocoa in full sun kept higher sap flux; soil water content was higher in full sun, which the authors link to competition for water in the shaded systems [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. A multi-species silvopasture trial on degraded rangeland in arid India found the same kind of reversal in a grazing system: understorey herbage yield fell further under drought beneath every tree and shrub species than in the treeless control pasture, attributed by the authors to shading and competition for soil moisture; the trees did supply extra dry-season browse fodder, a trade-off kept separate from the herbage finding [ev_drought_hazard_singhrao08_1]. Elsewhere, a review says tree shade could decrease understorey yields under normal rainfall, and the Senegal review reports no clear consensus on windbreaks in drought, some studies finding higher yields in drier years and others harm to rainfed crops [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17]. In Kenya the link between agroforestry and perceived drought held in Burat but not in Kinna, and one Kenyan unit states only that agroforestry has been proposed for resilience [ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. Few units give a size, so the class is slight. Most units are reviews repeating earlier studies or household perception, the Canadian trial is high-income evidence, and the Kenyan FMNR unit is a practitioner judgement on a technology sheet, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The household evidence comes largely from lower-middle-income Kenya, inside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10]. The Indian silvopasture result is likewise lower-middle-income evidence, inside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_drought_hazard_singhrao08_1]. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. The French result is a relative cushioning of the drought impact, not a stated yield advantage over full sun, from a single season and site, and it is high-income evidence, outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3].

agroforestry__drought_hazard__farming_sy.mechanism: In an eastern Canadian soybean intercrop, experimentally induced drought caused crop losses in the monocrop system only, while nitrogen fixation declined in both systems [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. In a French walnut-based alley-cropping system, an imposed spring drought cut pea yield by 22% compared with rainfed conditions, while the agroforestry yield was relatively improved by 12 to 20% against its own rainfed baseline [ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3].
agroforestry__drought_hazard__farming_sy.conditionality: A Senegal review finds no clear consensus on windbreak hedges in drought, with some studies reporting higher yields in drier years and others harm to rainfed crops, so this unit does not set a direction either way [ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17]. The Canadian and French trials are high-income evidence (Canada, France), outside the LIC/LMIC target, and carry most of the pooled weight in this row, while the Honduran and Senegalese evidence sits inside or adjacent to it, which is why the row as a whole transfers out of context. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. The French result is a relative cushioning of the drought impact from a single season and site, not an absolute yield advantage over full sun [ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3].

agroforestry__flood__mixed_crop_livestoc.conditionality: Apart from the meta-analysis, all units come from a single household study in Kenya based on farmer interviews and surveys, so the flood benefit is largely self-reported [ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6, ev_t3_flood_erosion_table_quandt17_13, ev_t3_flood_conclusion_quandt17_11]. A review reports, citing Nguyen et al. 2013, that in Vietnam extreme flooding from heavy rainfall caused yield losses in regionally cultivated crops while farms with trees were less affected [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_11], and, citing Eychène et al. 2014, that coffee-based agroforestry in Mesoamerica can help prevent flood occurrences and reduce the adverse impact of extreme rainfall events [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12]. agroforestry__food_insecurity.mechanism: Across contexts, agroforestry raises household food security mainly through tree products adding to diets and smoothing shortfalls. In Malawi, fertilizer-tree adopters had food crop value 35% higher than non-adopters, driving greater food security [ev_t6_foodsec_ferttree_castle21_8]. In Kenya, agrosilvopastoral extension advice raised the household dietary diversity score by 1.22 points and the number of food groups consumed by 2.291, out of 12 analysed [ev_food_security_castle21s_1]. In Zambia, improved fallows raised the number of months per year with enough grown food by 1.069 months [ev_food_security_castle21s_3]. Across the Regreening Africa endline survey (Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Mali, Niger, Rwanda, Senegal, Somalia), the share of respondents meeting the minimum-dietary-diversity cut-off rose from 16 to 21%, a 31% relative increase, and households that intensified tree-product use saw significant dietary-diversity gains in Ethiopia, Ghana, Niger, Rwanda and Senegal [ev_food_security_rgaf23_8, ev_food_security_rgaf23_10]. A World Vision multi-country meta-analysis found project participants' months of food shortage significantly lower, by 0.26 months, than non-participants [ev_food_security_wvfmnr19_9]. In Senegal, only 3% of FMNR adopters failed to meet annual food needs for more than 4 months against 14% of non-adopters in one zone, and 0% versus 4% in another [ev_food_security_seghieri19_13]. In Nepal, the share of households food-sufficient rose from 52% to 69% after a market-oriented agroforestry intervention, a highly significant change [ev_food_security_pandit19_1], and in Tanzania, improved agroforestry secured enough food year-round for 40% of households against 18% on traditional farms [ev_food_security_reyes05_1]. In Kenya, fruit from on-farm trees was some farmers' only steady food source during the floods, and agroforestry-project households used fewer detrimental coping strategies during the drought and flood hunger periods that followed [ev_food_security_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_2]. In Rwanda, a positive association between tree density and food security was found in two of six agroecologies [ev_food_security_ndoli21_1]. Reviews summarise the same mechanism: the IPCC AR6 chapter links increased food security and household income to diversification of production avoiding trade-offs between crop and tree products [ev_food_security_ipccar6ch5_7], and a review states agroforestry could help up to 1.3 billion people on degrading agricultural land in food-security terms [ev_food_security_ipccsrccl6_6]. A synthesis across East African studies names fodder, food, firewood and income as the main livelihood benefits, diversifying livelihoods and acting as safety nets in times of climate shocks [ev_food_security_muthuri23_1]. In Niger, during the 2005 food crisis, farmers practising farmer-managed natural regeneration were less severely affected than other farmers and recorded relatively lower infant mortality, through income from selling wood and other forest products [ev_food_security_boton10_2].
agroforestry__food_insecurity.conditionality: Against this, the same Rwandan study found the opposite in a third agroecology, with increasing tree density associated with lower food security in the Buberuka Highlands even as it raised food security in Congo Nile — measured harm for some households [ev_food_security_ndoli21_2]. Several units find no effect: Kenyan improved fallow showed no significant nutritional results [ev_food_security_castle21s_2], the Regreening Africa endline's food-insecurity-experience-scale score showed no substantial change [ev_food_security_rgaf23_9], Nigerien FMNR did not reduce months of perceived food shortage though it raised crop diversity [ev_food_security_haglund11_1], and the Sahel food-consumption-score gains were not statistically significant under the authors' own convention, though the authors describe them as increases [ev_food_security_bina15_7, ev_food_security_bina15_8, ev_food_security_bina15_9]. The Talensi and Nepali/Tanzanian gains come from before-and-after project self-evaluations or non-randomised comparisons with no control group, and the World Vision multi-country brief and the Nguyen review both note their findings cannot be fully disentangled from other project activities or, in the review's case, were guaranteed by its own inclusion rule (only studies already showing a food-security improvement were selected) [ev_food_security_talensi21_3, ev_food_security_talensi21_4, ev_food_security_wvfmnr19_9, ev_food_security_nguy24n_1]. Most units describe direction without a size; where sizes are given (Malawi, Regreening Africa), the gains sit in low and lower-middle-income African and South Asian contexts, in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_t6_foodsec_ferttree_castle21_8, ev_food_security_rgaf23_8, ev_food_security_pandit19_1].

agroforestry__food_insecurity__farming_s.mechanism: Two Sahelian sources on farmer-managed natural regeneration agree that it eases household food shortages. In Senegal, only 3% of adopters failed to meet annual food needs for more than 4 months in a first zone, against 14% of non-adopters, and 0% versus 4% in a second zone [ev_food_security_seghieri19_13]. In Niger, during the 2005 food crisis, farmers practising the regeneration were less severely affected than other farmers and recorded relatively lower infant mortality, through income from selling wood and other forest products [ev_food_security_boton10_2].
agroforestry__food_insecurity__farming_s.conditionality: The evidence base is thin: two sources, both from the Sahel. The Senegal comparison gives a measured share of households falling short; the Niger finding is a narrative account of the 2005 crisis with no comparative numbers, and its own mechanism is income from wood sales rather than food production itself. Both sit in low and lower-middle-income rainfed cropping systems, in context with the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__food_insecurity__farming_s.mechanism: Across mixed crop–livestock systems, agroforestry raises food security through added food sources and income. In Nepal, the share of households that were food-sufficient rose from 146 of 279 (52%) before a market-oriented agroforestry intervention to 192 of 279 (69%) after, a highly significant change [ev_food_security_pandit19_1]. In Tanzania, improved agroforestry was securing enough food throughout the year for 40% of households, against 18% of households on traditional farms [ev_food_security_reyes05_1]. In the Sahel, moving from low-intensity to young-level farmer-managed natural regeneration raised the household food consumption score by about 12% across Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger and Senegal [ev_food_security_bina15_7]. In Kenya, during floods, some farmers reported fruit from their on-farm trees as their only steady source of food while other crops were underwater or washed away, and agroforestry-project households used fewer detrimental coping strategies (such as consuming seed stock or selling oxen) during the drought and flood hunger periods that followed than a control group [ev_food_security_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_2]. In Rwanda, a positive association between tree density and food security was found in two of six agroecologies [ev_food_security_ndoli21_1].
agroforestry__food_insecurity__farming_s.conditionality: Against this, the same Rwandan study found the opposite in a third agroecology: increasing tree density was associated with lower food security in the Buberuka Highlands, even as it raised the probability of food security in Congo Nile — the practice worsening the outcome for some households, which the engine counts as measured harm [ev_food_security_ndoli21_2]. The Sahelian gain from low to continuous FMNR showed no significant food-consumption-score gain in any country, and a separate measure, months with a household food deficit, found no significant effect for any FMNR intensity, though the authors read the communities as more resilient during food shortages as an inference rather than a measured result [ev_food_security_bina15_8, ev_food_security_bina15_9]. The Nepali and Tanzanian gains come from before-and-after or non-randomised comparisons with no control group, and the Tanzanian 'improved' farms were also larger, more often in the highlands and kept more dairy cattle and off-farm income, so some of the gain is not attributable to the trees alone [ev_food_security_pandit19_1, ev_food_security_reyes05_1]. All units sit in low and lower-middle-income Sub-Saharan African and South Asian mixed crop–livestock systems, in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_food_security_bina15_7, ev_food_security_pandit19_1, ev_food_security_reyes05_1].
