agroforestry__gender_inequity.mechanism: A gender review finds agroforestry can offer substantial benefits to women, but their participation is low in enterprises considered men's domain such as timber and in the area and number of trees they commit [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_1]. It reports, second-hand, that management labour often falls on women (in 89% of Embu households using calliandra fodder, females managed it) [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_2], that 32% of males and 23% of females planted improved fallows in four Zambian villages [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_3], and that in farmer-managed trials women had somewhat higher Sesbania survival than men [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_4]. A CILSS regional synthesis adds a further, more recent Sahelian observation: in Niger's re-greened farmer-managed natural regeneration zones, the increase in on-farm trees has, in many cases, sharply cut the time women spend collecting firewood for the household, from an average of 2.5 hours a day twenty years ago to 0.5 hour a day now [ev_gender_inequity_botreij09_34].
agroforestry__gender_inequity.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a class: every unit comes from a single narrative review of sub-Saharan African studies, read second-hand, with no measured finding of its own [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_1, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_2, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_3, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_4]. A further independent source or a measured change in inequity is what is missing. The cited figures point both ways (labour and uptake gaps against women, a trial advantage for women) and are shares of households or participants, not changes caused by agroforestry [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_2, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_3, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_4]. That is a before/after regional account with no control, and it adds a case where the gender effect runs the other way from the labour-burden units above, towards less time on a task that falls mainly to women, rather than confirming them [ev_gender_inequity_botreij09_34].

agroforestry__gender_inequity__income_gr.mechanism: A gender review finds agroforestry can offer substantial benefits to women, but their participation is low in enterprises considered men's domain such as timber and in the area and number of trees they commit [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_1]. It reports, second-hand, that management labour often falls on women (in 89% of Embu households using calliandra fodder, females managed it) [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_2], that 32% of males and 23% of females planted improved fallows in four Zambian villages [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_3], and that in farmer-managed trials women had somewhat higher Sesbania survival than men [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_4]. A CILSS regional synthesis adds a further, more recent Sahelian observation: in Niger's re-greened farmer-managed natural regeneration zones, the increase in on-farm trees has, in many cases, sharply cut the time women spend collecting firewood for the household, from an average of 2.5 hours a day twenty years ago to 0.5 hour a day now [ev_gender_inequity_botreij09_34].
agroforestry__gender_inequity__income_gr.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a class: every unit comes from a single narrative review of sub-Saharan African studies, read second-hand, with no measured finding of its own [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_1, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_2, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_3, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_4]. A further independent source or a measured change in inequity is what is missing. The cited figures point both ways (labour and uptake gaps against women, a trial advantage for women) and are shares of households or participants, not changes caused by agroforestry [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_2, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_3, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_4]. That is a before/after regional account with no control, and it adds a case where the gender effect runs the other way from the labour-burden units above, towards less time on a task that falls mainly to women, rather than confirming them [ev_gender_inequity_botreij09_34].

agroforestry__heat_stress__agro_pastoral.mechanism: In Senegal's Ferlo, air under Acacia tortilis ranged between 29 °C and 36 °C against 26 °C and 42 °C outside [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6]. Tree shade lowers the temperature crops and animals experience: IPCC and other reviews state that agroforestry reduces ambient temperature and crop heat stress, with over-storey shade moderating severe temperature effects by 2–4°C and tree shading lowering air temperature by 4°C [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, maximum daily temperature fell by an average of 1–2.5 °C and minimum air humidity rose by up to 5%, with stronger differences on hotter and drier days [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2]. For livestock, an IPCC AR5 assessment reports that increased shade from trees or cost-effective structures can substantially reduce the incidence of high heat-stress days, reduce animal stress and increase productivity [ev_livestock_productivity_porter14_1].
agroforestry__heat_stress__agro_pastoral.conditionality: The Senegal Ferlo and Sahelian parkland units come from agro-pastoral systems; the rest are general reviews applied here by default [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2]. All units report cooling or animal comfort, entering as components of heat-stress impact, and all are reviews or assessments citing earlier studies, the Ferlo temperatures repeating Akpo et al. [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6]. The livestock-shade statement is a global IPCC assessment citing underlying feedlot and modelling studies rather than tree-canopy measurements directly, and it does not say how large the productivity gain is [ev_livestock_productivity_porter14_1].

agroforestry__heat_stress__all.mechanism: Trees and shrubs shade crops, pasture and livestock, which lowers air and soil temperature compared with open conditions. Under tree crowns, researchers recorded temperature reductions of 2 to 9 degrees Celsius relative to open pasture in a review covering Costa Rica, Colombia and Nicaragua [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1], up to 13 degrees Celsius on the hottest days in a systematic review of silvopastoral systems [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1], and up to 6 degrees Celsius at midday under Faidherbia albida parkland trees in Ethiopia, where open-field temperatures reached 36 degrees Celsius against 29 degrees Celsius under the canopy [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1]. Shade-tree cover in cocoa agroforestry buffers daily maximum and minimum temperatures compared with monoculture [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1], and shelterbelts in China significantly lowered summer air temperature by 4.01% and raised relative humidity by 13.45% [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. This cooling reduces heat stress in livestock and raised milk production by 29% and 15% in two Latin American reviews of silvopastoral systems [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2], and a reduction in heat load is linked to a 6.8% rise in wheat grain yield under an agroforestry system in India [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6].
agroforestry__heat_stress__all.conditionality: The measured evidence is not uniformly positive. In Senegal, windbreak hedges were reported to generally cause a slight rise in temperature in protected plots rather than cooling, with effects varying by crop and growth stage [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. A modelled sensitivity analysis under Faidherbia albida in Ethiopia found that without applied nitrogen fertiliser, the cooling under tree shade produced no yield response at all, because yield was limited by nutrients rather than heat [ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. No unit in this row measures mitigation under a severe or extreme heat event; the quantified cooling and livestock-productivity figures come mostly from pastoral and tree-perennial systems across Latin America, West Africa and China, spanning low- to high-income countries, with only a minority of sources set in the low- and lower-middle-income countries this scoping tool targets.

agroforestry__heat_stress__all__income_g.mechanism: On hot summer days, a poplar alley-cropping system in Germany was 3.4°C cooler than a sole wheat system [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4]. In Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture, and cited studies found milk production more than 15% higher for cows grazing silvopasture than for cows in full sun [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2]. In Costa Rican coffee, measured shade cut maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C against full-sun plots [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].
agroforestry__heat_stress__all__income_g.conditionality: All units come from Germany or Costa Rica, recorded as high income and outside the LIC/LMIC target; all but the coffee measurement are earlier studies cited in reviews [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4]. The coffee unit is crop-specific and enters because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4]. They report air temperature or milk yield rather than measured heat-stress losses, live fences gave the smallest cooling of the arrangements compared, and the milk gain is not separated from other effects of the trees [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2].

agroforestry__heat_stress__all__income_g.mechanism: In Ethiopia, Faidherbia albida trees cut the radiation reaching the wheat canopy and made the wheat 6°C cooler than open wheat [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_5]. In the Ferlo, Senegal, air temperatures under Acacia tortilis ranged less widely than outside the canopy, and in Kenya shade trees are described as producing microclimates that buffer temperature fluctuations and can reduce evapotranspiration [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3].
agroforestry__heat_stress__all__income_g.conditionality: Windbreak hedges in Senegal pull the other way, generally raising temperature in protected plots with impacts that depend on the crop and its growth stage, so the evidence pools opposite signs [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. All four units are from LIC/LMIC countries (Ethiopia, Kenya, Senegal), but all are reported second-hand from earlier studies and rest on temperature or microclimate, a component of heat-stress impact [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_5, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3].

agroforestry__heat_stress__all__income_g.mechanism: Silvopastoral systems cut heat stress in cattle: intensive shrub–tree–rotational pasture models in the dry Colombian Caribbean reduce it, and eucalyptus–brachiaria systems in Brazil reduced the area at critical animal thermal-comfort levels by 20 to 100% against monoculture pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. In Cuba, live fences came to be used to shade cattle and avoid stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3].
agroforestry__heat_stress__all__income_g.conditionality: All units are reviews citing earlier studies, and they report animal comfort rather than measured production losses avoided [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10].

agroforestry__heat_stress__cropping_irri.mechanism: Reviews report that tree shade buffers severe temperature effects on understorey crops and lowers ambient temperature by 4°C, that agroforestry reduces ambient temperatures and crop heat stress, and that shade trees buffer rising temperatures to stabilise yields of crops like coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1]. Shade from live fences is reported to reduce cattle heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8].
agroforestry__heat_stress__cropping_irri.conditionality: No unit records irrigated cropping; the evidence is applied here by default, and the cattle-shade units concern livestock rather than irrigated crops [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. The only recorded country is Cuba (upper-middle income); the other five units have no country or income group, so the transfer is classed adjacent [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. All units are reviews citing earlier studies and rest on temperature buffering, a component of heat-stress impact [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1].

agroforestry__heat_stress__cropping_rain.mechanism: Measured cooling reaches crops: midday air temperature under Faidherbia albida canopies on Ethiopian wheat farms was up to 6°C lower than in the open field, poplar alley cropping in Germany was 3.4°C cooler than sole wheat on hot days, and lower heat load under Populus deltoides in India raised wheat grain yield by 6.8% [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6]. In the same Ethiopian study, a crop model found that the lower temperature under F. albida shade raised simulated wheat yield when nitrogen was applied, but without applied N simulated yield was extremely small and did not respond to temperature [ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. Tree shade lowers the temperature crops and animals experience: IPCC and other reviews state that agroforestry reduces ambient temperature and crop heat stress, with over-storey shade moderating severe temperature effects by 2–4°C and tree shading lowering air temperature by 4°C [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. A meta-analysis of field studies on Chinese farmland found summer air temperature 4.01% lower and relative humidity 13.45% higher in shelterbelt-protected than in unsheltered fields [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. For livestock, an IPCC climate-impacts assessment reports more generally that increased shade from trees or cost-effective structures can substantially reduce the incidence of high heat-stress days, reduce animal stress and increase productivity [ev_livestock_productivity_porter14_1].
agroforestry__heat_stress__cropping_rain.conditionality: Windbreak hedges in Senegal generally cause a slight temperature rise in the protected plots, with effects that vary by crop and growth stage [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. The Ethiopian, German, Indian, Senegalese and Chinese units come from rainfed cropping, and the German unit is high-income temperate evidence; the yield gain applies to hot conditions only [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6, ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. Most units are reviews citing earlier studies and report cooling, a component of heat-stress impact [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1]. The shelterbelt cooling is a pooled meta-analysis result from upper-middle-income China, expressed as a modest percentage change in air temperature rather than a measured heat-stress loss [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. The Ethiopian cooling was measured on farm, but its yield link is modelled, and the model's null without applied N is among the no-benefit results in this row [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. The livestock-shade statement applies here by default: it is a global assessment about livestock shade, not a crop finding, citing underlying feedlot and modelling studies rather than tree-canopy measurements directly, and names no size [ev_livestock_productivity_porter14_1].

agroforestry__heat_stress__mixed_crop_li.mechanism: Tree shade physically cools the microclimate crops and livestock sit in: reviews report that over-storey shade moderates severe temperature effects (2–4°C) on understorey crops in wheat, coffee and silvopasture systems, that tree shading can lower ambient temperatures by 4°C and soil temperatures by 6–10°C, and that shade trees buffer rising temperatures to stabilise yields such as coffee and raise food-staple yield by lowering daytime temperature and heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1]. The IPCC AR6 AFOLU chapter states in the same terms that agroforestry reduces ambient temperatures and crop heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1]. In mixed crop–livestock systems in Brazil, comparing eucalyptus agroforestry with monoculture pasture, the area reaching critical thermal-comfort levels for animals fell by 20 to 100%, with lower thermal-comfort index, black-globe humidity index and radiant thermal load throughout [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. An IPCC climate-impacts assessment separately reports that increased shade from trees or cost-effective structures can substantially reduce the incidence of high heat-stress days for livestock, reduce animal stress and increase productivity [ev_livestock_productivity_porter14_1].
agroforestry__heat_stress__mixed_crop_li.conditionality: All but the Brazilian unit — including a further global IPCC livestock-shade assessment — are reviews restating other studies' findings rather than measuring heat stress directly, so none of them name a country or farming system [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_livestock_productivity_porter14_1]. The single primary measurement is upper-middle-income Brazilian silvopasture, outside the LIC/LMIC target, which is why the row transfers only as adjacent [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. No unit in this row measures a severe or extreme heat event.

agroforestry__heat_stress__pastoral_rang.mechanism: Silvopastoral and pasture trees cut cattle heat stress: intensive shrub–tree–rotational pasture models in the dry Colombian Caribbean reduce it (Ocampo et al. 2012) [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1]. Tree shade in pastures is associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain (Abreu 2002) [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. In Nicaragua, Betancourt et al. 2003 found milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover, attributed to less heat stress and more foliage and fruit, and other studies found increases above 15% for cows grazing silvopasture compared with cows in full sun (Souza et al. 2000) [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2]. General reviews report the same cooling: over-storey shade moderates severe temperature (2–4°C) effects in silvopasture as well as crop systems, and tree shading can lower ambient temperature by 4°C [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1]. An IPCC climate-impacts assessment reports more generally that increased shade from trees or cost-effective structures can substantially reduce the incidence of high heat-stress days for livestock, reduce animal stress and increase productivity [ev_livestock_productivity_porter14_1].
agroforestry__heat_stress__pastoral_rang.conditionality: Every unit reports a benefit, but none measures it in a heat event the authors call severe or extreme, and the transfer to LIC/LMIC rangelands is not direct: almost all the weight sits in upper-middle-income Brazil and Colombia, high-income Costa Rica and unlocated reviews, with Nicaragua the only lower-middle-income site [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1]. The Latin American silvopastoral units come from pastoral rangeland; the general reviews are applied here by default [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1]. Most units are reviews citing earlier studies, and the milk and weight-gain figures are associations with shade rather than measured heat-stress losses avoided [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. The milk gains mix relief from heat with extra foliage and fruit, so they are not a pure heat-stress effect [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2]. The IPCC livestock-shade statement is a global assessment citing underlying feedlot and modelling studies rather than tree-canopy measurements directly, and names no size [ev_livestock_productivity_porter14_1].

agroforestry__heat_stress__pastoral_rang.mechanism: Intensive shrub–tree–rotational pasture models in the dry Colombian Caribbean reduce cattle heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3].
agroforestry__heat_stress__pastoral_rang.conditionality: The Colombian unit is a review citing an earlier study (Ocampo et al.) that reports animal comfort without a size, and the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1]. The Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself, though its comparison of woody-cover levels is cited from an earlier study [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. The evidence is from upper-middle-income Latin America, outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1].

agroforestry__heat_stress__tree_perennia.mechanism: Across tree-based perennial cropping and silvopastoral systems, overstorey tree shade moderates temperature extremes on the crop or pasture below and can reduce heat stress in grazing livestock. A review found tree shade moderates temperature effects of 2 to 4 degrees Celsius on understorey crops in wheat, coffee and silvopasture systems [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1], and a synthesis of empirical co-benefits separately found shade trees reduce canopy temperatures by 2 to 4 degrees Celsius, mitigating heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4]; tree shading can also lower ambient temperatures by 4 degrees Celsius and soil temperatures by 6 to 10 degrees Celsius [ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. In cocoa agroforestry, canopy shade buffers daily maximum and minimum temperatures compared with monoculture, with the potential to reduce the impact of rising mean temperatures and temperature extremes [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1]. Increased shade provision for livestock, through trees or cost-effective structures, can substantially reduce the incidence of high heat stress days and animal stress [ev_livestock_productivity_porter14_1].
agroforestry__heat_stress__tree_perennia.conditionality: This evidence covers tree-perennial cropping and silvopastoral systems only, and none of the sources measures mitigation under a severe or extreme heat event specifically: the cooling and shading effects above are moderate-weather or general-climate findings, not tests against a named heatwave. The livestock-shade evidence mixes built shade structures with tree shade, so the share of the benefit coming from trees specifically is unclear [ev_livestock_productivity_porter14_1].

agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard.mechanism: Shade from trees and shelterbelts lowers air and soil temperature, reducing heat stress for crops and livestock across many systems. Oil-palm alley cropping with black pepper or cacao in Malaysia cooled air by 1.3 degrees Celsius and soil surface by 2.1 degrees Celsius compared with a 15-year oil-palm monoculture [ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_3]; silvopastoral arrangements in Colombia and Costa Rica cooled paddocks by 1.7 to 3.6 degrees Celsius relative to open pasture, with tree groups giving the largest effect [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]; shelterbelts in China significantly lowered summer air temperature by 4.01% and raised relative humidity by 13.45% [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]; and under Faidherbia albida parkland trees in Ethiopia, midday air temperature fell by up to 6 degrees Celsius, with the open field reaching 36 degrees Celsius against 29 degrees Celsius under the canopy [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1]. A systematic review of silvopastoral studies found silvopastoral systems were mostly (57%) measured as having lower air temperature, soil-surface temperature and radiant heat load than treeless pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_1].
agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard.conditionality: The same shade can also warm conditions or show no significant effect, depending on species, age and season. In the Malaysian oil-palm trial, alleys intercropped with bamboo or bactris palm were significantly hotter (up to 37.0 degrees Celsius air temperature) than the monocultures, and the authors judged these two species unsuitable intercrops because of the increased air temperature [ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_4]. A Mexican coffee shade-gradient study found no significant difference in mean air temperature between high- and low-shade sites in either the wet or dry season, even though the high-shade site fluctuated less around the optimum temperature [ev_microclimate_buffering_lin07_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_lin07_2]. In Senegal, windbreak hedges were reported to generally cause a slight rise in temperature in protected plots rather than cooling, with effects varying by crop and growth stage [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. In the systematic review of silvopastoral systems, four of the seven cattle studies using the temperature-humidity index found no significant difference between silvopastoral and treeless pasture, partly because that index does not capture solar radiation, the main pathway through which trees reduce heat load [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_2]. Most of the quantified cooling is measured in upper-middle- and high-income countries (Malaysia, Brazil, Germany, China); evidence from low-income parkland systems in Ethiopia and the Sahel is present but thinner.

agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.mechanism: Under Sahelian parkland trees, maximum daily temperature fell by an average of 1–2.5 °C and minimum air humidity rose by up to 5%, with stronger differences on hotter and drier days [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2]. In Senegal's Ferlo, minimum and maximum air temperatures under the canopy of Acacia tortilis ranged between 29 °C and 36 °C, against 26 °C to 42 °C outside the cover [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6].
agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.conditionality: Both units are earlier studies cited in reviews and report air temperature under tree canopies, a component of heat-stress impact rather than a measured heat-stress outcome [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6]. In the Ferlo the canopy narrowed the range in both directions, with a higher minimum as well as a lower maximum under the trees [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6].

agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.mechanism: In rainfed cropping, trees and shelterbelts cool the crop. Under Faidherbia albida parkland trees in Ethiopia, midday air temperature at wheat floral height was lowered by up to 6°C against the open field, peaking at 29oC under the canopy versus 36oC outside [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1]. A meta-analysis of Chinese farmland found shelterbelts reduced summer air temperature by 4.01% against unsheltered fields [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1], and a review reports, second-hand, that poplar alley cropping in Germany was 3.4°C cooler than sole wheat on hot summer days [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4]. In semi-arid Kenya, dispersed Grevillea robusta trees over maize lowered the maize's own seasonal mean maximum growing-point temperature by 2.5 to 6.0 degrees C compared with unshaded sole maize, depending on the season [ev_microclimate_buffering_lott09_5].
agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.conditionality: The row carries a harm signal: an FAO review in Senegal states, second-hand, that windbreak hedges generally cause a slight rise in temperature in the protected plots, with impacts varying by crop and growth stage, so shelter designs that cut wind may warm rather than cool [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. The units measure air temperature, a component of heat-stress impact, not heat-stress yield losses [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. The Brazilian unit is upper-middle income and the Kenyan unit lower-middle income [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3].

agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.mechanism: Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. In Cuba live fences came to be used to shade cattle and avoid stress, and Neotropical livestock keepers value shade because it reduces heat stress and supports reproduction, weight gain and milk production [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8]. agroforestry__heat_stress_hazard__farmin.conditionality: Not every heat measure moved: in the same review, results for the temperature humidity index were unclear, with four of the seven studies that used it finding no significant difference from treeless pasture; the authors attribute this partly to that index leaving out solar radiation, the main pathway through which trees cut heat load [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_2]. The evidence is adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target; the only named country is upper-middle-income Cuba [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3]. No unit is from a tree-perennial system; the evidence is applied to tree-perennial systems by default [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8].

agroforestry__linear_boundary__heat_stre.mechanism: For linear plantings specifically, the clearest cooling evidence comes from denser shelterbelts: in China, a meta-analysis of farmland shelterbelts found summer air temperature significantly reduced by 4.01% compared with unsheltered farmland [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. In Cuba and across the Neotropics, live fences re-purposed to shade cattle are reported to reduce heat stress and improve comfort, reproduction, weight gain and milk production [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__heat_stre.conditionality: Against this, in Senegal windbreak hedges are reported to generally cause a slight rise in temperature in the protected plots rather than cooling them, with impacts varying by crop and growth stage — the practice worsening the outcome for some adopters, which the engine counts as measured harm [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. The split looks structural rather than random: a dense shelterbelt that also shades the ground, as in the Chinese study, cools the field, while an open windbreak hedge that mainly slows airflow without shading the plot can trap heat instead. None of the four units states a size tied to a severe heat event, and the live-fence evidence is a pantropical review rather than a site measurement, so the row sits adjacent to, not squarely inside, the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__linear_boundary__productio.mechanism: A line of trees or shrubs beside a field acts in two opposing ways on crop and forage production. Downwind of the belt, slower wind speed, trapped snow and a milder microclimate can raise yield: in a classic pooled dataset of US and Canadian shelterbelt trials, the weighted mean yield increase was 20.8% in regions with persistent winter snow and 12.5% without it [ev_crop_yield_kort88_6, ev_crop_yield_kort88_7], and in north-east China maize yield across a whole sheltered field rose by 16.57% [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1]. Close to the belt itself, the trees instead compete with the crop for light, water, nutrients and physical space: in the same pooled dataset the zone from half to one tree height out of the belt lost 50% of its yield to competition before the shelter effect took over further out, leaving a net field-level gain of about 3.5% [ev_crop_yield_kort88_3, ev_crop_yield_kort88_5], and in the China study the edge zone next to the shelterbelt lost 20.47% even as the wider field gained [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]. In Saskatchewan, yields were depressed out to about 10 m from the shelterbelt before an above-average zone began further downwind [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__productio.conditionality: Whether the net balance comes out positive depends on where yield is measured, how much water or wind stress the system faces, and the farming system. A global review of windbreak paddocks found crop yield averaged 8.3% lower than treeless paddocks when measured across the whole protected paddock, including the competition zone next to the trees [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1], a crop-specific effect since pasture yield in the same dataset rose by 3.1% [ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_4]; modelled instead as a response curve across a transect of tree heights downwind, the same data gave a net gain of 8.04% [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5]. In Saskatchewan, the competition strip and the sheltered gain beyond it both showed in a dry growing season, but the sheltered gain disappeared in a wet year when water was not limiting [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_3]. In Senegal, yield fell within 10 metres of hedges during the rainy season but rose by 23% across protected plots in the dry season [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13], while at Bambey the same hedges were reported to have a neutral effect on groundnut yield [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_14]. Pooled across many agroforestry studies, hedgerow systems specifically showed a lower yield response than other agroforestry practices in the same analysis [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_5]. In pasture systems, shade from live fences can reduce forage availability along the pasture edge [ev_forage_productivity_garbach12_1] and, if excessive, the overall productive pasture area of the farm [ev_livestock_productivity_moran18_14]. Benefit is more likely where the windbreak tree roots sit deeper than the crop roots, reducing below-ground competition [ev_crop_yield_moran18_11]. Most of the quantified evidence is from temperate, high-income systems in Canada, the United States and China; a fodder-tree feeding trial in Cambodia found cattle fed leucaena from living-fence stock gained weight while cattle on the standard dry-season diet lost weight [ev_livestock_productivity_gill20_1], but the low- and lower-middle-income evidence base for crop yield itself is thinner.

agroforestry__linear_boundary__rural_pov.mechanism: Boundary and line plantings earn money from the tree products. A windbreak hedge in irrigated rice in the Senegal River valley had an internal rate of return of 36 per cent, or 58 per cent counting its woody products [ev_economic_return_faosen24_15]. Neotropical farmers perceive live fences as a source of additional income, for example from timber sales [ev_household_income_moran18_7].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__rural_pov.conditionality: Both remaining units are second-hand or a perception: the Senegalese return is a financial indicator and the Neotropical income claim a farmer perception, each used as a proxy for poverty, and neither measures household poverty or how the gain is shared [ev_economic_return_faosen24_15, ev_household_income_moran18_7]. The strength is therefore not quantified. The Senegalese financial result comes from irrigated rice in a lower-middle-income country within the LIC/LMIC target [ev_economic_return_faosen24_15].

agroforestry__linear_boundary__soil_eros.mechanism: Live fences of Gliricidia sepium are used in Colombia, Mexico and Nigeria to prevent erosion and retain soil moisture, live fences in India reduce erosion by lowering runoff velocity, and Kenyan farmers report that planting trees in a line prevents soil being swept away by water [ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_2, ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_5, ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6]. A global review of plot and field studies found linear tree plantings (windbreaks, shelterbelts, living fences and hedgerows) cut soil loss by 55% on average against land without them, the lowest of the agroforestry systems compared though the differences among systems were not significant [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_3]. On Saskatchewan prairie fields with old shelterbelts planted to reduce wind erosion, erosion midway between the belts has generally been much less than in unsheltered fields, judged from depth to carbonates and 137Cs, and the authors expect soil productivity there to be higher than in open fields [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5]. In China, windbreak patches reduced average wind-erosion soil loss by 20% compared with open farmland [ev_erosion_hazard_chang21_1].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__soil_eros.conditionality: Only the compiled review and the Chinese windbreak measurement state a size; the live-fence and lined-tree citations and the Kenyan farmer's account give no erosion rate [ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_2, ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_5, ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6]. The 55% figure is an average of compiled study reductions across temperate and tropical sites, not a weighted meta-analytic effect, and it is not specific to low-income settings [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_3]. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt unit is high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target; it infers past erosion from soil markers rather than stating a measured erosion rate [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5]. The Chinese windbreak measurement is upper-middle-income evidence, adding to the mix already in this row [ev_erosion_hazard_chang21_1]. The pooled countries span high-income Canada, upper-middle-income China, and lower-middle-income India and Kenya, so the row transfers only as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target rather than squarely in context.

agroforestry__linear_boundary__water_qua.mechanism: Windbreaks, shelterbelts, living fences and hedgerows on farmland hold soil and nutrients on the field through surface cover and fine roots. A review compiling plot and field studies found linear tree plantings decreased the average nutrient loss from leaching and runoff by 16% and 33% respectively, against land without them [ev_nutrient_removal_zhu19_2].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__water_qua.conditionality: Confidence is very low: the row rests on a single review with few case studies for linear plantings, the percentages are averages of compiled study results rather than weighted meta-analytic effects, and no country or income group is given [ev_nutrient_removal_zhu19_2]. The ranges across studies are wide and include no change: phosphorus losses fell by 0–50%, and the nitrogen range runs from an increase to a large decrease [ev_nutrient_removal_zhu19_2]. The review also reports that linear plantings reduced nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium losses less than the other agroforestry systems it covered. The unit measures nutrient loss leaving the field, which is the pathway to water quality downstream, not stream or groundwater quality itself.

agroforestry__linear_boundary__water_str.mechanism: One study links field shelterbelts to more water stress, through less soil water next to the trees. Beside Saskatchewan field shelterbelts, spring soil water content in 1990 dropped noticeably from 0.1 to 0.05 relative distance from the belt, which the authors put down, tentatively, to uptake by the trees and grasses in the previous fallow year; in 1989 the pattern differed, with a slight trend of decreasing available water from the field edge to the centre [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. The engine reads a slight, unquantified increase in water stress; the counterfactual is soil further into the same field, not an unsheltered field.
agroforestry__linear_boundary__water_str.conditionality: This rests on one source. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt unit is high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target; it measures soil water close to the belt rather than crop water stress, the drop appeared in 1990, not in 1989, and the authors hedge its cause [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. Missing: measured soil water or crop water stress beside windbreaks, live fences or hedgerows in low- or lower-middle-income settings, and any study that compares sheltered with unsheltered fields.

agroforestry__linear_boundary__waterlogg.mechanism: Deep-rooted, fast-growing boundary trees can drain waterlogged fields by transpiring excess soil water (biodrainage). A review of biodrainage cites a study by Ram et al. (2011) in canal-irrigated waterlogged fields at Hisar, Haryana, India: parallel strip plantations of Eucalyptus tereticornis along farm boundaries, spaced at 66 m at a density of 300 plants per hectare, lowered the groundwater table beneath the strips by 85 cm compared with adjacent unvegetated fields in 3 years, with wheat grown between the strips [ev_waterlogging_hazard_singhlal18_1].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__waterlogg.conditionality: No class is set because the row rests on one second-hand reading of one Indian study. What is missing is a second independent source or a direct measurement, ideally one that reports crop yield or farm income on the drained land rather than water-table depth alone; the water-table fall is measured under the strips, and how far it extends into the cropped inter-spaces is not stated [ev_waterlogging_hazard_singhlal18_1].

What is missing is a second independent source or a direct measurement, ideally one that reports crop yield or farm income on the drained land rather than water-table depth alone; the water-table fall is measured under the strips, and how far it extends into the cropped inter-spaces is not stated [ev_waterlogging_hazard_singhlal18_1]. The study was in canal-irrigated fields, so it matches this farming system directly.

agroforestry__linear_boundary__wind_cycl.mechanism: Windbreaks reduce wind speed over a zone that typically extends 10 to 20 tree heights downwind, so large landscapes need multiple barriers to control wind erosion [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15]. Live fences in India serve as windbreaks and raise soil moisture retention through litter build-up [ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__wind_cycl.conditionality: Both units are reviews citing earlier studies and concern wind erosion and sheltering, not cyclone damage [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15, ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4]. Only the Indian unit names a country (lower-middle income) [ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4]. No unit is from an agro-pastoral system; the evidence is applied to agro-pastoral systems by default [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15, ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4].

agroforestry__linear_boundary__wind_cycl.mechanism: Windbreaks and shelterbelts work mechanically, by slowing the wind reaching the sheltered crop. A review on windbreak airflow states that a major effect of a windbreak is to reduce the incidence of low-frequency, high-magnitude damage events such as sandblasting or lodging [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_cleugh98_3]. The zone of reduced wind speed behind a windbreak typically extends 10 to 20 tree heights downwind, so large fields often need multiple barriers [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15]. In China, farmland shelterbelts cut wind speed by 35.8% compared with unsheltered farmland [ev_windbreak_protection_hao26_1]. In Senegal, windbreak hedges are described as having a major impact on wind and playing an important role in protecting sandy, degraded soils from wind erosion [ev_windbreak_protection_faosen24_12]. In India, live fences are used as windbreaks and to raise soil-moisture retention through litter accumulation [ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4].
agroforestry__linear_boundary__wind_cycl.conditionality: None of the five units measures a severe or extreme wind or cyclone event — the evidence covers routine wind and erosion control. Only the Chinese shelterbelt study states a size; the rest describe mechanism or role without a magnitude, which caps the class at moderate. The Chinese unit is upper-middle income, the Senegalese and Indian units lower-middle income, so the row sits adjacent to, not squarely inside, the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__biodi.mechanism: On red and lateritic soils in Jhargram, West Bengal, India, an agri-horti-silviculture system of Gmelina arborea and grafted mango trees with pigeon pea grown in the alleys had the highest earthworm diversity of the systems compared, with a Simpson's diversity index of 0.62 against 0.41 in sole pigeon pea [ev_biodiversity_outcome_biswas22_1]. Tree prunings and leaf fall were kept in the field.
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__biodi.conditionality: The strong class rests on a single trial and a single taxon: earthworm diversity is a soil-biodiversity indicator, not a measure of wider farm or landscape biodiversity, and statistical significance of the difference is not reported [ev_biodiversity_outcome_biswas22_1]. The system was fertilised and given need-based irrigation at tree establishment, so the result applies to managed alley systems on degraded lateritic soils in lower-middle-income settings; further studies, on other taxa, are needed before this reads as a general effect.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__carbo.mechanism: In planted silvoarable systems (crops grown alongside deliberately planted trees), tree litter and root inputs raise soil organic carbon under the tree-crop system relative to cropland without trees. A global review found conversion from cropland to agroforestry generally increased soil carbon storage, and a legume-diversified intercrop trial in Malawi showed a trend toward higher soil carbon under the tree-crop system.
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__carbo.conditionality: The signal is not universal: a Niger trial found no significant difference in soil carbon or nitrogen between the tree-based system and the conventional comparison after four years, and the Malawi result itself was only a trend (P = 0.10), not a conventional statistically significant difference. Evidence comes from only a small number of countries (India, Malawi, Niger), so transfer beyond them is uncertain.
evidence_summary: Ma et al. (global tree-based agroforestry review): conversion from cropland to agroforestry generally increased soil organic carbon storage; conversion from pasture did not.
Snapp et al. (Songani, Malawi): a trend toward higher soil carbon under a legume-diversified intercrop (P = 0.10), not a conventional significant difference.
Bado et al. (Sahel, Niger): no significant soil-carbon or nitrogen difference between the tree-based (zero-till) and conventional system after four years.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__cost_.mechanism: The Regreening Africa cost-efficiency analysis reports that adopting land restoration practices in Rwanda, where the arm was tree-planting agroforestry, cost $201 per household [ev_project_cost_crs23_3].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__cost_.conditionality: This is a programme expenditure per adopting household for one low-income country arm of one programme, so it does not pool with other sources [ev_project_cost_crs23_3]. The same quote attributes Rwanda's higher per-household cost than Ghana's FMNR to tree-planting agroforestry where average land size per household is much more limited [ev_project_cost_crs23_3].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__cost_.mechanism: The Regreening Africa cost-efficiency analysis reports that adopting land restoration practices in Rwanda, where the arm was tree-planting agroforestry, cost $1,387 per hectare [ev_project_cost_crs23_4].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__cost_.conditionality: This is a programme expenditure per hectare where at least one practice was adopted, from one low-income country arm of one programme, so it does not pool with other sources [ev_project_cost_crs23_4]. The same quote notes the much more limited average land size per household in Rwanda and gives $58 per hectare for FMNR in Ghana [ev_project_cost_crs23_4].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__cost_.mechanism: Planted tree-crop systems in annual cropping add labour, and costs rise with it. In Cameroon, Leucaena alley cropping in a maize/groundnut intercrop raised labour from 75 to 104 person-days per hectare a year (38%), and, averaged over 3 years, raised variable costs by 34% against the traditional system [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. In Nigeria, maize plots mulched with tree prunings required higher labour input than the fertilizer and untreated controls, 96% of it for collecting and managing mulch and only 4% for weeding [ev_project_cost_korm99_4]. A Nigerian alley-cropping model adds two further labour-cost readings, both increases: annual labour for maize production under 4 m-spaced Leucaena alley cropping is reported increased by 53 percent against the traditional bush-fallow control, because of the added labour for hedgerow pruning, and under the closer 2 m spacing the model assumes total labour increases by 87 percent, since more hedgerows need pruning [ev_project_cost_ehui90_5, ev_project_cost_ehui90_6].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__cost_.conditionality: The cost rise comes from the work of cutting, carrying and spreading prunings, so the design and harvest regime of the hedgerows set the bill [ev_project_cost_korm99_4, ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. The Cameroon variable costs mix hedgerow establishment with recurrent pruning, and they decreased from the first to the third year, so the 34% is an average that is heavier early on [ev_project_cost_tonye95_1]. In the Nigerian trial the trees were grown on a separate plot and the prunings carried in, a biomass-transfer design rather than trees in the field itself [ev_project_cost_korm99_4]. Both are on-station or researcher-run trials in lower-middle-income West and Central Africa; the size rests on the Cameroon figure alone, and neither unit is a cost saving. Both readings add to the cost-increase side of this row rather than the cost-saving side: like the Cameroon and Nigeria mulching evidence already here, the extra labour is pruning and handling tree biomass, not time saved on weeding. The 4 m figure is drawn from an earlier cited labour study rather than measured by the modelling authors themselves, and the 2 m figure is the modelling authors' own assumption (more hedgerows to prune at closer spacing), not a measurement. Both are lower-middle-income Nigerian evidence, within the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__droug.mechanism: The only unit names income growth through commercial agroforestry as one option that reduced vulnerability to climate shocks (drought) in some Ethiopian communities; it gives no biophysical mechanism [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__droug.conditionality: The rated effect belongs to a bundled sustainable-land-management programme assessed through stakeholder responses, not to agroforestry alone, and it does not describe a planted silvoarable design [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4]. The evidence is from Ethiopia (low income), within the LIC/LMIC target [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4]. No unit is from an agro-pastoral system; the evidence is applied to agro-pastoral systems by default [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__droug.mechanism: Within planted silvoarable systems, trees are reported to help crops reach water and recover from drought stress. In an experimentally induced drought in an eastern Canadian soybean-intercropping system, crop losses occurred only in the monocrop, not in the agroforestry system [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4]. In Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, said deep-rooted mango, papaya and banana trees get water from deep down and do not dry up fast, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind; the study concludes that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought, citing deep root systems that use a greater soil volume for water [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10, ev_t3_drought_roots_quandt17_2, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. In a French walnut-based alley-cropping system, imposed spring drought cut full-sun pea yield by 22% while the alley-cropped yield rose 12 to 20% relative to its own rainfed baseline, though alley-cropped pea still yielded less overall than the full-sun control in both rainfall regimes [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__droug.conditionality: Set against this, a reversal is measured directly in Kenya: in a growing season that received only 317 mm of rain, maize under dispersed Grevillea robusta trees yielded 0.02 t/ha against 1.53 t/ha in unshaded sole maize, a near-total loss [ev_crop_yield_lott09_4]. In semi-arid Brazil, in a low-rainfall year, maize yielded very little whether or not it was grown among alley-cropped trees, with no significant difference between the two systems — the drought year erased the tree benefit rather than reversing it [ev_crop_yield_martins13_2]. The Kenyan household link to perceived drought held in Burat but not in Kinna, and one Kenyan unit only states that agroforestry has been proposed for resilience rather than measuring it [ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. Measured harm (maladaptation) — the practice reducing production for some adopters — appears in 14 sources within this family. A Kenyan on-station alley-cropping trial in Embu adds a direct species contrast within one experiment: maize alley-cropped with leucaena yielded significantly more than both the unfertilised and fertilised maize-monoculture controls, while the same maize alley-cropped with calliandra yielded less than the unfertilised control — same site, same design, opposite signs by hedgerow species [ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_1, ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_2].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__recur.mechanism: In degraded lateritic soils of West Bengal, India, an alley-cropping system of Gmelina arborea trees, grafted mango and pigeon pea cost US$482 per hectare per year to run, the highest cost of production among the systems compared, averaged over a multi-year trial [ev_project_cost_biswas22_1].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__recur.conditionality: This single estimate mixes establishment and recurrent cost items (seedlings, fertiliser, pesticide, irrigation, labour, machinery) averaged over the full multi-year trial, so it is a broad cost-of-production figure rather than a narrowly defined recurring annual cost, and it comes from one site and one farming system. A second independent source would be needed before agreement can be stated on the size of the recurring cost for this sub-practice.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__rural.mechanism: Planted silvoarable systems, trees grown in rows with arable crops, raise income mainly through fertiliser-tree soil fertility effects, intercrop diversification, and eventual timber or fruit harvests on top of the annual crop. Net revenue from a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea intercrop in India was reported as up to 2.66 times higher than the pigeon pea sole crop [ev_economic_return_biswas22_1], and alley cropping with Acacia senegal in Sudan raised sorghum net revenue from 501 to 558 Sudanese pounds per hectare [ev_economic_return_fadl13_4]. Eucalyptus timber intercropped with field crops in India gave a benefit-cost ratio of 3.5 to 1, compared with 1.3 to 1 for agricultural crops alone [ev_economic_return_ram11_4], and alley cropping in Nigeria returned a net present value of 1755 Nigerian naira per hectare, more than the no-till and other alley-cropping comparators [ev_economic_return_ehui90_7]. Fertiliser trees also protect farmers against drought-year crop failure: in Zambia, a farmer who had planted fertiliser trees lost only 90 US dollars in sunk cost when a crop failed, against 164 US dollars for a farmer who had invested in inorganic fertiliser [ev_economic_return_chaudhury11_1].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__rural.conditionality: The benefit depends on which intercrop combination and management regime is used, and is not universal. A meta-analysis found that crop-fruit tree intercropping in China had a negative effect on productivity [ev_household_income_castle21s_2], and the same Indian Gmelina trial's higher net returns were measured against a high-cost mango sole crop, so the size of the gain depends on the alternative crop chosen [ev_economic_return_biswas22_2]. In Nigeria, net present value for sweet orange monocropped or intercropped was negative for the monocrop and for one intercrop combination, and positive only with cassava and maize or with chilli pepper and amaranthus [ev_economic_return_aiyel01_1]. Alley cropping with nitrogen-fixing trees and mulch from multi-purpose trees was profitable in land- and labour-abundant conditions [ev_economic_return_korm99_5] but, as the same source separately records, not where land is a scarce resource [ev_economic_return_korm99_6]. An improved-fallow system in Malawi stayed profitable, with a value-cost ratio above 4.0, only while fertiliser prices were low; when fertiliser prices rose, the comparable rotation fell to a value-cost ratio at or below 2.5 [ev_economic_return_snapp10_1]. Adoption of improved fallows and biomass transfer in Kenya remained too small in area after six years to produce a significant household-level welfare impact [ev_household_income_place05_2]. Most of the quantified gains are from low- and lower-middle-income countries in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, with one upper-middle-income harm finding from China.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__soil_.mechanism: Trees combined with crops, as alley cropping or contour hedgerow intercropping, protect the soil surface with living plants, litter and mulch and bind it with extended fine roots. A review compiling plot and field studies against sole crops found silvoarable agroforestry cut soil loss by 66% on average and water loss by 43% [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_2]. The same Nigerian alley-cropping model also projects soil loss directly: over a 20-year horizon on a sloping field, 2 m-spaced Leucaena alley cropping gives the lowest predicted cumulative soil loss of the systems compared (2.5 t/ha), against 17.8 t/ha for the traditional short-cycle bush fallow it is compared with; 4 m spacing follows at 9.9 t/ha, still below the no-till (14 t/ha) and bush-fallow controls [ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_1, ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_2, ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_3]. On a steep hillslope in Laguna, the Philippines, a randomised trial of contour hedgerows (Desmanthus virgatus) on maize-mungbean alleys found annual soil loss fell step-wise with each added practice: from 124 t/ha/yr under the farmer's up-and-down-slope tillage, to 40 t/ha/yr once contour hedgerows and contour tillage were added, to 3 t/ha/yr once the hedgerow trimmings and crop residues were also spread as mulch, to 0.2 t/ha/yr once zero tillage was added on top of hedgerows and mulch; the hedgerow-plus-contour-tillage treatment alone also produced only about half as much annual runoff as the farmer's practice [ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_1, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_2, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_3, ev_runoff_reduction_paningbatan95_4]. In Jiangxi Province, China, a randomised trial intercropping peanut with Choerospondias axillaris trees on a sloping field found mean soil loss per rainfall event fell by 25.3% with younger trees and by 32.0% with older trees compared with mono-cropped peanut [ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_1, ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_2].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__soil_.conditionality: The review-based average rests on a single review whose percentages are averages of compiled study reductions, not weighted meta-analytic effects, and which gives no country or income-group breakdown [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2]. The newer field and modelled evidence now carries most of the weight in this row and points the same way: in Nigeria, a modelled 2 m alley-cropping system gives the lowest predicted 20-year cumulative soil loss of the systems compared, and in the Philippines, a hillside field trial found soil loss fall from 124 to 40 t/ha/yr once contour hedgerows and contour tillage were added to the farmer's practice, falling further to 3 and then 0.2 t/ha/yr as mulch and zero tillage were added on top [ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_1, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_1, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_2, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_3]. The Nigerian erosion figures are modelled, not measured, running a simplified USLE-based erosion model calibrated to plot-level erosion rates from the same research station, and the model's own ranking shows erosion as time-dependent: initial erosion rates are lower under no-till than under the 4 m alley, with the alley only overtaking by the end of the 20-year horizon. The Philippines result is bundled: each successive treatment adds a co-practice (contour tillage, then mulch from the hedgerow trimmings and crop residues, then zero tillage) on top of the hedgerows, so the hedgerow-alone share of the reduction cannot be separated from the tillage and mulch changes that go with it, and even the hedgerow-plus-contour-tillage treatment is still called 'considerable' soil loss by the authors, not yet a tolerable rate. Both the Philippines and Nigeria results sit inside the LIC/LMIC target; the Chinese trial is upper-middle-income evidence. The same Chinese trial found a reversal on runoff: mean runoff per event was higher in both tree-intercropped treatments than in mono-cropped peanut, even though soil loss was lower — the authors attribute the higher runoff to surface seals and crusts forming on the untilled soil under and between the tree rows, while tillage of the peanut area itself raised infiltration there; the engine counts this as measured harm for some adopters [ev_runoff_reduction_wei07_3]. In China, mean soil loss per rainfall event fell with both younger and older intercropped trees against mono-cropped peanut, but mean runoff per event was higher in both tree treatments than in the mono-crop — a reversal the authors attribute to surface seals forming on the untilled soil near the trees rather than to the trees raising runoff generally [ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_1, ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_2].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__water.mechanism: In rainfed cropland, the measured evidence points both ways depending on whether water-use efficiency or soil moisture itself is measured. At Sadore in the Nigerien Sahel, Ziziphus mauritiana trees in millet fields raised the rainwater-use efficiency of millet by 17 to 47% depending on fertiliser treatment, and of a millet/cowpea intercrop by 11 to 17% [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_2]. In a long-running Gliricidia + maize trial at Makoka, Malawi, system water-use efficiency (above-ground biomass including the tree, per unit of seasonal water use) was strongly and significantly higher in every season for gliricidia-based systems than for sole maize or maize-pigeonpea [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_6]. At the same site, available soil water was also greater in the gliricidia+maize+pigeonpea system at the peak of the recharge phase in two seasons, attributed to increased infiltration and reduced soil evaporation, and higher below 60 cm in the second season's May reading [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8]. In a German alley-cropping trial in a drought year, soil water content remained lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In Jiangxi Province, China, a peanut-tree alley-cropping trial found the profile-mean (0-150 cm) soil water potential drier in both tree-intercropped treatments than in mono-cropped peanut or either tree monoculture, consistent with tree-crop competition for water, with the difference larger in the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_wei07_4].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__water.conditionality: Against this, at the start of the cropping season available soil water was generally lower in the tree-based Makoka systems, consistent with the trees depleting moisture through the dry season, and the March-to-August decline was most pronounced in the gliricidia-based treatments [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5]; several other season-level readings found no significant difference [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_1, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_6, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_7, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_9, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11], and the authors conclude that gliricidia pruned before and during the cropping season does not provoke undue competition for water with the associated crop. In France, a walnut-alley trial found a depth split: soil water in the plough layer was drier under the trees than the full-sun control through spring, while at depth (50 cm or more) soil water dynamics were very similar between the two systems [ev_soil_moisture_blan22_4, ev_soil_moisture_blan22_5]. The water-use-efficiency figures are total above-ground biomass of trees and crops together per unit of water use, not grain per unit of water, so the tree's own biomass lifts the tree-system values; the Niger figures, by contrast, count crop biomass only per mm of rainfall, so they show the crop itself using rain more efficiently with trees nearby [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1]. The German and French units are high-income temperate evidence, each from a single season and site, outside the LIC/LMIC target; the Niger and Malawi evidence (low income) sits inside it, which is why this row transfers in_context overall. This Chinese result is the deciding addition for this row: benefit and harm/no-effect units in this sub-practice were already close in weight, split between the water-use-efficiency gains (which credit the tree's own biomass, not just the crop's) and the direct soil-moisture readings that show trees depleting water at the start of the season. Adding this one further harm reading — drier soil profiles under intercropped trees than under mono-cropped peanut — is now enough to tip the balance from a row that read a moderate net benefit into one where neither side has enough weight to set a direction, which is why the class changes to conflicting evidence rather than staying a moderate gain. This is upper-middle-income Chinese evidence, consistent with the row's existing transfer.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__water.mechanism: Under waterlogging in Punjab, India, agroforestry systems had higher evapotranspiration than sole crops, removing excess water from the soil and creating a better soil environment for plant growth, as a review reports from Dhillon et al. (2010) [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__water.conditionality: The cell is data deficient, not a finding of no effect: the only evidence is a single Indian study (lower-middle income, within the LIC/LMIC target) reported second-hand in a review, with no size stated [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9]. What is missing is a measured comparison of crop or farm output under waterlogging with and without trees, or a second independent source; the primary Dhillon et al. study itself would be the first place to look. The study system is irrigated cropping, applied here to all farming systems by default [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__water.mechanism: Under waterlogging in Punjab, India, agroforestry systems had higher evapotranspiration than sole crops, removing excess water from the soil and creating a better soil environment for plant growth, as a review reports from Dhillon et al. (2010) [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__water.conditionality: The cell is data deficient, not a finding of no effect: the only evidence is a single Indian study (lower-middle income, within the LIC/LMIC target) reported second-hand in a review, with no size stated [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9]. What is missing is a measured comparison of crop or farm output under waterlogging with and without trees, or a second independent source; the primary Dhillon et al. study itself would be the first place to look.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__wind_.mechanism: The only evidence is a background statement in a Kenyan livelihood-resilience study that trees have the ability to buffer crops from storms, citing earlier work [ev_t3_wind_buffer_quandt17_4].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__wind_.conditionality: It is not a measurement made in that study, refers to crops rather than livestock or structures, and gives no tree arrangement, species or storm intensity [ev_t3_wind_buffer_quandt17_4]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__wind_.mechanism: The only evidence is a background statement in a Kenyan livelihood-resilience study that trees have the ability to buffer crops from storms, citing earlier work [ev_t3_wind_buffer_quandt17_4].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__wind_.conditionality: It is not a measurement made in that study, refers to crops rather than livestock or structures, and gives no tree arrangement, species or storm intensity [ev_t3_wind_buffer_quandt17_4]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

agroforestry__production_gap.mechanism: Agroforestry's effect on the crop-yield gap depends heavily on how close the trees stand to the crop. In a global review of windbreak and alley systems, wider tree spacing lifted yield — modelling predicted an 8.04% yield gain over a 20 tree-height buffer for windbreaks, and a 13% gain at 15 tree-heights for alley systems [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_8]. The same review found the opposite at close spacing: alleys under 10 tree-heights had reduced yields, and those under 2.5 tree-heights lost more than 25% [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_7]. In dryland agriculture, a separate literature review reported agroforestry techniques raising cereal yields by 69% on average [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14].
agroforestry__production_gap.conditionality: At the whole-agroforestry level the sub-practices disagree with one another, so the roll-up states conflicting evidence rather than picking a side: alley/boundary tree systems and shaded-perennial systems split between gain and loss by spacing and shade design, while regeneration-based systems point positive. Measured harm (maladaptation) — the practice reducing production for some adopters — appears in 40 sources. A livestock-yield check on linear agroforestry, drawn from only 12 publications covering 36 paddock-years, could not establish an effect in either direction [ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_13]. A Kenyan on-station alley-cropping trial in Embu adds a direct species contrast within one experiment: maize alley-cropped with leucaena yielded significantly more than both the unfertilised and fertilised maize-monoculture controls, while the same maize alley-cropped with calliandra yielded less than the unfertilised control — same site, same design, opposite signs by hedgerow species [ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_1, ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_2]. In Niger, millet yields on fields with regenerated trees (100 to 370 kg/ha) were higher than on control fields without trees (50 to 270 kg/ha), a gain of 50 to 100 kg/ha the authors attribute to tree presence, and the same protected trees supply dry-season fodder that eases the feed shortage common at that time of year [ev_crop_yield_boton10_1, ev_forage_productivity_boton10_7]. Shade level splits the result within one crop too: in southern Brazil coffee shaded by Mimosa scabrella accumulated more clean coffee over the harvests than unshaded coffee, a gain the authors tie to less frost damage, while the same paper reports from earlier trials that excessive, permanent shade caused coffee production losses comparable to those caused by frosts [ev_crop_yield_caramori96_1, ev_crop_yield_caramori96_2].

agroforestry__production_gap__aez-humid_.mechanism: In humid tropical farming systems, trees contribute nitrogen (through litter, pruning residues and nitrogen-fixing species) and other soil benefits that narrow the gap between actual and potential crop yields. A pantropical synthesis of sub-Saharan African sites found trees raised both yield and soil nitrogen, with a weighted yield ratio of about 2.0 for humid conditions, and separate meta-analyses covering 48 and 34 studies found overall mean increases in total and available soil nitrogen under trees in humid and sub-humid tropical settings.
agroforestry__production_gap__aez-humid_.conditionality: This result is reported at the agro-ecological-zone (humid tropics) level, one step removed from a direct country match, so it transfers to a specific farming system with some uncertainty. The soil-nitrogen gains come from pantropical meta-analyses pooling many sites and study designs, not from a single matched-yield field trial repeated in every target country.

agroforestry__production_gap__aez-semi_a.mechanism: In semi-arid farming systems, scattered shrubs and trees raise soil nutrients near their canopies — a Sahelian study measured soil nitrogen and phosphorus 38% and 51% higher under shrub canopies than in open fields — and millet and sorghum yields were often higher close to trees, giving a weighted yield ratio of about 1.9 for semi-arid conditions in a sub-Saharan Africa synthesis.
agroforestry__production_gap__aez-semi_a.conditionality: The benefit is markedly variable at the field scale: the same Sudano-Sahelian dataset found yield changes under trees ranging from about -100% to +200% between fields, so the slight overall gain is an average across a wide spread, not a reliable result for every plot — some fields see no benefit or a loss.

agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.mechanism: Parkland trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, crucial in the dry season and during drought, and in Senegal access to cool zones under trees reduces livestock heat stress and so raises animal productivity [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1, ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22]. Under parkland trees, tuber yield is improved (+0.40 to +1.67 t ha-1) and legumes are less affected by tree cover [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1].
agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.conditionality: Cereals lose out: grain yield ranged from a loss of 0.54 t ha-1 under Balanites aegyptiaca to a gain of 0.24 t ha-1 under F. albida, with reductions attributed to competition for light, nutrients and water, so the net effect depends on which crops dominate [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1]. All units are reviews citing earlier studies from the Sahel and Senegal, and the fodder and livestock gains are stated without a size [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1, ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22].

agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.mechanism: In irrigated cropping, trees compete with the crop for water, nutrients and light.
