Between rows of juvenile plumcot trees in drip-irrigated, semi-arid Xinjiang, China, intercropped soybean yielded 46.03% less and intercropped alfalfa 51.83% less than the same crops grown alone, over two years [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]. In village irrigated perimeters of the Senegal River valley, hedges cut yields up to 10 metres from the hedge in the rainy season, while total yields across the protected plots rose 23 per cent in the off-season, as an FAO review reports from earlier work (Tamba; Samba et al.) [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13]. In canal-irrigated Haryana, India, a Eucalyptus biodrainage planting along field boundaries lowered the water table and raised wheat grain yield 3.4 times over compared with adjacent waterlogged fields without the plantation, though near the tree lines shading and root competition cut wheat yield by an estimated 11.7% [ev_crop_yield_ram11_2, ev_crop_yield_ram11_3].
agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.conditionality: The class rests on a single Chinese experiment with young trees, so confidence is low and the size may not hold as the trees mature or in other designs [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1]. Part of the Chinese loss reflects the smaller cropped area and the lower seeding rate and irrigation given to the intercropped soybean, and yields are per unit of total plot area, so the tree rows count against the crop [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]. The Senegal result runs the other way over the whole protected plot, which separates the two: hedges bordering a plot lose crop near the hedge but can raise the plot total, while trees planted through the plot at close spacing take crop area and water directly [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13]. The Senegal figure is a second-hand reading in grey literature with no comparator stated beyond the unprotected plots. China is upper-middle income, outside the LIC/LMIC target; Senegal is lower-middle income, within it [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13]. The Indian biodrainage yield gain is attributed to relief from waterlogging through a lowered water table, not to any general shade or nutrient mechanism, and comes from a single planting in one location [ev_crop_yield_ram11_2, ev_crop_yield_ram11_3]. India, like Senegal, is lower-middle income, within the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.mechanism: In mixed crop-livestock systems, agroforestry raises total farm output by supplying fodder, soil fertility and dry-season tree products alongside crops and livestock, so productivity gains are measured across multiple farm components rather than one crop alone.
agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.conditionality: One study in this pool found non-adopting farmers saw a drop in productivity specifically when required to switch to fertiliser-tree systems — the single harm finding here — which does not reflect a typical voluntary-adoption outcome.

agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.mechanism: Across silvopastoral systems, tree cover consistently raises forage and livestock output relative to open pasture. In Senegal, herbaceous biomass under Acacia tortilis and Balanites aegyptiaca canopies reached 2 to 5 times that measured in treeless areas, and tree leaves, fruit and pods make up about 40% of cattle diet and 80% of small-ruminant diet in the dry-to-wet-season transition [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_20, ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21]. Reviews report tree shade in pastures associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain generally [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4], and in Nicaragua and Costa Rica, milk production was 29% and over 15% higher on high tree-density or silvopasture compared with low-cover or full-sun pasture, with dry-season liveweight gains 2 to 5% higher on high-tree-density pasture, attributed to lower heat stress and more available foliage and fruit [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. In Colombia, intensive silvopasture raised milk production 32.1% over the same pasture grasses without shrubs or trees, raised milk per hectare per year under Leucaena against an open-field system, and a review reports beef output 12-fold higher per unit of land than traditional grazing, also higher than improved treeless pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Intensive silvopasture is also reported to raise stocking rate several-fold over extensive grazing, with proportional gains in meat and milk output, and better cattle feeding in critical drought periods is said to reduce seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. During a severe drought, Colombian silvopastoral forage production held steady while grass-monoculture biomass fell to a quarter, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are described as more drought-tolerant, giving more stable dry-season forage volumes [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. A review also reports that integrating a grazed fodder bank — fodder trees or shrubs established on part of the pasture and then grazed — repeatedly raises animal production, though the gain is delayed by the trees' establishment period and by taking part of the pasture out of use while they establish [ev_livestock_productivity_dagang03_5]. In arid India, trees and shrubs lopped for green leaf fodder supply sheep, goats and camels with browse in drought years, when grass is scarce [ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_2].
agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.conditionality: Gains are not universal. Under high-density Acacia decurrens silvopasture in Colombia, milk per cow per day was lower than in the open field, though a lower-density silvopasture at the same site still out-performed the open field, showing tree density itself can flip the sign [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. A review of Brazilian silvopastoral thermal-comfort and production studies found no significant difference in milk production in the studies that measured it [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. During El Niño events, silvopastoral systems in Colombia still lost milk production, just less than conventional systems did [ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1]. The Argentine multi-site forage evidence is the clearest statement that the benefit is severity- and site-dependent: it held in humid areas in both normal and dry years, showed no difference in semi-arid areas, and reversed from a slight gain to an 89% loss in a dry year at one semi-arid site, with denser canopy generally associated with lower relative forage production across sites [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_7]. Most of the Latin American livestock units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume rather than new primary measurements, and the clearest primary magnitudes (Colombia, Nicaragua, Costa Rica) are upper-middle or high income, while the Senegalese fodder evidence is lower-middle income, which is why this row's evidence sits adjacent to, rather than squarely inside, the LIC/LMIC target. Against this, a review of a regional silvopastoral conservation project in Esparza, Costa Rica reports that unpruned multistrata live fences can reduce forage availability by shading out the grasses along pasture edges [ev_forage_productivity_garbach12_1]. The same arid-India trial that supplies the browse-fodder finding also measured lower understorey herbage yield under every tree and shrub species than in a treeless control during drought years, a trade-off between the forage layers that this row's gain does not net off [ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_2].

agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.mechanism: In coffee and cocoa agroforestry, shade trees compete with the crop for light while also buffering climate stress and adding nutrients, and both effects show up in the evidence. On the loss side, a pan-tropical review found shaded coffee and cocoa yielded 26% less per hectare than conventional, unshaded systems [ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1]; a pan-tropical cocoa meta-analysis found cocoa bean yield 25% lower in agroforestry than in monoculture, though total system yield (cocoa plus the other products) was about ten times higher [ev_crop_yield_niether20_1]; and in Bolivia, full-sun cacao monocultures were 41% more productive in cacao alone than agroforestry plots, attributed to greater light reaching the trees [ev_crop_yield_armengot16_1]. On the gain side, a global meta-analysis of coffee systems found the odds of climate-related yield loss were lower under agroforestry than under conventional coffee, an odds ratio of 0.69 [ev_crop_yield_patil25_1], and in Rwanda, intercropping coffee with Tephrosia (a nitrogen-fixing shrub) mulch raised coffee yield by 23% to 36%, rising to 25% to 42% when fertiliser was added too [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_1].
agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.conditionality: The same Bolivia cacao trial that found lower cacao yield under shade also found that selling the plantain and banana grown alongside the cacao more than made up for the lost cacao revenue [ev_agricultural_production_value_armengot16_1] — so a crop-yield loss does not always mean a production loss once the other products in the system are counted. The direction in this cell turns on the shade and nutrient balance of the specific sub-practice and the crop and shade level studied, which is why no single direction is reported.

agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.mechanism: In high-income, often mechanised cropping systems, trees compete with the adjacent crop for light, water and nutrients. Canadian Prairie shelterbelt studies found a competition zone of reduced crop yield close to the trees and a wind-sheltered zone further out with above-average yields, but the net effect across the field was often a loss — one study estimated a net yield loss equivalent to the width of the shelterbelt. Pea yields under trees fell by 25% to 77% depending on rainfall regime, and a Brazilian shaded-coffee comparison found a 30% yield reduction in the shaded system relative to monoculture.
agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.conditionality: The direction is not uniform even within high-income systems: several Costa Rican shaded-coffee comparisons found no significant yield difference against full sun, and non-grain or livestock components improved under trees even as grain and legume yields fell — tuber and bean yields rose at a subarctic Ontario site, and cattle weight gains and milk yield were reported higher under trees in Costa Rica. The negative result is strongest for annual grain and legume intercrops competing directly with tree roots and shade, not for every component of these farming systems.
agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.agreement_note: Agreement is only medium: the competition-driven yield losses (several Canadian Prairie and French pea studies, a cacao comparison) sit alongside null results (several Costa Rican shaded-coffee comparisons with no yield difference) and gains in non-grain components (bean, tuber and livestock yields), so the net increase in the production gap reflects a weight-of-evidence judgement, not a unanimous finding.

agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.mechanism: Among low- and lower-middle-income contexts, agroforestry's yield effect is positive on average but varies sharply by sub-practice. Pooled across studies, the standardized effect on crop yield was +1.16 (Hedges' g), with a 95% confidence interval of −0.35 to 2.67 [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_1]; a single Malawi study of fertiliser-tree fallows rotated with maize found a much larger effect of 3.85 on crop value, used as a proxy for yield [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_3]. In the shrub- and tree-parklands of Sudano-Sahelian West Africa, millet and sorghum yields ranged from 25% lower to 120% higher where shrubs grew in the fields, and were even more variable — 100% lower to 200% higher — where trees rather than shrubs were present [ev_crop_yield_felix18_2]. In Niger, millet yields on fields with regenerated trees (100 to 370 kg/ha) were higher than on control fields without trees (50 to 270 kg/ha), a gain of 50 to 100 kg/ha the authors attribute to tree presence, and the same protected trees supply dry-season fodder that eases the feed shortage common at that time of year [ev_crop_yield_boton10_1, ev_forage_productivity_boton10_7].
agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.conditionality: The gains are not universal: a hedgerow-intercropping subgroup in a sub-Saharan Africa review found a crop-yield response ratio of only 0.9 (95% CI 0.9 to 1.0), spanning the no-effect value of 1 — the one configuration in that dataset where agroforestry did not lift yield [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_5]; and a payment-for-ecosystem-services tree-planting programme showed an effect as low as −0.33 (Hedges' g) at the low end of the same review's range [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_2]. Measured harm (maladaptation) — the practice reducing production for some adopters — appears in 18 sources. A Kenyan on-station alley-cropping trial in Embu adds a direct species contrast within one experiment: maize alley-cropped with leucaena yielded significantly more than both the unfertilised and fertilised maize-monoculture controls, while the same maize alley-cropped with calliandra yielded less than the unfertilised control — same site, same design, opposite signs by hedgerow species [ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_1, ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_2].

agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.mechanism: A review of the worldwide windbreak literature finds field and forage crop yield generally higher in sheltered fields than unsheltered ones, with whole-field weighted mean yield gains of 20.8% in regions with persistent winter snow and 12.5% in regions without it [ev_crop_yield_kort88_1, ev_crop_yield_kort88_6, ev_crop_yield_kort88_7]. A hedgerow meta-analysis found soil total nitrogen significantly higher under plant hedgerows than in farmland without them, attributed to hedgerow litter inputs and capture of nutrient-laden runoff [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1].
agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.conditionality: Set against this, the same windbreak review notes that land occupied by the trees and tree-crop competition can turn the shelter yield gain into a net loss in some studies [ev_crop_yield_kort88_2], and a coffee/cocoa review found dry-bean yield per hectare 26% lower under shade than in conventional, unshaded systems [ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1]. None of the climate-zone windbreak figures gives a country, and they are weighted averages across many studies rather than a single measured site, so the practical gain for a given field is not guaranteed [ev_crop_yield_kort88_6, ev_crop_yield_kort88_7]. The hedgerow meta-analysis mixes grass-only strips with woody hedgerows and measures soil nitrogen, a component of the production gap, not yield itself [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1]. All units in this scope row report a 'mixed' income classification (pooling evidence across several income bands in the source itself) rather than a single country or income group, so the row cannot be placed more precisely within the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.mechanism: In upper-middle-income contexts, several studies show agroforestry or silvopasture raising production. In China, a national meta-analysis found crop yield 16.57% higher within sheltered farmland than unsheltered [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1], and a separate study of shelterbelt-protected maize in northeast China found yield gains of 4.28 to 9.45% at the optimal level of tree protection across climatic-productivity zones, highest in the semi-arid west [ev_crop_yield_zheng16_1, ev_crop_yield_zheng16_2, ev_crop_yield_zheng16_3]. In Iran, intercropped wheat and barley yielded 35% and 39% higher near trees than in their respective monocultures [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_2]. In Brazil, second-year coffee yield under the best-performing shade-tree species reached up to 101.99 kg/ha while the unshaded monoculture control yielded nothing in the same year [ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1]. For livestock, Colombian intensive silvopasture raised milk production 32.1% over the same pasture grasses without shrubs or trees, and milk production still rose 10% in the lowest-rainfall year in several decades after a switch to intensive silvopasture that also allowed irrigation to be dropped [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Leucaena-based silvopasture in Colombia raised stocking rate and milk output while eliminating chemical fertiliser, and a review reports silvopasture beef output 12-fold higher per unit of land than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. In mixed crop-livestock Brazil, cattle in silvopasture gained 512 g/animal/day against 452 g/day in monoculture, and tree leaves added about 40 kg/ha of nitrogen in a cactus-pear-and-buffel-grass system, with potential to cut fertiliser costs [ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]. In Argentina, forage production under trees exceeded treeless grassland or pasture at drought intensities at or below the authors' dry-year threshold [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1], and in Colombia forage production held steady through intense drought while grass monoculture biomass fell to a quarter [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. In a mixed pasture of leucaena (Leucaena leucocephala) and the grass Setaria sphacelata, reported from Sri Lanka in the same review, nitrogen transferred from the tree gave the grass a 16% higher nitrogen yield than in monoculture, with 21% of the grass's nitrogen traced to the leucaena [ev_forage_productivity_dagang03_2]. A review also reports that integrating a grazed fodder bank — fodder trees or shrubs established on part of the pasture and then grazed — repeatedly raises animal production, though the gain is delayed by the trees' establishment period and by taking part of the pasture out of use while they establish [ev_livestock_productivity_dagang03_5]. In Brazil's semi-arid Cariri Paraibano, alley cropping cut maize-plus-bean biomass by about 38% against crops grown without trees over the whole experiment, though counting the trees' own leaf, twig and fuelwood biomass, total productivity in the tree system was 260% higher than in the treeless system, with biomass productivity also varying far less year to year (a coefficient of variation of 18.2% against 89.5%) [ev_crop_yield_martins13_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_martins13_1, ev_yield_stability_martins13_1]. On a set of monitored Bahia cocoa farms, removing shade trees entirely alongside fertiliser use nearly doubled cocoa bean yield [ev_crop_yield_vaast14_3].
agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.conditionality: Against this, the same Chinese shelterbelt study that found a 16.57% gain within the sheltered field also found yield 20.47% lower in the edge zone immediately next to the shelterbelt, where trees compete directly with the crop [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2], and the northeast China maize study found yield falling once shelterbelt density rose above the optimum [ev_crop_yield_zheng16_4]. In China, juvenile plumcot rows cut intercropped soybean yield by 46.03% and alfalfa hay yield by 51.83% against sole cropping, partly because the intercrop had less cropped area and a lower seeding rate [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]. In China, apricot-wheat intercropping significantly reduced wheat grain yield and its components in both years measured [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3]. In Brazilian agroforestry, soybean yielded only 500 to 700 kg/ha against about 2700 to 3000 kg/ha in monoculture over two seasons [ev_crop_yield_santos25_5]. In Indonesia, agroforestry maize yield was significantly lower by the third harvest, though soybean yield in the same system was unaffected across all three harvests [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_4]. In Brazilian dairy, a review of silvopastoral studies found no significant difference in milk production in the studies that measured it, and under high-density Acacia decurrens silvopasture in Colombia, milk per cow per day was lower than in the open field, though lower-density silvopasture there still out-performed the open field [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. During El Niño events, silvopastoral systems in Colombia lost less milk production than conventional systems, but still recorded a loss, not a gain [ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1]. In Brazil, drought-induced cocoa yield loss showed no relationship with shade-tree ground cover (p = 0.64), and in Mexico coffee harvest loss was unrelated to vegetation management, with all farms losing 18 to 40% of the harvest regardless of shade complexity [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. In Argentina, the forage benefit itself is conditional and sometimes reverses: it held in very humid areas in both normal and dry years, showed no difference between systems in semi-arid areas, and at the semi-arid Santiago del Estero site swung from a slight gain in normal years to an 89% loss in a dry year, with denser tree canopy associated with lower relative forage production across sites [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_7]. All of this evidence is upper-middle income by definition of the scope row (China, Iran, Brazil, Colombia, Argentina, Sri Lanka), so it transfers in_context to its own scope but is not automatically representative of the LIC/LMIC target. The Brazilian alley-cropping figures are a single trial, and its higher total-productivity and stability figures only hold once the trees' own fuelwood and fodder biomass are counted alongside the food crop, not for the food crop alone [ev_crop_yield_martins13_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_martins13_1, ev_yield_stability_martins13_1]. The Bahia shade-removal finding is a second-hand citation in a review editorial and is confounded with a simultaneous fertiliser change, so the yield gain cannot be attributed to shade removal alone [ev_crop_yield_vaast14_3].

agroforestry__recurrent_cost.mechanism: The main recurring cost agroforestry adds is caring for and harvesting the system's extra components (tree and crop combined) each year. In degraded lateritic soils of West Bengal, India, a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea agroforestry system cost US$482 per hectare per year to run, more than any of the sole-crop comparisons in the same trial [ev_project_cost_biswas22_1]. In north-central Nicaragua, the in-kind cost of family labour on the most diversified shaded coffee plots was US$498 per hectare per year, against US$54 per hectare per year on full-sun coffee, while cash costs for fungicide, fertiliser and hired labour were not significantly different between the two [ev_project_cost_pinoar14_1].
agroforestry__recurrent_cost.conditionality: The Nicaraguan figure is specifically the value of unpaid family labour, not a cash outlay, and the author notes that the shaded plots' higher family-labour use is what drives down their net income relative to full-sun coffee, even though cash costs were similar [ev_project_cost_pinoar14_1]. The Indian figure averages cultivation cost (seedlings, fertiliser, pesticide, irrigation, labour, machinery) over a multi-year trial and mixes establishment and recurrent items together, so it is a broad cost-of-production figure rather than a narrowly defined recurring cost [ev_project_cost_biswas22_1].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.mechanism: The compiler of the Burkina Faso WOCAT sheet on assisted natural regeneration of degraded land judged that the technology copes well with local rainstorm [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1358_2017_local_rainstorm].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.conditionality: The cell rests on a single practitioner judgement from a documented technology sheet in low-income Burkina Faso, not measured damage, and the rating itself describes good coping [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1358_2017_local_rainstorm].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.mechanism: Fire is named among the factors behind the lack of regeneration in ageing agroforestry parklands, alongside climate change, grazing, removal of spontaneous shoots and the forest code [ev_fire_hazard_seghieri19_16]. The compiler of the Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet judged that the technology copes not well with forest fire or land fire [ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_forest_fire, ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_land_fire].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.conditionality: Fire is among several listed threats and its separate effect is not measured; the parkland unit is from lower-middle-income Senegal, within the LIC/LMIC target, and concerns long-term parkland persistence [ev_fire_hazard_seghieri19_16]. The Kenyan coping ratings are practitioner judgements from the same technology sheet, not measured damage [ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_forest_fire, ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_land_fire].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.mechanism: WOCAT compilers judged assisted natural regeneration of degraded land in Burkina Faso to cope well with general river flood, and FMNR in Kenya to cope moderately with flash flood [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1358_2017_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_507_2019_flash_flood].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.conditionality: Both units are practitioner judgements on documented technology sheets, not measured damage, from regeneration practices in low-income Burkina Faso and lower-middle-income Kenya [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1358_2017_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_507_2019_flash_flood].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.mechanism: The compiler of the Burkina Faso WOCAT sheet on assisted natural regeneration of degraded land judged that the technology copes well with local windstorm [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1358_2017_local_windstorm].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a sensitivity for this cell: it is a single practitioner rating on a technology sheet from low-income Burkina Faso, about local windstorms rather than cyclones, with no measured damage, so it does not show the regenerated trees are undamaged [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1358_2017_local_windstorm]. A second independent source or one measured finding of wind damage to regenerated trees would let the cell state a sensitivity.

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__bio.mechanism: The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet rates gains in animal and habitat diversity, its compiler noting that many animal species find safe habitats in new FMNR sites and that, compared with degraded sites, FMNR sites provide more habitats in the trees or soil [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_habitat_diversity]. In Niger's Maradi region, FMNR adoption appears to raise tree diversity by between one and three species per farm and tree density by between 12 and 16 trees per hectare compared with matched non-adopters [ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1]. In Maradi's Dan Saga and Aguié villages, the same regeneration took local woody species richness from only a few types of tree in the 1980s to at least 30 tree species today, with farmers reintroducing species that had disappeared [ev_biodiversity_outcome_boton10_4].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__bio.conditionality: The Kenyan units come from a WOCAT technology sheet for FMNR in lower-middle-income Kenya and are compiler judgements comparing regenerated with degraded sites, not species surveys [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_habitat_diversity]. The Niger result is a matched comparison of adopters with non-adopters that counts tree species on farms, not wider biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1]. The evidence comes from a narrow base: Kenya and Niger only, a handful of sources in total. The same Sahelian synthesis also cautions that the biodiversity gain is not guaranteed: in some regions farmers protect Faidherbia albida with priority over other species, producing something closer to a monoculture than a diverse parkland [ev_biodiversity_outcome_boton10_5].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__car.mechanism: In Sudano-Sahelian cropland, shrubs and trees on agricultural fields had an overall positive but variable effect on soil total carbon (+ 20 to 75%), and a cited meta-analysis reports that soil under Faidherbia albida canopy holds on average 46 per cent more organic carbon than outside it [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1]. The externally audited Humbo FMNR project in Ethiopia reports CO2 sequestered since 2007 [ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT compiler adds that increasing tree cover through FMNR is one of the ways to sequester carbon in biomass [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_507_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. In Lempira, Honduras, soil organic matter under the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system, monitored for four years in three places, increased from 2.4% to 4.5% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__car.conditionality: Two literature units measure soil carbon under trees (a component of sequestration), and the Humbo figure is a project total from a World Vision self-evaluation with no per-hectare or per-year denominator [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11]. The literature is from semi-arid West Africa and Ethiopia (low- and lower-middle-income countries) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11]. The WOCAT unit is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet, not a measured stock or rate [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_507_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. Measured directly on Ethiopian wheat farms, soil organic C did not differ significantly under and outside the Faidherbia albida canopy at the end of the 2013 cropping season, so the cited 46 per cent canopy gain was not reproduced at that site; this null lowers the agreement rather than the class [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sida18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1]. The Honduran figure is soil organic matter used as a proxy for soil organic carbon, measured before and after on the same plots with no concurrent slash-and-burn control; it comes from a promoter-written grey-literature article, and the system bundles the trees with mulch, zero tillage and no burning [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__cat.mechanism: A review reports that Ilstedt et al., combining canopy interception and transpiration data of trees with their effects on water infiltration, derived an optimal intermediate tree density for parklands from a groundwater-recharge perspective; recharge is read here as a component of catchment water yield [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_vannoordwijk21_6].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__cat.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state an effect for this cell: it is one modelling result read second-hand, with no measured finding and no country, and it points to an intermediate optimum rather than more trees always raising recharge [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_vannoordwijk21_6]. A second independent source or one measured finding on water yield or recharge under regenerated farmland trees would let the cell state a class.

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__cos.mechanism: The Regreening Africa cost-efficiency analysis reports that adopting land restoration practices in Ghana, where the arm was mainly FMNR, cost $66 per household, a programme cost per adopting household [ev_project_cost_crs23_1].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__cos.conditionality: This is a programme expenditure per adopting household for one lower-middle-income country arm of one programme, so it does not pool with other sources [ev_project_cost_crs23_1]. The same quote notes FMNR in Ghana cost less per household than tree-planting agroforestry in Rwanda [ev_project_cost_crs23_1].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__cos.mechanism: The Regreening Africa cost-efficiency analysis reports that adopting land restoration practices in Ghana, mainly FMNR, cost $58 per hectare [ev_project_cost_crs23_2].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__cos.conditionality: This is a programme expenditure per hectare where at least one practice was adopted, from one lower-middle-income country arm of one programme, so it does not pool with other sources [ev_project_cost_crs23_2]. The same quote gives $1,387 per hectare for tree-planting agroforestry in Rwanda [ev_project_cost_crs23_2].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__dro.mechanism: In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. The Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates the impact of droughts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__dro.conditionality: The parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. The Kenyan FMNR unit is a compiler rating on a technology sheet, not a measurement, and neither unit puts a size on the drought benefit [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. Only the Sahelian parkland unit is recorded in an agro-pastoral system; the Kenyan rating is applied here by default [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. With two units, one a review citation and one a rating, the cell lacks any measured drought loss with and without trees.

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__dro.mechanism: On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. Hydraulic redistribution in Sahelian parklands lets crop roots use deep soil moisture reached only by tree roots [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3]. The Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__dro.conditionality: Apart from the Ethiopian paired-plot study, which is a drought-year result reported as an 'up to' figure with its normal-season gain reported separately [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2], the literature units are reviews citing earlier work, and the deep-water unit enters as a component of drought impact rather than a measured drought loss [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3]. The FMNR unit is a compiler rating of a slight benefit on a technology sheet, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__dro.mechanism: On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. Parkland hydraulic redistribution lets crops use deep soil moisture reached only by tree roots [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3], and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__dro.conditionality: The Ethiopian paired-plot study is the measured result here: a drought-year comparison reported as an 'up to' figure, with the normal-season gain reported separately in the same study [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. The other literature unit is a review describing a soil-water process in West African Sahel parklands, used as a component of drought impact rather than a measured drought loss [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3]. The FMNR unit is a single compiler rating of a slight benefit, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__dro.mechanism: In Senegal's sylvopastoral zone, tree leaves, fruits and pods make up about 40 per cent of cattle diet and 80 per cent of small-ruminant diet in the run-up to the rains [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21]. The Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__dro.conditionality: The Senegal diet-share estimate is a second-hand figure entering as a component of drought impact rather than a measured drought loss [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21]. The Kenyan FMNR unit is a compiler rating of a slight benefit, not a measurement, and is applied to pastoral rangeland by default [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The Honduran point is an earlier observation cited in an ICRAF working paper, and it does not come from a pastoral rangeland system, so it is applied here by default [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__dro.mechanism: Two sources point to a slight reduction in drought damage. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet rates drought impacts as decreased, its compiler judging that FMNR improves the micro-climate and soil moisture and therefore mitigates the impact of droughts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__dro.conditionality: The cell is thin: one compiler judgement on a WOCAT technology sheet from lower-middle-income Kenya [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts] and one promoter-written practitioner account from Honduras. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. Neither unit puts a size on the benefit or measures drought losses with and without the practice in a controlled comparison; an independent measured study is what is missing.

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__est.mechanism: The Regreening Africa cost-efficiency analysis reports that adopting land restoration practices in Ghana, where the arm was mainly FMNR, cost $66 per household, a programme cost per adopting household [ev_project_cost_crs23_1].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__est.conditionality: The figure is a programme cost per adopting household, not a per-hectare establishment cost, so it fits this indicator only loosely and comes from one country arm [ev_project_cost_crs23_1]. The same quote notes FMNR in Ghana cost less per household than tree-planting agroforestry in Rwanda [ev_project_cost_crs23_1].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__fir.mechanism: The only evidence is the compiler of the Kenyan WOCAT sheet on Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR), who comments that tree cover can increase the risk of major wildfires and advises fire breaks for larger FMNR sites [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_507_2019_fire_risk].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__fir.conditionality: The cell rests on a single practitioner judgement from a documented technology sheet in lower-middle-income Kenya, not a measured change in fire occurrence or damage [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_507_2019_fire_risk]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__flo.mechanism: The only evidence is the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR), who states that it also mitigates the impact of annual floods on crops and settlements [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_507_2019_flood_impacts].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__flo.conditionality: This is a single compiler rating on a technology sheet, not a measurement [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_507_2019_flood_impacts]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__flo.mechanism: The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet rates flood impacts as decreased, its compiler noting that FMNR also mitigates the impact of annual floods on crops and settlements [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_507_2019_flood_impacts].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__flo.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a class: the cell rests on a single compiler judgement on a WOCAT technology sheet from lower-middle-income Kenya, not a measured reduction in flood damage; a further independent source or a measured finding is what is missing [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_507_2019_flood_impacts].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__foo.mechanism: Across regeneration-based farmland (FMNR), several sources find fewer households going hungry. A World Vision meta-brief across seven African and one Timorese project catchments found project participants reported significantly fewer months of food shortage, by 0.26 months, than non-participants [ev_food_security_wvfmnr19_9]. In Senegal, only 3% of FMNR adopters failed to meet annual food needs for more than 4 months in one zone, against 14% of non-adopters, and 0% versus 4% in another zone [ev_food_security_seghieri19_13]. In the Sahel, moving from low-intensity to young-level FMNR raised the household food consumption score by about 12% [ev_food_security_bina15_7]. In Ghana's Talensi project, households with sufficient diet diversity rose from 44.5% at baseline to 55.8% at endline, and households with one or more hungry months in the previous year fell from 68.2% to 41%, though this project bundled FMNR with savings groups, post-harvest storage and value-chain and livestock work, so the gain is not attributable to FMNR alone [ev_food_security_talensi21_3, ev_food_security_talensi21_4]. A WOCAT compiler for Kenyan FMNR rates food security and self-sufficiency improved, reasoning that more diversified livelihoods reduce the risk of food insecurity [ev_food_security_wocat_507_2019_food_security_selfsufficiency]. In Niger, during the 2005 food crisis, farmers practising the regeneration were less severely affected than other farmers and recorded relatively lower infant mortality, through income from selling wood and other forest products [ev_food_security_boton10_2].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__foo.conditionality: The class stays slight rather than higher because some units find no effect: in Niger, FMNR does not appear to reduce the number of months of perceived food shortage, though it does seem to raise crop diversity, and in the Sahel the number of months with a household food deficit showed no significant effect for any FMNR intensity, with resilience during shortages read by the authors as an inference rather than a measured result [ev_food_security_haglund11_1, ev_food_security_bina15_9]. The Sahel food-consumption-score gain from low to continuous FMNR was also not significant [ev_food_security_bina15_8]. The Talensi gains are a World Vision self-evaluation, before-and-after with no control group and an acknowledged change in sampling, and the project itself attributes part of the hungry-months improvement to better food storage rather than FMNR [ev_food_security_talensi21_3, ev_food_security_talensi21_4]; the World Vision multi-country figure likewise notes the FMNR effect cannot be fully disentangled from other project activities [ev_food_security_wvfmnr19_9]. The WOCAT rating is a compiler's assessment on a technology sheet, not a measurement [ev_food_security_wocat_507_2019_food_security_selfsufficiency]. All units sit in low, lower-middle and LIC/LMIC-pooled African and Timorese contexts, in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_food_security_wvfmnr19_9, ev_food_security_seghieri19_13, ev_food_security_talensi21_3].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__gen.mechanism: A CILSS regional synthesis reports that, in Niger's re-greened farmer-managed natural regeneration zones, the increase in on-farm trees has, in many cases, sharply cut the time women spend collecting firewood for the household: from an average of 2.5 hours a day twenty years ago to 0.5 hour a day now [ev_gender_inequity_botreij09_34].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__gen.conditionality: The row carries this one evidence unit from one source: a regional synthesis citing a national study team's report, a before/after regional account with no control village and no measure of how the saved time was used. A second independent source, or one measured finding against a control, would let this cell state a class [ev_gender_inequity_botreij09_34].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__hea.mechanism: In Senegal's Ferlo, air under Acacia tortilis ranged between 29 °C and 36 °C against 26 °C and 42 °C outside [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, maximum daily temperature fell by an average of 1–2.5 °C and minimum air humidity rose by up to 5%, with stronger differences on hotter and drier days [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__hea.conditionality: The Senegal units come from a review citing earlier studies and the Sahelian parkland figure is likewise a cited result; both report canopy-air temperature rather than a direct livelihood outcome [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__hea.mechanism: Parkland trees cool crops and livestock: midday air temperature under Faidherbia albida canopies on Ethiopian wheat farms was up to 6°C lower than in the open field, peaking at 29 °C under the canopy against 36 °C outside [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1]. In the same Ethiopian study, a crop model found that the lower temperature under F. albida shade raised simulated wheat yield when nitrogen was applied, but without applied N simulated yield was extremely small and did not respond to temperature [ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. In Senegal's Ferlo, air under Acacia tortilis ranged between 29 °C and 36 °C against 26 °C and 42 °C outside [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, maximum daily temperature fell by an average of 1–2.5 °C and minimum air humidity rose by up to 5%, with stronger differences on hotter and drier days [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__hea.conditionality: The Ethiopian cooling was measured directly on farm; the other units are reviews citing earlier studies, and all report canopy temperature or animal comfort, entering as components of heat-stress impact [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2]. The yield link is modelled rather than measured, and the model's null without applied N is the no-benefit result that discounts the class: on unfertilised wheat the cooling did not carry through to simulated yield [ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__hea.mechanism: Faidherbia albida parkland trees on Ethiopian wheat farms lowered midday air temperature by up to 6°C against the open field: it peaked at 36 °C in the open and at 29 °C under the canopy, and exceeded 28 °C for about six hours a day in the open against less than two hours under the trees [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1]. A crop model in the same study found that this cooling raised simulated wheat yield when nitrogen was applied [ev_crop_yield_sida18_3].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__hea.conditionality: Without applied N, simulated wheat yield was extremely small and did not respond to temperature, so the benefit depends on fertilisation; this modelled null is the no-benefit result that discounts the class [ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. All units come from a single Ethiopian on-farm study in low-income rainfed cropping, within the LIC/LMIC target; the cooling was measured, the yield response modelled [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_3].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__hea.mechanism: Faidherbia albida parkland trees on Ethiopian wheat farms lowered midday air temperature by up to 6°C, peaking at 29 °C under the canopy against 36 °C in the open field, and in Senegal's Ferlo air temperatures under Acacia tortilis ranged between 29 °C and 36 °C against 26 °C to 42 °C outside the cover [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, maximum daily temperature fell by an average of 1–2.5 °C and minimum air humidity rose by up to 5%, with stronger differences on hotter and drier days [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__hea.conditionality: These are temperature measurements under tree canopies (the Ethiopian one measured on farm, the Senegalese and Sahelian ones cited from earlier studies), linked to heat stress through microclimate buffering rather than a measured heat-stress outcome [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2]. They come from low-income Ethiopia, lower-middle-income Senegal and the wider Sahel [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__pro.mechanism: Regeneration-based agroforestry (farmer-managed natural regeneration and similar on-farm tree regrowth) raises farm productivity mainly through soil-fertility gains under scattered trees and diversified tree products, not necessarily through higher grain yield directly beneath the trees — in Niger, farmer-managed natural regeneration did not significantly increase grain yields, with the added value instead coming from higher yields of other crops such as cowpea. In Niger, millet yields on fields with regenerated trees (100 to 370 kg/ha) were higher than on control fields without trees (50 to 270 kg/ha), a gain of 50 to 100 kg/ha the authors attribute to tree presence, and the same protected trees supply dry-season fodder that eases the feed shortage common at that time of year [ev_crop_yield_boton10_1, ev_forage_productivity_boton10_7].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__pro.conditionality: Two sources measured harm: cereal yield reductions have been observed under specific tree species in the Sahel, and groundnut yields fell under one native tree's canopy. Effects vary strongly by tree species and distance from the trunk — some species are associated with cereal yield gains, others with losses — and a modelled Ethiopian trial found wheat yield did not respond to temperature change without added nitrogen, so the benefit depends on fertility management as much as on regeneration itself.

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__rur.mechanism: FMNR and related regeneration-based farmland raise rural household income through tree products and diversified livelihoods. In the Sahel, moving from low to continuous Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) practice is associated with an increase in gross household income per capita of about 13%, through sale and own use of fuelwood, fodder, fruit, leaves and other products from the regenerated trees, and moving from low to new/young practice with a 10% increase in gross income through the same pathway [ev_household_income_bina15_2, ev_household_income_bina15_1]. In Niger, FMNR adoption raised gross annual household income by between 22,805 and 27,950 FCFA (46 to 56 USD) per capita, an 18 to 24% increase, with an estimated annual benefit-cost ratio of 2.5 to 3.0 and a 20-year net present value of €772/ha [ev_household_income_haglund11_1, ev_economic_return_haglund11_1, ev_economic_return_abasse23_1]. Sale of fuelwood and service wood from FMNR is reported to raise income across all social categories, including the very vulnerable [ev_household_income_abasse23_1]; a separate estimate put the annual value of FMNR, through improved soil fertility, firewood, fodder and other products, at US$56 per hectare in Niger [ev_economic_return_wvfmnr19_7], and the social return on investment of a Ghanaian FMNR project at US$655-887 per household per year [ev_economic_return_wvfmnr19_8]. In Senegal, FMNR-adopting households gained on average 72.65 USD per season from selling non-timber forest products, against 29.73 USD for non-adopters [ev_household_income_seghieri19_12]. In Honduras, farmers using the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system gained a new income stream from renting their land for livestock grazing, because the system produces more stover [ev_household_income_welc02_7]. Across its project countries, a World Vision meta-analysis found participants 15 percentage points more likely than non-participants to report an increase in household income and nine percentage points more likely to report a decrease in community poverty, an effect reported similarly by poorer households, female-headed households and female respondents [ev_household_income_wvfmnr19_5, ev_rural_poverty_wvfmnr19_10]. A WOCAT compiler for Kenyan FMNR rates farm income increased, noting diversified income from wood, honey, medicinal products and other non-wood products [ev_household_income_wocat_507_2019_farm_income]. A CILSS regional synthesis adds further Sahelian returns. For protecting natural regeneration on farmland in Niger, the internal rate of return was 31 percent, built from an initial investment of about 24 person-days of labour per hectare (1,000 FCFA per day, so 24,000 FCFA to start) against 20 years of wood production and a 5 percent millet and stalk gain in the first 4 years; fodder and soil-fertility benefits were left out of the calculation, so the authors consider the return an underestimate [ev_economic_return_botreij09_28]. On Burkina Faso's Central Plateau, farmer-managed natural regeneration returned an internal rate of 24 percent [ev_economic_return_botreij09_33]. A separate Sahelian estimate puts a Nigerien farmer's wood-sales income from the regeneration at more than 100 000 FCFA of fuelwood and construction wood after 5 years, rising as the regeneration ages [ev_household_income_boton10_8].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__rur.conditionality: Against this, the same World Vision multi-country meta-analysis finds Uganda a clear outlier: participant households there were significantly less likely to report income improvements, which the authors attribute partly to participants being poorer households with different income-generation opportunities — the practice worsening the outcome for some adopters, counted here as measured harm [ev_household_income_wvfmnr19_6]. Several Sahel income gains are not statistically significant under the authors' own 5% convention (the 10% and 13% gross-income figures, and the low-to-young tree-product-value gain), though the authors describe them as increases [ev_household_income_bina15_1, ev_household_income_bina15_2, ev_household_income_bina15_4]. The Honduran and Ghanaian/Nigerien World Vision figures are grey-literature project self-evaluations or practitioner articles by project-promoter staff, with a positive-bias discount, and the World Vision brief itself states the FMNR effect cannot be fully disentangled from other project activities [ev_household_income_welc02_7, ev_economic_return_wvfmnr19_7, ev_economic_return_wvfmnr19_8, ev_household_income_wvfmnr19_5]. All units sit in low and lower-middle-income Sub-Saharan African, South Asian and Southeast Asian contexts (Niger, Burkina Faso, Mali, Senegal, Honduras, Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, Timor-Leste), in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_household_income_haglund11_1, ev_household_income_bina15_1, ev_household_income_welc02_7, ev_household_income_wvfmnr19_5]. Both are internal-rate-of-return figures from project tables with no significance test, read ordinally rather than compared in absolute terms with the currency figures elsewhere in this row [ev_economic_return_botreij09_28, ev_economic_return_botreij09_33].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__soi.mechanism: Across World Vision FMNR projects, participants were 10 percent points more likely than non-participants to report a reduction in erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_wvfmnr19_3]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT compiler adds that, due to less wind and water erosion, the siltation of ponds and water pans is reduced [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. During Hurricane Mitch in October 1998, Honduran farmers practising the Quesungual system suffered less landslide damage than those using traditional slash-and-burn [ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual system report that soil erosion has been nearly stopped, and estimate nutrient loss through erosion at more than 10 times lower than under slash-and-burn [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4]. In Niger, farmers and reviewers describe the regenerated trees protecting against wind, reducing erosion and evaporation, and enriching the soil through litter decomposition and nutrients from livestock sheltering in their shade [ev_erosion_hazard_boton10_6].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__soi.conditionality: The World Vision result is a reported perception from a self-evaluation in which the FMNR effect cannot be fully separated from other project activities [ev_erosion_hazard_wvfmnr19_3]. The WOCAT unit is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet, not an erosion measurement, and the siltation rating enters as a component [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. The Honduran landslide result is an earlier observation cited in a working paper, for a slash-and-mulch system under very intense rainfall [ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1]. The Honduran erosion claim is a narrative from a promoter-written grey-literature article with no measured erosion rate, and the effect belongs to the whole bundle of trees, mulch cover, zero tillage and no burning [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__wat.mechanism: The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet rates reduced downstream siltation, its compiler noting that less wind and water erosion reduces the siltation of ponds and water pans [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__wat.conditionality: The cell rests on a single compiler judgement from a technology sheet in lower-middle-income Kenya, with no measurement behind it; siltation enters as a component of water-quality risk, and no unit measures water quality itself [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. What is missing is a measured sediment or water-quality comparison downstream of regenerated farmland against comparable farmland without regeneration, or a second independent source; this is a gap in the evidence, not a finding of no effect.

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__wat.mechanism: Studies of trees on regenerated farmland disagree on soil water, so no direction is stated. On the side of more water stress, under Faidherbia albida parkland in Ethiopia soil moisture in the sub-soil was the least for wheat with tree, intermediate for sole tree and the highest for open field, while the authors observed no variation in topsoil moisture content between treatments [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_2]. On the side of less, in Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual system report 23% soil humidity in the driest month (April) against 8% in a traditional slash-and-burn field, a difference equivalent to 20mm of rainfall, or 20 more days that crops can be sustained without rain; they explain it by better infiltration through the soil cover and more soil organic matter [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet also points that way, its compiler crediting an increase in water retention which increases the ground water levels [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__wat.conditionality: The sides differ in system and in what is measured. The Ethiopian result is a measured subsoil draw-down under heavily pruned parkland trees with a growing wheat crop [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]; the Honduran result is driest-month soil humidity in a slash-and-mulch system against slash-and-burn, which the authors credit to soil cover and soil organic matter [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1]; and the WOCAT unit speaks of groundwater, not crop-root-zone moisture [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. The Honduran soil-humidity figures come from a grey-literature article by the project's own promoters, report no replication or significance, and compare a bundle (trees with mulch, zero tillage and no burning) against slash-and-burn, so the trees cannot be credited alone [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1]. The WOCAT unit is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet rather than a soil-moisture measurement [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. Whether pruning or tree density changes the subsoil draw-down is not tested [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]. The cited parkland tree-density result for groundwater recharge sits in the regeneration catchment water yield row.

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__win.mechanism: Practitioner ratings on WOCAT sheets for regeneration practices in Burkina Faso and Kenya record reduced wind speed, the Kenyan compiler noting that FMNR trees serve as a windbreak protecting houses, greenhouses and crop fields against heavy winds [ev_windbreak_protection_wocat_1358_2017_wind_velocity, ev_windbreak_protection_wocat_507_2019_wind_velocity].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__win.conditionality: Both units are compiler judgements of wind speed on documented technology sheets for regeneration practices in low-income Burkina Faso and lower-middle-income Kenya, not measured storm or cyclone losses [ev_windbreak_protection_wocat_1358_2017_wind_velocity, ev_windbreak_protection_wocat_507_2019_wind_velocity].

agroforestry__rural_poverty.mechanism: Agroforestry raises rural household income mainly through diversified and higher-value production. Pooling adoption studies across 13 Sub-Saharan African countries, agroforestry adoption had a positive effect on income of 0.28 (Cohen's d, 95% confidence interval 0.13 to 0.44) [ev_household_income_jemaneh26_1]; a broader pooled estimate across contexts found a smaller effect of 0.12 standardized mean difference, with a 95% confidence interval of −0.06 to 0.30 [ev_household_income_castle21s_1]. In western Kenya, fallow systems returned $2.17 per labour-day, 33% higher than continuous maize cropping with no inputs [ev_economic_return_place05_3]. A separate Sahelian estimate puts a Nigerien farmer's wood-sales income from the regeneration at more than 100 000 FCFA of fuelwood and construction wood after 5 years, rising as the regeneration ages [ev_household_income_boton10_8].
agroforestry__rural_poverty.conditionality: The gains are not universal. In China, fruit-tree/crop intercropping measured a −0.29 reduction in household income (95% CI −0.52 to −0.07) tied to lost off-farm income and tree-crop competition, against a +0.52 gain found elsewhere in the same review for a Kenyan climate-vulnerability agroforestry programme [ev_household_income_castle21s_2]. A pan-tropical review of cocoa agroforestry found that, although total system production was higher under shade trees, this was not reflected in higher revenues, net present values, or lower costs [ev_economic_return_niether20_1]. Measured harm (maladaptation) — the practice reducing income for some adopters — appears in 10 sources.

agroforestry__rural_poverty__farming_sys.mechanism: In irrigated cropland, trees bring returns from wood, fodder or fruit on top of the crop. A Senegalese review cites Fall et al. (2002) estimating that in the Senegal River valley a windbreak hedge in irrigated rice had an internal rate of return of 36 per cent, or 58 per cent when the woody products of the hedge were counted (Satin, 1998) [ev_economic_return_faosen24_15]. In canal-irrigated waterlogged fields at Hisar, India, a biodrainage study by Ram et al. found a benefit-cost ratio of 3.5:1 for the first rotation of Eucalyptus boundary strips, well above the 1.3:1 the same authors report for ordinary agricultural crops in Haryana, with returns from selling the trees after only an initial planting and maintenance cost [ev_economic_return_ram11_4]. In a drip-irrigated trial in Xinjiang, China, juvenile plumcot trees intercropped with alfalfa or soybean gave a higher average cash flow than the corresponding sole crops [ev_economic_return_wang23_1].
agroforestry__rural_poverty__farming_sys.conditionality: How big the poverty effect is cannot be stated: the units report returns on investment or cash flow, components of household income rather than measured poverty change. The Senegalese figure is an earlier study read second-hand in a review [ev_economic_return_faosen24_15]. The Indian figure now comes from the original Ram et al. study rather than a second-hand reading, but it is still a single planting's first-rotation harvest, not a repeated or ongoing return [ev_economic_return_ram11_4]. The Chinese trial covers only the establishment years, and in the same trial the intercropped soybean and alfalfa yielded much less than sole crops, so the cash-flow gain comes from the fruit trees rather than from the crop [ev_economic_return_wang23_1]. The evidence comes from lower-middle-income Senegal and India and upper-middle-income China.

agroforestry__rural_poverty__farming_sys.mechanism: In Senegal's southern-centre groundnut basin, households practising intensive FMNR earned on average 72.65 USD per season from selling non-timber products against 29.73 USD for other households [ev_household_income_seghieri19_12]. In southern Malawi, under higher fertiliser prices the value-cost ratio of a Tephrosia vogelii relay intercrop with maize stayed above 4.0, which the authors call a profitable scenario, while the higher prices pulled monoculture maize down to 2.5 or less [ev_economic_return_snapp10_1].
agroforestry__rural_poverty__farming_sys.conditionality: Income and returns stand in for poverty here rather than measuring it, and the strength of the effect is not quantified against a poverty measure. The Senegal figures are an adopter versus non-adopter survey comparison with no stated significance test, taken from an English abstract inside a French volume, and the Malawian ratio is a fertiliser-price scenario on on-farm trial data rather than measured household income [ev_household_income_seghieri19_12, ev_economic_return_snapp10_1]. The FMNR and Tephrosia results come from different sub-practices, regeneration-based farmland in Senegal and a planted relay intercrop in Malawi, which agree in direction only.

agroforestry__rural_poverty__farming_sys.mechanism: In Rwanda, tree products are a safety net: food-insecure farmers more often sold tree products for income than food-secure farmers, and tree density was positively associated with food security in some agroecologies [ev_household_income_ndoli21_1, ev_food_security_ndoli21_1]. In Nyando District, Kenya, agroforestry-project households typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods, sold fuel wood and timber to buy food during the drought, relied on tree fruit when floods washed crops away, and in Lower Nyando held more livestock wealth than control households [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_1, ev_household_income_thorlak12_2].
agroforestry__rural_poverty__farming_sys.conditionality: The Rwandan effect varied by agroecology: more trees went with higher food security in Congo Nile but lower food security in the Buberuka Highlands [ev_food_security_ndoli21_2]. The Lower Nyando livestock-wealth difference, used by the authors as an income surrogate, was not significant at conventional levels, and the timber-sales and flood-fruit findings are farmer-reported [ev_household_income_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_1]. Household income, wealth and food security are used here as proxies for rural poverty, and the Rwandan units are cross-sectional associations rather than a comparison during a shock [ev_household_income_ndoli21_1, ev_food_security_ndoli21_1, ev_household_income_thorlak12_2].

agroforestry__rural_poverty__farming_sys.mechanism: In pastoral rangeland systems, silvopastoral conversion mostly pays once established. In Peru and Colombia, an intensive silvopastoral system had an operating benefit-cost ratio of 2.8 against 1.34 for a traditional system [ev_economic_return_saucedo23_1]. In the Colombian Amazon, producer income from milk sales rose 42.12 percent under an intensive silvopastoral system owing to its higher carrying capacity of 2.71 against 1.84 animal units for the intensive system and grass monoculture respectively [ev_household_income_montagnini15_1]. In Nicaragua, a modelled 20-hectare beef and dairy farm found silvopastoral net income overtaking traditional pasture income only in the fifth year after establishment [ev_economic_return_diasf08_2].
agroforestry__rural_poverty__farming_sys.conditionality: Against this, in Brazil a review of barriers to silvopastoral adoption states that, for this reason, farm income in the first years after establishing a silvopastoral system would be comparatively lower than under traditional pasture [ev_economic_return_diasf08_1]. The Brazilian and Nicaraguan units are an expert review and a modelled single-farm case rather than measured trials, the Peru-Colombia benefit-cost ratio is cited within a systematic review, and the milk-income gain already carries the cattle-stocking change that drives it, so the finding is reported as an establishment-phase income dip followed by a payback once the system matures [ev_economic_return_diasf08_1, ev_economic_return_diasf08_2].

agroforestry__rural_poverty__farming_sys.mechanism: Returns in tree-perennial agroforestry have been reported both above and below the alternative. In Bolivia the return on labour over the years was almost twice as high in agroforestry systems as in monocultures [ev_economic_return_dsantos23_7]. In a Brazilian system at Tomé-Açu, the rice component showed negative economic performance and black pepper was unprofitable in low-price cycles [ev_economic_return_ferraz24_6].
agroforestry__rural_poverty__farming_sys.conditionality: The two units measure different things: the Bolivian gain is a whole-system return per day of labour against monoculture, while the Brazilian loss is the performance of single components, which the authors say need adjustment in production, technology or management, and which depends on price cycles [ev_economic_return_dsantos23_7, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_6]. Component choice and exposure to price swings are therefore what a project would need to check. Both units are reviews citing earlier studies with no effect sizes and measure returns as a proxy, not poverty; they come from Bolivia (lower-middle income) and Brazil (upper-middle) [ev_economic_return_dsantos23_7, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_6].

agroforestry__rural_poverty__income_grou.mechanism: Agroforestry adds income and food through tree products and yields: FMNR in Niger is valued at US$56 per hectare a year in soil fertility, firewood, fodder and other products, FMNR-adopting households in Senegal earn 72.65 USD per season from non-timber products against 29.73 USD for others, and calliandra fodder raises farmers' net income in Kenya and Uganda by about US$ 101–122 a year by replacing dairy meal [ev_economic_return_wvfmnr19_7, ev_household_income_seghieri19_12, ev_household_income_kiptot11_1]. Food-security gains include a dietary diversity score raised by 1.22 under Vi Agroforestry advice in Kenya, food crop value raised by 35% by fertilizer trees in Malawi, fewer months of food shortage among FMNR participants, and diet diversity rising with use of tree products [ev_food_security_castle21s_1, ev_t6_foodsec_ferttree_castle21_8, ev_food_security_wvfmnr19_9, ev_food_security_rgaf23_10]. A systematic review concludes that incomes improved through higher yields, payments for ecosystem services or higher prices from eco-certification [ev_t6_income_pathway_castle21_5].
agroforestry__rural_poverty__income_grou.conditionality: The pooled income effect is small and not significant (0.12 SMD, 95% CI -0.06 to 0.30), the meta-analysis ratios for revenue, profit and benefit-cost are not significant, and several units are null: tree-product income per household stayed at USD 82 PPP, food-insecurity scores barely changed, income change was not expected within the programme period, and improved fallows did not translate into household welfare on small farms [ev_household_income_castle21s_1, ev_economic_return_steward23wp_1, ev_economic_return_steward23wp_2, ev_economic_return_steward23wp_3, ev_household_income_rgaf23_6, ev_food_security_rgaf23_9, ev_household_income_crs23_5, ev_household_income_place05_2]. One unit points the other way: in Uganda, FMNR participants, who were often the poorer households, were less likely to report income gains [ev_household_income_wvfmnr19_6]. All evidence is from LIC/LMIC settings, but most units measure proxies for poverty (income, returns, food security) rather than poverty itself, and some results are bundled project outcomes or modelled scenarios, such as the Talensi diet and hungry-month changes and a Nigerian climate model [ev_economic_return_wvfmnr19_7, ev_food_security_castle21s_1, ev_food_security_talensi21_3, ev_food_security_talensi21_4, ev_household_income_watts22_14].

agroforestry__rural_poverty__income_grou.mechanism: Household income and economic returns stand in for poverty in this evidence, and they move in both directions. Gains: an integrative review of Brazilian family-farm agroforestry viability studies found all indices positive, with internal rates of return always above 7% and benefit-cost ratios above 1, most between 1.20 and 2.50 and some above 3.00; individual systems in Pará reached a benefit-cost ratio of 2.5 and an internal rate of return of 15%, or cleared a 10% hurdle rate [ev_economic_return_ferraz24_1, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_2, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_7, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_8]. In Colombia, silvopasture raised income through better animal nutrition, productivity and fertility and higher carrying capacity: a Bank-commissioned business case estimates up to US$523/ha more annual income with production costs US$127/ha lower, intensive silvopasture had an operating benefit-cost ratio of 2.8 against 1.34, milk-sale income was 42.12% higher than under pasture monoculture, and Caquetá farms in silvopastoral projects saw higher income from animal sales [ev_household_income_cmscr20_6, ev_economic_return_saucedo23_1, ev_household_income_montagnini15_1, ev_household_income_bur24_1]. A Brazilian review also cites potential to raise profitability in municipalities prone to climate variation [ev_economic_return_ribeiro22_2]. Losses: crop–fruit tree intercropping in Xinjiang, China lowered gross household income (−0.29 SMD) [ev_household_income_castle21s_2]; silvopasture income lags traditional pasture in the first years after establishment [ev_economic_return_diasf08_1]; an organic agroforestry system in Paraná collapsed from the seventh year through lack of long-term management and planning, the rice component at Tomé-Açu lost money and black pepper did so in low-price cycles, and a multistrata coconut, lemon, passionfruit, cowpea and cassava system gave the lowest return of those assessed [ev_economic_return_ferraz24_5, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_6, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_9]. For Indonesian social-forestry permits, profitability was no better for permit holders than for households without one [ev_economic_return_castle21s_4].
