agroforestry__rural_poverty__income_grou.conditionality: What separates the sides, where the evidence says: time since establishment, since silvopasture income lags in the early years and the Colombian completion report found no measured poverty reduction at closing because many systems were still being established and effects could not be separated from drought [ev_economic_return_diasf08_1, ev_rural_poverty_cmscr20_9]; long-term management and planning, the stated cause of the Paraná collapse [ev_economic_return_ferraz24_5]; the choice of components and their prices, with rice and black pepper losing and one multistrata mix earning least [ev_economic_return_ferraz24_6, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_9]; and system type, with the Colombian silvopasture gains set against the Xinjiang crop–fruit tree intercropping loss [ev_household_income_castle21s_2]. For a Task Team Leader the practical points are to plan for an establishment-period income gap and to vet component choice and long-term management. On evidence quality, the gain side leans on grey-literature Brazilian viability studies, earlier results cited in reviews, a modelled business case for the US$523/ha figure, and a brief with no effect size [ev_economic_return_ferraz24_1, ev_household_income_cmscr20_6, ev_household_income_bur24_1, ev_economic_return_saucedo23_1, ev_household_income_montagnini15_1]; the Xinjiang loss is a quantified estimate from a systematic review, while the other losses are narrative case reports. All units measure income or returns rather than poverty itself.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__asset_th.mechanism: In cabruca cocoa agroforests in southern Bahia, Brazil, the El Niño drought of 2015 and 2016 killed 15% of cocoa trees against under 1% normally and 7% of the 317 woody shade trees, with no shade-tree species particularly affected; potential yield fell from 242 to 26 kg/ha, an 89% reduction, and was still 83% lower nine months after the drought ended [ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_1, ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__asset_th.conditionality: The engine sets the threat class at high, but the whole row is one observational study of one drought event in Bahia [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1]. It has no unshaded comparator, so it shows the damage to the shaded system, not that shade caused it. Cocoa units are crop-specific and enter under the shaded-perennial crop-scope ruling. Brazil is upper-middle income, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_1]. No second independent drought study of a shaded perennial system is in the pool, and none from a low- or lower-middle-income country.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__asset_th.mechanism: A tropics review, citing earlier studies, reports that flooding increases tree mortality in cacao agroforests, with older systems potentially more vulnerable [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_6].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__asset_th.conditionality: The two units point different ways: a coconut review from Kerala, India, reports second-hand that the coconut palm withstands typhoons and flooding [ev_flood_hazard_kumar22_2], while the cacao mortality finding is the least robust grade in the review's own scheme [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_6]. Both are second-hand readings and crop-specific, entering under the shaded-perennial crop-scope ruling; neither measures how much damage a flood does. India is lower-middle income [ev_flood_hazard_kumar22_2].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__asset_th.mechanism: In shaded coffee in Soconusco, Chiapas, Mexico, a field study found minimal vegetation damage as a result of the hurricane, and no small landslides within the study plots [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_7]. A coconut review from Kerala, India, reports, citing earlier work, that the coconut palm can withstand natural calamities like typhoons and flooding [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_kumar22_1].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__asset_th.conditionality: The measured finding comes from a single hurricane whose winds the unit records as mild, so it does not show shaded perennials withstand a severe cyclone [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_7]. The coconut statement is a second-hand review claim about the palm itself, not a measurement [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_kumar22_1]. Both are crop-specific and enter under the shaded-perennial crop-scope ruling. Mexico is upper-middle income and India lower-middle income, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_7, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_kumar22_1].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__biodiver.mechanism: In shaded coffee and cacao systems, more structurally complex agroforestry supports more species than simpler, intensified alternatives. A ten-country cocoa meta-analysis found cocoa agroforestry held a significantly higher number of animal species, pooled across taxa, than cocoa monoculture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1]. A review of shaded coffee systems found bird diversity 120 to 306% higher in three shaded coffee systems of varying complexity than in conventional coffee [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2]. Comparing coffee/cacao agroforest against a more intensified sparse-shade plantation, a response-ratio study found total species richness and forest-species richness both significantly higher under agroforest [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_2]. Along a Mexican coffee-intensification gradient (forest, traditional polyculture, commercial polyculture, shaded monoculture), estimated ant, butterfly and bird richness was higher at the less-intensified, more complex-shade end of the gradient that agroforestry occupies [ev_biodiversity_outcome_perf05_1].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__biodiver.conditionality: Set against the gains, the same response-ratio study found coffee/cacao agroforest itself held significantly lower richness than standing natural forest — 11% lower for total species richness and 35% lower for forest-species richness — so the biodiversity benefit is relative to a more intensified system, not to the forest it may have replaced [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_4]. In Cameroon, cocoa yields above 1 t/ha were not attainable with more than 10 associated tree species, a direct trade-off between tree diversity and cocoa yield that growers face as they add species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seghieri19_7]. Most units describe a significant difference without naming every taxon or giving a consistent metric across studies, and the certification, intensification-gradient and cocoa meta-analysis evidence does not enumerate study countries in the cited text, so the row sits in_context with, but is not a close match for, the LIC/LMIC target as a whole [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_1].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__carbon_s.mechanism: Carbon sequestration potential needs a net greenhouse-gas balance: carbon dioxide removed in biomass and soil, minus any methane and nitrous oxide the system emits. Most of what this cell's evidence measures is only one part of that balance, a biomass or soil carbon stock. A pan-tropical cocoa meta-analysis found 2.5 times more total biomass carbon in agroforestry than in monoculture [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1], and East African perennial tree-crop systems held an average of 29.9 Mg of carbon per hectare aboveground [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_4]. But a synthesis of agroforestry methane and nitrous oxide data found that shifting to shaded perennial-crop systems can increase net soil methane emissions rather than reduce them, because nitrogen from nitrogen-fixing shade trees can inhibit the soil bacteria that oxidise methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_kim16_4]. Only one unit in this row states a net greenhouse-gas balance that combines carbon removals with methane and nitrous oxide: a modelled estimate for Ghanaian cocoa of a 127% greater GHG removal under moderate shade than under near-full-sun management [ev_carbon_sequestration_hawkins24_1].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__carbon_s.conditionality: Because almost all of the row's units report only a carbon-stock or single-gas figure, they cannot set the cell's class: a higher biomass-carbon stock is not evidence of a higher net removal once a system's methane and nitrous oxide emissions are counted, and the one unit that does report the combined balance is a model, not a field measurement. A measured net greenhouse-gas balance for a shaded perennial-crop system, or a second independent source backing the Ghana model, would let this cell state a class.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__cost_red.mechanism: In southern Rwanda, sowing the legume shrub Tephrosia vogelii between rows of smallholder coffee and using it as mulch required 30 man-days ha−1 less than current farmer management because it reduced weeding, with benefit–cost ratios between 3.4 and 5.5 [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3]. A pan-tropical meta-analysis of cocoa agroforestry against full-sun cocoa monocultures found that the higher total system production of agroforestry is not reflected in revenues, net present values or production costs: costs did not differ significantly between the systems [ev_project_cost_niether20_1].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__cost_red.conditionality: The sources point in different directions for different reasons: the Rwandan saving comes from weed suppression by a mulch-producing legume intercrop, not from shade trees, while the cocoa meta-analysis compares shade-tree agroforestry with full-sun monoculture and finds no significant cost difference [ev_project_cost_bucagu13_3, ev_project_cost_niether20_1]. Both are crop-specific (coffee and cocoa), from low- and lower-middle-income producing countries, and both concern recurrent production costs (labour, inputs), not establishment costs.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__drought_.mechanism: Under drought, shade over cocoa and coffee has been found to protect the crop, to compete with it for water, and to make no difference. On the protective side, in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly raised coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; a review cites a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season (Lin 2006) [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8]; and another cites low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia (Schwendenmann et al. 2010; Köhler et al. 2010) [ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11]. On the competing side, the strongest measurement is a Ghana field study of a cocoa plantation through the extreme 2015/16 El Niño drought: all cocoa plants under the shade tree Albizia ferruginea died, cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality with sap flux density cut to 115 g cm2 day1 against 170 in full sun, sap-flux recovery afterwards was 163 in full sun against 37 under Antiaris, and soil water was higher in full sun, which the authors link to strong competition for soil water [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. A review adds that under warmer, water-limited conditions tree-cacao competition can push soil moisture and cacao yields below open-sun farms (Blaser et al. 2018) [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8]. Between them sit no-effect findings: in a Ghana rainwater-suppression experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced yield decline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the Ethiopian study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in the extreme climate shock [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]; and across cabruca cocoa farms in southern Bahia, Brazil, drought yield loss was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__drought_.conditionality: Studies disagree, and what separates the sides, as far as the evidence says, is twofold. First, whether the shade trees draw on the same scarce soil water as the crop: the losses, including the Ghana die-off, are attributed to that competition [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1, ev_crop_yield_watts22_8], while the gains come with a named companion tree (Gliricidia) or a shade-management setting (canopy openness) [ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]. Shade-tree species, density and canopy management are therefore the design questions; in the Ghana study the outcome differed by shade-tree species, total loss under one and heavy loss under the other [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. Second, a higher yield under shade is not the same as protection from drought: the Ghana experiment found the better performance of cocoa under shade can only partly compensate for the reduced yield during drought episodes [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. The Ghana experiment's shade came from artificial shade nets, not shade trees, so it has no below-ground competition and its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. All units are crop-specific (cocoa or coffee) and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop. The Ghana die-off was measured in an extreme drought; most other units do not say how severe the drought was [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]. The review units are second-hand readings of earlier studies, and only the evapotranspiration figure carries a size [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11, ev_crop_yield_watts22_8]. The field units are from upper-middle-income Brazil, low-income Ethiopia and lower-middle-income Ghana; the review units record no country [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__drought_.mechanism: In a cocoa plantation in Ghana's Ashanti region, shade trees competed with cocoa for soil water through the extreme 2015/16 El Niño drought. All cocoa plants under the recommended leguminous shade tree Albizia ferruginea died; cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria, the most common shade tree, suffered 77% mortality and massive stress, with sap flux density cut to 115 g cm2 day1 against 170 in full sun; and sap-flux recovery after the drought was 163 in full sun against 37 under Antiaris. Soil water content was higher in full sun than under the shade trees, which the authors link to strong competition for soil water [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__drought_.conditionality: This is a single measured study on a single farm with a few replicate shade trees per species, so the row gives a direction only, with no size class [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. The shade-tree species is part of the result: the loss was total under Albizia and heavy under Antiaris, so other shade species, densities or pruning regimes may behave differently. The drought was extreme; the same plots were also measured through wet and normal dry periods, which separates the drought response from ordinary shade effects [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. The finding is crop-specific (cocoa) and enters under the shaded-perennial crop-scope ruling; Ghana is lower-middle income, within the LIC/LMIC target. A financed shade-cocoa system in a drought-prone area carries this as a risk to the planted asset and the crop.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__flood__a.mechanism: The only evidence is a review's second-hand statement that in Mesoamerica coffee-based agroforestry can help prevent flood occurrences, reducing the adverse impact of extreme rainfall events [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__flood__a.conditionality: This single unit is crop-specific (coffee) and enters because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; it records no country or income group and no measured flood loss [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__flood__t.mechanism: The only evidence is a review's second-hand statement that in Mesoamerica coffee-based agroforestry can help prevent flood occurrences, reducing the adverse impact of extreme rainfall events [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__flood__t.conditionality: This single unit is crop-specific (coffee) and enters because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; it records no country or income group and no measured flood loss [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__flood_ha.mechanism: A review reports, second-hand, that coffee-based agroforestry in Mesoamerica can regulate ecological services including preventing flood occurrences, helping reduce the adverse impact of extreme rainfall events [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__flood_ha.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a class: it is a single second-hand review sentence with no effect size, no country or income group, and a general claim about what coffee agroforestry can do rather than a measured flood outcome [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12]. A further independent source or a measured finding for shaded perennial systems is what is missing.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__heat_str.mechanism: Shade trees cool the understorey crop in shaded perennial systems. In cocoa agroforestry, canopy shade provides a more stable microclimate, with lower and more buffered maximum and minimum temperatures than in monoculture [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1]. A synthesis of empirical co-benefits found shade trees reduce canopy temperatures by 2 to 4 degrees Celsius, mitigating heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4], and a shaded coffee plot in Costa Rica measured a 1.7 degree Celsius reduction in maximum air temperature compared with full sun [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__heat_str.conditionality: This evidence base is limited to shaded perennial-crop systems (cocoa and coffee) and does not cover severe or extreme heat events: none of the cited sources measures mitigation under an intense heat episode, so the cooling shown here is a moderate-weather finding, not a tested defence against a heatwave.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__heat_str.mechanism: Shade trees cool the understorey crop in shaded perennial systems. In cocoa agroforestry, canopy shade provides a more stable microclimate, with lower and more buffered maximum and minimum temperatures than in monoculture [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1]. A synthesis of empirical co-benefits found shade trees reduce canopy temperatures by 2 to 4 degrees Celsius, mitigating heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4], and a shaded coffee plot in Costa Rica measured a 1.7 degree Celsius reduction in maximum air temperature compared with full sun [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__heat_str.conditionality: This evidence base is limited to shaded perennial-crop systems (cocoa and coffee) and does not cover severe or extreme heat events: none of the cited sources measures mitigation under an intense heat episode, so the cooling shown here is a moderate-weather finding, not a tested defence against a heatwave.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__heat_str.mechanism: In shaded perennial-crop systems specifically, canopy shade lowers temperature around the crop. Oil-palm alleys intercropped with black pepper or cacao in Malaysia cooled air by 1.3 degrees Celsius and soil surface by 2.1 degrees Celsius against a 15-year monoculture [ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_3]; studies of tropical agroforestry under canopy trees averaging 20 metres tall found a temperature reduction of about 2 degrees Celsius compared with a site without trees [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_2]; and a synthesis of empirical co-benefits found shade trees reduce canopy temperatures by 2 to 4 degrees Celsius, mitigating heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__heat_str.conditionality: As in the wider tree-perennial evidence, the benefit is not universal: in the same Malaysian trial, alleys intercropped with bamboo or bactris palm were significantly hotter than the monocultures, judged unsuitable intercrops because of the increased air temperature [ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_4], and a Mexican coffee shade-gradient study found no significant difference in mean temperature between high- and low-shade sites in either season [ev_microclimate_buffering_lin07_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_lin07_2]. None of the units measures mitigation under a severe or extreme heat event.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__producti.mechanism: Within shaded perennial-crop systems (coffee, cocoa, coconut), the crop's yield response to the shade trees runs both ways depending on shade density and the companion species. Coffee under 40-60% Erythrina shade cover produced 41% fewer fruits per bush than coffee under a maximum of 20% shade cover [ev_crop_yield_villa20_1]; a pan-tropical cocoa meta-analysis found cocoa bean yield 25% lower in agroforestry than monoculture, though total system yield was about ten times higher once the other products are counted [ev_crop_yield_niether20_1]; and in Bolivia, full-sun cacao monocultures were 41% more productive in cacao alone than agroforestry, attributed to greater light reaching the trees [ev_crop_yield_armengot16_1]. Against this, intercropping coconut with pasture grasses, black pepper and coffee was reported to increase coconut nut yield in Sri Lanka [ev_crop_yield_kumar22_1], and in Rwanda, intercropping coffee with nitrogen-fixing Tephrosia mulch raised coffee yield by 23% to 36% [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_1]. In southern Brazil, coffee shaded by Mimosa scabrella trees accumulated 6584 kg/ha of clean coffee over the harvests at the lowest density of 50 trees/ha against 4340 kg/ha unshaded, a response the authors relate closely to frost damage to the productive branches and floral buds [ev_crop_yield_caramori96_1]; the same paper reports from earlier trials that excessive, permanent shade caused coffee production losses comparable to those caused by frosts, because too little light at the canopy shifts bud differentiation away from flower buds [ev_crop_yield_caramori96_2].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__producti.conditionality: As with the Bolivia cacao case, a crop-yield loss does not always mean a production loss: the same trial found that selling the plantain and banana grown alongside the cacao more than made up for the lower cacao revenue [ev_agricultural_production_value_armengot16_1]. A weak negative relationship between shade-tree diversity and coffee productivity was also reported in Nicaragua, though the authors describe it as only weakly significant [ev_crop_yield_hagg17_1]. The Brazilian shaded-coffee gain comes from a single experimental farm with one plot per treatment and no yield statistics, in an upper-middle-income subtropical setting where the benefit is frost protection, and shaded coffee was not higher in every year, so its transfer to LIC/LMIC shaded coffee is uncertain [ev_crop_yield_caramori96_1]; the excess-shade loss is second-hand, summarised from earlier cited studies [ev_crop_yield_caramori96_2]. The net direction for this family depends on shade density, the companion species used, and whether the other products of the system (fruit, pepper, timber, bananas) are counted alongside the main crop.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__recurren.mechanism: In north-central Nicaragua, the in-kind cost of family labour (unpaid household labour valued at its market rate) was highest on the most diversified shaded coffee plots, at US$498 per hectare per year, against US$54 per hectare per year on full-sun coffee; cash costs for fungicide, fertiliser, pest control and hired labour were not significantly different between the shaded and full-sun systems [ev_project_cost_pinoar14_1].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__recurren.conditionality: The source states this is the value of family labour, not a cash cost, and the author attributes the shaded system's lower net income to this higher family-labour use rather than to higher cash spending [ev_project_cost_pinoar14_1]. This is one site in one country, so no cost class is stated here, and a second independent source is needed before a cost size can be agreed for this family.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__rural_po.mechanism: In shaded coffee and cocoa systems, farm profit depends on whether the extra products and resilience from the shade trees outweigh what is given up in crop yield. A pan-tropical review found shaded coffee and cocoa farms had net returns 23% higher than conventional, sun-grown systems [ev_economic_return_jezeer17_1]. In Ghana, moderate-shade cocoa plots had 65% higher value of production than near-full-sun cocoa plots once cocoa, intercrops, fruit, fuelwood and timber are all counted [ev_economic_return_hawkins24_3]. In Costa Rica and Guatemala, modelled long-run returns for low-investment coffee farms were positive under high shade but negative on average under low shade [ev_economic_return_lalani24_1]. Against this, in Nicaragua a multiple regression found coffee net revenue fell as shade-tree diversity rose [ev_economic_return_hagg17_1]; in Ghana, modelling found Rainforest-Alliance-certified shaded cocoa less profitable than an intensive full-sun monoculture assumed to yield 20% more [ev_economic_return_vaast14_4]; and in Ecuador, net margin per hectare was lower under organic cacao agroforestry (US$1,565) than under technified full-sun cacao (US$2,323) [ev_economic_return_perezneira16_1].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__rural_po.conditionality: The gains above come from counting the whole system's products (shade-tree fruit, timber, fuelwood) or from a resilience advantage (the high-shade coffee farms' positive long-run return); the losses come from comparisons against an intensively managed or input-heavy full-sun alternative, where the certification premium or extra yield does not fully offset agroforestry's lower yield of the main crop. Whether shaded perennial systems reduce poverty depends on market access for the secondary products and on what the comparison system assumes.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__soil_ero.mechanism: In shaded coffee, a study on a Costa Rican farm found shade trees reduced sheet erosion by a factor of 2 against full-sun plots [ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1], with runoff and erosion attenuated by close to a factor of two [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3]; reviews state that shade trees protect soil from erosion through the leaves and branches they add, and that reduced erosion and enhanced infiltration are commonly documented under coffee agroforestry [ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11, ev_erosion_hazard_patil25_6]. After Hurricane Stan in Chiapas, Mexico, coffee farms with more complex vegetation suffered less landslide damage, and the farm area hit by landslides rose as vegetation complexity fell [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_10, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_2, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3]. In Misiones, Argentina, a cited study found the erosion and soil exhaustion of yerba mate monoculture much smaller when the crop is associated with trees [ev_erosion_hazard_montagnini15_1]. In Brazilian coffee, accumulated soil loss under shade was 26% of the loss measured in the unshaded area, and accumulated water loss was 44% of the unshaded area's, over the same rainy season [ev_erosion_hazard_decarvalho21_1, ev_runoff_reduction_decarvalho21_2].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__soil_ero.conditionality: The Costa Rican runoff source notes the plot-scale benefit represents little at catchment scale on its soils, and that evidence is high-income [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1]. The Chiapas landslide results come from a single hurricane: the landslide-volume and landslide-size trends were only marginal (P = 0.062), and nearby forest cover did not influence landslide frequency or extent [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_5, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_4]. The review statements give no size [ev_erosion_hazard_patil25_6, ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11]. The evidence is crop-specific and from upper-middle- and high-income countries, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target. The yerba mate unit is read second-hand from a CATIE edited volume [ev_erosion_hazard_montagnini15_1]. Absolute losses were small in both the shaded and unshaded plots on this farm, so the shaded advantage sits on a very low base, and the comparison is a single-farm case study with no replication or significance test, upper-middle-income Brazilian evidence [ev_erosion_hazard_decarvalho21_1].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__water_st.mechanism: In tree-crop systems, shade and tree water use change soil moisture in opposing ways. A multi-country meta-analysis of cocoa agroforestry across Ghana, Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire, Indonesia, Malaysia, Costa Rica, Panama, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia found soils under agroforestry have a significantly lower volumetric water content than under monocultures [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]. In Ghana, the combined transpiration of shade trees and cocoa plants raised water uptake, with a consequent reduction in soil water compared with full-sun cocoa [ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]. Against this, in a Mexican coffee lysimeter study, soil water losses and gains fluctuated far more at the low-shade site than at the medium- and high-shade sites, showing that shade can buffer soil moisture loss through evaporation [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. In Malaysian oil palm, alley-cropping with black pepper or cacao measured significantly wetter topsoil than the monocultures, attributed to greater leaf area, lower light penetration and reduced wind cutting evaporation from exposed soil — the one unit in this row's newer evidence that reads as a soil-moisture benefit [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_1].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__water_st.conditionality: This is the shaded perennial-crop family's own row; cocoa and coffee are this family's crops, so the same three units apply directly. Most of the units measure less soil water under shade — the multi-country cocoa meta-analysis and the Ghana study — so the class is a slight increase in water stress rather than a benefit, and the Mexican coffee buffering result is the one offsetting signal, which keeps agreement at high rather than a stronger reading [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. None of the three states a size for the difference, and none measures a drought or other named water-stress hazard — all describe ordinary dry-season soil moisture [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. The Mexican result is a slower rate of loss and smaller swings under shade, not a higher measured moisture level, and the same site gained less water after rain through canopy interception [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. The cocoa evidence sits in lower- and upper-middle-income countries across Latin America, West Africa and Southeast Asia, in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. Every other new unit adds to the drying side already dominant in this row: the same Malaysian trial found bamboo alleys measured significantly drier topsoil than the monocultures, attributed to bamboo's sparse canopy leaving the ground exposed [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_2]; and in Brazilian coffee, soil moisture under shade was measured lower than under the unshaded area at every depth throughout the monitoring period, with the drying most pronounced soon after rain in drier periods — shade drying the soil rather than conserving it, even though the authors separately argue tree-coffee water-use complementarity kept available water sufficient for the coffee through the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_5, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_6, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_7]. None of the new units states a size or names a drought, and both sources are upper-middle-income evidence (Malaysia, Brazil), consistent with this row's existing transfer.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__wind_cyc.mechanism: The row rests on one study of hurricane-hit coffee farms in Soconusco, Chiapas, Mexico, which compared farms of differing vegetation management. It found significant effects of vegetation management on landslides but not on coffee harvest lost, with all farms reporting yield losses between 18 and 40% [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. For the farmer's harvest, shade trees made no measured difference.
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__wind_cyc.conditionality: This is a no-mitigation result from the primary study. A review's second-hand reading of the same study, that more diverse coffee systems suffered less hurricane damage, was dropped from the evidence because the primary does not support it: the difference the study found was in landslides, not in the harvest. The 18 to 40% range is the loss across all farms, not an effect of the trees [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. The unit is crop-specific (coffee) and counts because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; it is a single study in upper-middle-income Mexico, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target, and does not state the hurricane's severity [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__wind_cyc.mechanism: One study of hurricane-hit coffee farms in Chiapas, Mexico, compared farms of differing vegetation management and found significant effects of vegetation management on landslides but not on coffee harvest lost, with all farms losing between 18 and 40% of harvest [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. Shade trees did not reduce the hurricane's toll on the coffee harvest in that study.
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__wind_cyc.conditionality: The row rests on the primary study's null result, so no mitigation of hurricane harvest loss in shaded coffee is established. A review's second-hand reading of the same study, reporting less damage in more diverse coffee systems, was dropped because the primary does not support it. The 18 to 40% range is the loss on all farms, not an effect of the trees [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. The evidence is coffee-specific, counted under the ruling that shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop, from a single study in upper-middle-income Mexico, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.mechanism: In a severe drought, the area under the most recently planted intensive silvopastoral systems fell by 45 percent across surveyed farms in a Colombian payment-for-ecosystem-services programme [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.conditionality: The loss is in the establishment phase: the source notes established systems were more resilient to drought than traditional pastures [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4]. The evidence is from upper-middle-income Colombia, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.mechanism: A Brazilian review, citing Vosti et al. (1998), states that accidental fire is a constant concern for silvopastoral producers because of the damage it could cause to trees and crops, and that post-fire re-establishment costs could be quite high [ev_fire_hazard_diasf08_3].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a sensitivity for this cell: it is a second-hand comment on producer concern, not a measured loss, from upper-middle-income Brazil, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_fire_hazard_diasf08_3]. A second independent source or one measured finding of fire damage to silvopastoral trees would let the cell state a sensitivity.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.mechanism: In Brazil, a review of barriers to silvopastoral adoption notes that in the establishment phase, tree seedlings need protection from excess solar radiation and wind, alongside trampling, herbivory, weed competition and accidental fire [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_diasf08_4]. In a US silvopasture trial, heavy thinning of an even-aged stand to open the canopy for forage added extra risk of wind blowdown to the retained trees, with tree productivity in silvopasture described as at potential risk to this kind of damage, though the degree of risk and how management might mitigate it remains understudied [ev_climate_shock_orefice16_1].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.conditionality: Both units agree that silvopastoral trees are vulnerable to wind, which is why agreement reads as high despite there being only two units: the Brazilian unit lists wind among several establishment-phase vulnerabilities alongside trampling, herbivory, weeds and fire rather than measuring wind damage itself, and the US unit is an author assertion about risk, not an observed blowdown event. Brazil is upper-middle income and the USA high income, so this scope row sits outside the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__biodiversit.mechanism: In Colombian silvopastoral systems, biodiversity rises relative to open pasture, the land use the practice replaces. A global meta-analysis (47 publications, 279 comparisons) found silvopastoral systems supported 28.4% higher biodiversity than open pastures, with native-tree silvopasture raising biodiversity by 36.3% and planted-tree silvopasture by 20.9%, both against open pastures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_12]. Invertebrate abundance showed the largest taxon-specific gain against open pasture, 53.7% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_8]. In Colombia specifically, a World Bank project evaluation reports that silvopastoral systems played a major role in increasing and conserving biodiversity at farm and landscape level, raising the number of species (richness) and individuals observed (abundance), including forest-dependent and endangered species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8]; bird monitoring on Colombian cattle farms found intensive silvopasture had four times more birds and 35% higher species richness than grass monocultures, and ant species richness was 62% higher than in treeless pastures in the same landscape [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2]. Properties with silvopastoral intervention in the Colombian Amazon also significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. A tropical-agroforestry review states that pastures with isolated trees generally show higher bird diversity than pastures without them [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_1]. A further Colombian Andes study of dung beetles — an indicator of ecological-process recovery, not just species counts — found significantly more beetles caught per trap in intensive silvopasture than in the treeless improved pasture it replaced (275 individuals across five species against 143 across three species), with the same three species found in both land uses plus two additional species recorded only in the silvopastoral system [ev_biodiversity_outcome_giraldo10_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_giraldo10_2].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__biodiversit.conditionality: The same global meta-analysis measures silvopasture against a second, different benchmark — ungrazed native forest — and there the sign reverses: native-tree silvopasture held 18.1% lower overall biodiversity, 14.8% lower plant biodiversity and 24.4% lower invertebrate biodiversity than native forest, with invertebrate abundance 30.2% lower [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_4, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_5, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_9, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_11]. This is a conservation benchmark, not the intervention counterfactual: it means silvopasture holds less biodiversity than intact forest, not that converting grazing land to silvopasture reduces biodiversity, so the class is set from the open-pasture comparisons and these forest-benchmark units are held out of it. Two further forest-benchmark comparisons, for birds and bird species richness, found no significant difference, and the invertebrate-abundance gain against open pasture was itself not significant despite a large point estimate [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_6, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_7, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_10]. The meta-analysis does not report the countries behind its figures, so only the Colombian project evidence anchors this row to the LIC/LMIC target; as a pooled global figure it transfers only as adjacent [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8]. The bird-diversity review's single worked example compares recently abandoned pasture against actively grazed pasture, so grazing cessation is confounded with the trees themselves [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_1]. These two new dung-beetle units read as a benefit and are weighted heavily enough, alongside the existing Colombian evidence, to move this row's own class from a moderate to a strong gain; they do not touch the separate forest-benchmark comparisons already held out of the class above.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__carbon_sequ.mechanism: In Colombia and Costa Rica, silvopastoral systems are reported to raise carbon stocks and sequestration. The World Bank's Colombian Conservation and Sustainable Development of the Coffee Growing Regions project reports net accumulated CO2 removals of 1,131,056 t CO2e from converting pasturelands to dispersed trees in pasture, live fences, intensive silvopastoral systems and secondary-forest conservation [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10]. In Costa Rica, silvopastoral systems had a carbon storage potential of 1.2 to 4.5 Mg C/ha/yr, against below 1 Mg C/ha/yr in treeless pasture [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1]. A global meta-analysis of land-use conversions found soil organic carbon stocks rose 66% and 31% at different depths converting agriculture to silvopasture, 17% converting forest plantation to silvopasture, and 32% converting forest to silvopasture at the deepest sampled profile, where the authors note silvopasture held more SOC than the forest it replaced at that depth [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_27, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_39, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_24, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_38]. A Colombian review states a preliminary GHG balance where lower nitrogen losses and greater carbon capture in intensive silvopastoral systems offset livestock methane emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2], and silvopastoral systems built from degraded natural woodland are reported to mitigate climate change by increasing above- and below-ground carbon stocks [ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_4]. Among pasture-improvement practices assessed in a Colombian climate-smart-agriculture matrix, only tree-improved pastures and live fences showed a positive effect on the mitigation pillar [ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_6]. Properties with silvopastoral intervention in the Colombian Amazon also significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties, retaining forest carbon [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. In the Colombian Amazon (Caquetá), a chronosequence comparing silvopasture against the traditional pasture it replaced found no significant change in total soil organic carbon stock over the full sampled soil profile, but did find a gain confined to the deepest sampled layer, read by the authors as a sign the practice could turn the soil into a carbon sink in deeper layers over time [ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_2]. A review of pastures in semi-arid north-eastern Brazil reports a similar pattern: retaining native tree species (Ziziphus joazeiro and Spondias tuberosa) in pasture significantly raised total soil carbon compared with open pasture away from the trees, attributed to litterfall and fine-root turnover adding soil organic matter and to nitrogen fixation, though the review gives no carbon value [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dagang03_1].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__carbon_sequ.conditionality: Set against this, the same global meta-analysis found soil organic carbon fell 44% converting forest to silvopasture at a shallower sampled depth (against the 32% gain reported at the deepest profile) and fell 47% converting uncultivated or other land to silvopasture — a reversal the engine counts as measured harm, which the authors attribute to the heterogeneity of the uncultivated/other category (bare, degraded or control land) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_6, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_40]. Converting pasture or grassland to silvopasture showed no noticeable change in soil organic carbon in the same meta-analysis, and two further global meta-analyses likewise found no significant effect of converting pasture to agroforestry on soil carbon, attributing it to perennial grass roots already dominating belowground carbon inputs before trees are added [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_9, ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_4, ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_3]. The forest-to-silvopasture figures are measured against existing natural forest, a conservation benchmark, not the pasture-to-silvopasture adoption counterfactual that matters for the practice's climate-mitigation role. All of this is global meta-analysis evidence without a Colombia/Costa Rica-specific breakdown, so only the World Bank project and Costa Rican figures anchor the row to its stated countries; as pooled global findings the SOC units transfer only as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_27, ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1]. Two further readings from the same Colombian Amazon chronosequence measure silvopasture's shallow surface-layer soil carbon against standing native forest rather than against the pasture it replaced, with the traditional pasture on the same land showing a comparable or larger gain over forest in that layer; the engine holds these out of the class for the same reason as the earlier forest-benchmark comparisons in this row — they measure recovery toward a forest reference, not the pasture-to-silvopasture adoption counterfactual, and here the gain mostly reflects grass-root carbon inputs after conversion rather than the trees [ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_4]. The full-profile null and the unstated-size deeper-layer gain both count toward the same-direction pool without stating a size, which is why only a minority of the same-direction units in this row state how big the effect is, holding the class at moderate; the system is also bundled with tillage, lime and phosphate-rock application at establishment, so the gain cannot be credited to the trees alone. The Brazilian pasture finding is a narrative review citing an underlying primary study without giving its own carbon value or stating the study's duration, so it corroborates the direction of the SOC gain without adding a size [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dagang03_1].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__catchment_w.mechanism: In a New Zealand silvopasture trial, winter moisture available to recharge the soil profile was lower under silvopasture than under open pasture (113 against 142 mm in a normal-rainfall winter), which the authors attribute to the evergreen pine canopy intercepting rain and continuing to transpire through winter, so silvopasture water use stays higher than open pasture even in the cool season [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_pollock08_1]. After a wetter-than-usual winter, deep drainage below 2 m was detected only under open ryegrass/clover pasture, not under the silvopastures, which the authors read as the silvopastoral trees retaining and using most of the incoming rainfall except in exceptionally wet winters [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_pollock08_2].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__catchment_w.conditionality: Both readings come from one silvopasture experiment in the Canterbury Plains of New Zealand, high-income temperate evidence well outside the LIC/LMIC target, so the row transfers as out of context. Neither unit measures water leaving the catchment or reaching downstream users; both describe soil-profile recharge and drainage as components of catchment water yield. With only one independent source behind both readings, agreement here is read as low.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__cost_per_he.mechanism: In a US silvopasture establishment trial (forest converted to silvopasture in the Adirondack region of New York), the initial timber-harvesting cost to thin and clear the stand was $1,059 per hectare, which the authors attribute to equipment trucking for a small harvest area, small-diameter stems and research timing [ev_project_cost_orefice16_1]. Forage seeding (orchardgrass and white clover) cost a further $167.04 per hectare, and fencing and water infrastructure $185.33 per hectare, incurred at establishment and again at a mid-rotation replacement [ev_project_cost_orefice16_2, ev_project_cost_orefice16_3].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__cost_per_he.conditionality: All three figures are actual costs from a single US research trial, high-income temperate evidence well outside the LIC/LMIC target, and the timber-harvest cost applied equally to the open-pasture comparator the trial used, so it is not a cost specific to silvopasture. With only one independent source behind all three figures, agreement here is read as low, and the figures cannot be converted or pooled into a single range.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__cost_reduct.mechanism: A World Bank completion report for Colombia states that production costs were US$127/ha lower on average under silvopastoral systems than under traditional ranching, attributing the saving to improved animal nutrition, productivity and fertility and lower incidence of animal death and disease [ev_project_cost_cmscr20_7].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__cost_reduct.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a class: the figure is second-hand, an estimate the report takes from a Bank-commissioned business case rather than a measurement, and there is no other source to pool with [ev_project_cost_cmscr20_7]. A further independent source or a measured cost comparison is what is missing. It comes from upper-middle-income Colombia, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target, and is a recurrent production-cost saving, not an establishment cost [ev_project_cost_cmscr20_7].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__ag.mechanism: The only evidence is a US silvopasture study listing better water infiltration among silvopasture's general ecosystem-service benefits, without linking it to a drought outcome [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__ag.conditionality: This is a single cited-secondary statement from a high-income country, outside the LIC/LMIC target, and it names a soil-water process rather than a measured drought impact [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. A second independent source or one measured drought finding would let this cell state a class.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__al.mechanism: In silvopastoral systems, the benefit runs through fodder availability and herd condition during drought. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant through intense drought while grass monoculture biomass fell to a quarter [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in the lowest-rainfall year in several decades milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which is said to reduce seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. A US silvopasture study lists better water infiltration among silvopasture's services, used here as a soil-water component of drought [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. In a multi-site Argentine study, forage production under trees exceeded treeless grassland or pasture at drought intensities at or below the authors' dry-year threshold, and held up in very humid areas in both normal and dry years, a result corroborated by a companion reading of the same sites [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__al.conditionality: The evidence splits by drought severity and which forage layer is measured, rather than agreeing on one direction. On the benefit side, the Colombian and Argentine forage and milk gains above hold up to around the authors' dry-year threshold [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1]. On the harm side, the same Argentine study found the benefit reverses under severe drought at some sites: at semi-arid Santiago del Estero the relative forage response swung from +2% in normal years to -89% in a dry year, at the humid Chaco site it swung the other way (-15% to +26%), and in the semi-arid aridity category overall there was no significant difference between systems in either normal or dry years — the authors attribute the reversal to tree-forage competition for water overtaking facilitation above about 35% rainfall reduction [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_6]. A multi-species silvopasture trial on degraded rangeland in arid India adds a second harm result: understorey herbage yield fell further under drought beneath every tree and shrub species than in the treeless control, attributed by the authors to shading and competition for soil moisture, though the same trees supplied extra dry-season browse fodder not counted in that herbage comparison [ev_drought_hazard_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_2]. What separates both sides is drought intensity and which forage layer is counted: below a site-specific dry-year threshold, or when browse is counted alongside grass, silvopasture holds or gains; once drought crosses that threshold, or when only understorey herbage is counted, tree-grass competition for scarce water dominates and the system does worse than open pasture. The Latin American silvopastoral units are mostly earlier studies cited in a Spanish-language review and a CATIE edited volume rather than new primary measurements; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees, and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The clearest primary magnitudes (Argentina, Colombia, India) are upper-middle or lower-middle income, and the US unit is high income, so the row as a whole transfers only as adjacent [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_drought_hazard_singhrao08_1].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__mi.mechanism: The only evidence is a review's second-hand report that in Brazil's semi-arid region agroforestry systems had lower year-to-year variation in biomass productivity over 4 years than conventional systems (for example 16% against 91% for maize plus bean), attributed mainly to water availability [ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__mi.conditionality: This single unit concerns yield stability, not a measured drought impact, and comes from upper-middle-income Brazil, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought_haz.conditionality: This is a single primary measurement from lower-middle-income India, inside the LIC/LMIC target, but it covers herbage alone: the same trial found the trees also supplied extra dry-season browse fodder not counted here, so this result should not be read as agroforestry increasing drought vulnerability overall, only that it increased herbage loss specifically [ev_drought_hazard_singhrao08_1].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__fire__agro_.mechanism: Silvopasture has been compared with forest and other unmanaged vegetation, not with open pasture. In Washington State, USA, silvopasture management reduced grass biomass, litter and duff depth against non-grazed managed forest, and the authors conclude that managing overstory, understory and grazing together can reduce fuel loads and potential wildfire risk [ev_t3_fuel_load_abstract_batcheler24_1, ev_t3_litter_duff_batcheler24_5]. Rotational grazing removes understory biomass and herbaceous surface fuel, and the reduced, more variable overstory density has the potential to reduce fire frequency compared with other land uses [ev_t3_herbaceous_fuel_batcheler24_4, ev_t3_fire_freq_batcheler24_3]. Rate of fire spread and burn severity correlate with litter and duff depth in this forest type [ev_t3_fire_spread_batcheler24_6]. Across six European Mediterranean countries, an overlay of burnt areas on land use found that, corrected for land-use extent, shrublands carried a greater share of fires than forest, grassland and agroforestry: agroforestry occupied 12% of the area and was associated with 6% of the fires, while shrubland occupied 16% and was associated with 40% [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_1]. Agroforestry's lower share was not statistically different from that of forest and grassland [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_2], and without the area correction the average fire incidents were lowest for grasslands (11.2%) and agroforestry (20.2%) and highest for shrublands (36.7%) and forests (31.9%) [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_3].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__fire__agro_.conditionality: None of this evidence can set the class; the cell is data deficient. Every comparison is against the unmanaged state, while this cell asks how silvopasture compares with the open pasture of an agro-pastoral system. The US study compares silvopasture with non-grazed managed forest [ev_t3_fuel_load_abstract_batcheler24_1, ev_t3_litter_duff_batcheler24_5, ev_t3_select_fuels_batcheler24_8]; the Mediterranean study compares existing grazed wood-pasture with forest, shrubland and grassland [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_1]. The nearest thing to the right comparator is grassland, and there the Mediterranean study found no significant difference, with grassland showing the lowest raw fire incidence [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_2, ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_3]. Against treeless pasture the reading changes: trees add woody material, litter and duff that open pasture does not have, so having less fuel than a forest does not mean having less fuel than the pasture the practice replaces, and the fire-spread correlation with litter and duff depth would then point to added risk [ev_t3_fire_spread_batcheler24_6]. In the US study only select fuel types fell (1-, 10-, 100- and 1000-h fuels were similar between the management systems), and the fire-frequency statement is a potential effect, not a measurement [ev_t3_select_fuels_batcheler24_8, ev_t3_fire_freq_batcheler24_3]. The Mediterranean overlay is observational and the agroforestry it maps is existing dehesa- and montado-type grazed wood-pasture, not new planting [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_1]. Both studies are from high-income settings, outside the LIC/LMIC target. What would fill the gap is a fire-risk comparison (fuel load, fire frequency or burn severity) of silvopasture against treeless pasture, ideally in an LIC/LMIC agro-pastoral system.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__flood__all.mechanism: Colombian silvopastoral soils eroded 35.3 percent less than degraded pasture in the Coffee Ecoregion but only 5.4 percent less in the flatter Cesar River Valley [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__flood__all.conditionality: Both figures come from a single World Bank project report comparing silvopasture with degraded pasture rather than conventional pasture, and they measure erosion, a component of flood impact [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__food_insecu.mechanism: Integrated agrosilvopastoral extension may improve diets: a systematic review cites a Kenyan study in which receiving Vi Agroforestry advice raised the household dietary diversity score by 1.22 and the number of food groups consumed by 2.291, out of the 12 analysed [ev_food_security_castle21s_1].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__food_insecu.conditionality: This cell is data deficient, not evidence of no effect. It rests on a single study reported second-hand in a review, from West Pokot, Kenya, and on extension advice rather than silvopasture measured on the farm [ev_food_security_castle21s_1]. A second independent source, or the original study's own measurement, would let this cell state a class.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__heat_stress.mechanism: Silvopastoral systems cut heat stress in cattle: intensive shrub–tree–rotational pasture models in the dry Colombian Caribbean reduce it, and eucalyptus–brachiaria systems in Brazil reduced the area at critical animal thermal-comfort levels by 20 to 100% against monoculture pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. Tree shade in pastures is associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover, attributed to less heat stress and more foliage and fruit, and other studies found increases above 15% for cows grazing silvopasture compared with cows in full sun [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2]. An IPCC climate-impacts assessment reports more generally that increased shade from trees or cost-effective structures can substantially reduce the incidence of high heat-stress days for livestock, reduce animal stress and increase productivity [ev_livestock_productivity_porter14_1].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__heat_stress.conditionality: Most units are reviews citing earlier studies, and the shade-associated milk and weight-gain figures are associations rather than measured heat-stress losses avoided [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. The milk gains mix relief from heat with extra foliage and fruit, so they are not a pure heat-stress effect [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2]. The IPCC livestock-shade statement is a global assessment citing underlying feedlot and modelling studies rather than tree-canopy measurements directly, and names no size [ev_livestock_productivity_porter14_1].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__heat_stress.mechanism: Trees over pasture and livestock intercept solar radiation and lower the temperature animals are exposed to. The IPCC's livestock-adaptation chapter (a cited secondary assessment) states that shade from trees or cost-effective structures can substantially reduce the incidence of high heat-stress days and the productivity loss that comes with them. A Brazilian review found agroforestry systems cut the area of pasture reaching critical heat levels for livestock by 20 to 100% compared with monoculture pasture.
agroforestry__silvopastoral__heat_stress.conditionality: No study in this pool measured livestock at severe or extreme heat stress, only at high heat-stress levels, so the benefit at the most dangerous heat extremes is unproven. The IPCC statement groups shade trees together with built shade structures as a single adaptation option rather than isolating the tree effect, and is a secondary assessment rather than a herd trial.
evidence_summary: IPCC's livestock-adaptation chapter (cited secondary assessment): shade from trees or cost-effective structures can substantially reduce high heat-stress days and raise livestock productivity, with spraying rated a less effective alternative.
A Brazilian review (upper-middle-income context) reports that agroforestry systems cut the area of pasture reaching critical heat levels for livestock by 20-100% compared with monoculture.
agroforestry__silvopastoral__heat_stress.agreement_note: Both sources point the same way and neither reports a harmful or null result, but they measure different things (herd heat-stress days vs. area reaching critical heat), so the size of the benefit cannot be pooled into one number.
