An IPCC climate-impacts assessment reports more generally that increased shade from trees or cost-effective structures can substantially reduce the incidence of high heat-stress days for livestock, reduce animal stress and increase productivity [ev_livestock_productivity_porter14_1].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__heat_stress.conditionality: The Colombian units come from a review citing earlier studies, and the milk and weight-gain figures there are associations with tree shade in humid-tropic pastures rather than measured heat-stress losses avoided [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. The milk gains mix relief from heat with extra foliage and fruit, so they are not a pure heat-stress effect [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2]. The IPCC livestock-shade statement is a global assessment citing underlying feedlot and modelling studies rather than tree-canopy measurements directly, and names no size [ev_livestock_productivity_porter14_1].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__heat_stress.mechanism: In the dry Colombian Caribbean, silvopastoral models most intensive in shrubs, trees and rotational pasture reduce heat stress in cattle, and a Brazilian study found agroforestry reduced the area at critical thermal-comfort levels for animals by 20 to 100% compared with monoculture pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. In tropical silvopasture, temperatures under tree crowns can average 2-5°C lower than outside them throughout the year, depending on the characteristics of the trees [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_1]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. A systematic review of silvopasture and dairy cattle, mostly from Brazil, found the effect on the thermal environment was mostly (57%) favourable: silvopasture gave lower air temperature, black globe temperature, soil surface temperature and radiant thermal load than treeless pasture, and cows drank less often and had lower surface temperature and respiratory rate [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_1]. An older review cites Kelly et al. (1950) that trees are the most effective shade for cattle, adding evaporative cooling from the leaves to protection from sunlight [ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__heat_stress.conditionality: The Colombian and Brazilian review results are cited secondary findings from upper-middle-income settings, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. All units report air temperature, thermal indices or animal comfort, components of heat-stress impact rather than measured losses [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. Not every index moves: in the same systematic review, results for the temperature humidity index, which uses only air temperature and humidity, were unclear, with most of the studies that used it finding no significant difference between silvopasture and treeless pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_2]. The cattle-shade statement from Australia and the USA is an old citation without a tree system [ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__production_.mechanism: Trees in a pasture add shade, deep-rooted drought buffering and nitrogen transfer to the grass layer, but they also compete with pasture grasses for light, water and nutrients; which effect wins depends on tree density and age. A global meta-analysis of silvopastoral paddocks found pasture yield fell by an average of 20.8% across 345 paddock-years and by 30% once tree density exceeded 800 trees per hectare, while newly planted trees had no effect at all and the oldest trees reduced pasture yield to below 50% of the open-pasture control [ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_9, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_10, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_11, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_12]. Livestock yield across the same global dataset fell by 18.6% on average, but 33% of paddock-years still showed higher animal productivity under trees than in the open [ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14], and the decline levelled off once density passed about 300 trees per hectare [ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_15]. Nitrogen-fixing trees can also transfer nitrogen to companion grasses: Setaria grass grown with leucaena in Sri Lanka had a 16% higher nitrogen yield than a grass monoculture [ev_forage_productivity_dagang03_2].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__production_.conditionality: The sign flips with drought severity and site. Pooled across Argentine sites, silvopastoral forage production exceeded treeless grassland in both normal and dry years where the dry year's rainfall shortfall stayed at or below 35% of the long-term mean, but reversed into a competition process once the shortfall exceeded 35% [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2]. At one site the silvopastoral relative response went from +2% in normal years to -89% in a dry year, while at another site with a smaller shortfall the response went the opposite way, from -15% in normal years to +26% in the dry year [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_6]. The same study found forage production fell further as tree cover (shade intensity) increased, in both normal and dry years [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_7]. In arid India, herbage yield under most tree and shrub species was lower than the treeless control during drought years, significantly so for Acacia tortilis and Dichrostachys nutans, but the trees also produced leaf fodder that households cut for livestock during the same droughts, a trade-off of less grass for more browse [ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_2]. In New Zealand radiata-pine silvopasture, early complementarity between trees and pasture reversed as the trees matured, and by 15 years after planting the pasture had disappeared entirely under the trees [ev_forage_productivity_pollock08_1]. In a US silvopasture trial, forage was significantly lower under trees than in open pasture a year after establishment [ev_forage_productivity_orefice16_1], though the difference was no longer significant in the second year, with the authors citing the small sample size [ev_forage_productivity_orefice16_2]. At the high-intensity end, an intensive Colombian silvopastoral system raised stocking to 4.3 cows per hectare and milk production to 130% of the conventional baseline while eliminating chemical fertiliser, and kept forage production constant through intense drought when a grass monoculture lost 25% of its biomass [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1]. Most of the quantified evidence is from upper-middle- and high-income countries (Argentina, the United States, New Zealand); the arid-India and Sri Lanka units are the main lower-middle-income evidence.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__rural_pover.mechanism: Silvopastoral systems raise rural income chiefly through better animal nutrition and productivity. In Colombia, switching from traditional ranching to a silvopastoral system increased farmers' annual income by as much as $523 per hectare, with production costs $127 per hectare lower, attributed to improved animal nutrition, productivity and fertility and lower disease and death [ev_household_income_cmscr20_6]. In the Colombian Amazon, milk income rose 42.12% under an intensive silvopastoral system, linked to a higher stocking capacity of 2.71 animal units per hectare against 1.84 under pasture monoculture [ev_household_income_montagnini15_1]. A review across Peru and Colombia found an operating benefit-cost ratio of 2.8 for an intensive silvopastoral system against 1.34 for a traditional system [ev_economic_return_saucedo23_1].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__rural_pover.conditionality: The gain is not immediate everywhere: in Brazil, household income from silvopastoral systems was found comparatively lower than under traditional pasture in the first years after establishment, before the system matures [ev_economic_return_diasf08_1]. A World Bank project review in Colombia, where 47.2% of prospective beneficiaries were below the poverty line at baseline (3.6% in extreme poverty), could not yet separate the project's poverty impact from drought and other climatic shocks, since many systems were still in their establishment phase at project closing [ev_rural_poverty_cmscr20_9]. Measured harm (maladaptation) — the practice reducing this outcome for some adopters — appears in 1 source.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__soil_erosio.mechanism: Trees in pasture hold soil and water on the slope. In Colombia's Coffee Ecoregion, soils under silvopasture lost 12.3 t/ha a year against 19 t/ha for degraded pasture, a mean reduction in erosion of 35.3 percent; in the flatter Cesar River Valley the figures were 17.5 against 18.5 t/ha [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. A review compiling field studies of agroforestry against its controls found that silvopastoral systems reduced soil loss by 68% and water loss by 73% on average [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_1]. In Costa Rica and Nicaragua, runoff equalled 28-48% of rainfall on pastures without trees against less than 10% in silvopastoral systems [ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1]. Runoff was higher on grass pasture than in tree-dominated fodder banks, so tree cover attenuates runoff and the soil erosion it causes [ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__soil_erosio.conditionality: Slope sets how much there is to gain: the Colombian reduction was large in the hilly Coffee Ecoregion and small in the flatter Cesar River Valley, where the project notes less scope for improvement [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. The Colombian figures are project measurements against degraded pasture from upper-middle-income Colombia, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1]. The review percentages are simple averages of compiled study reductions, not weighted meta-analytic effects, they mix temperate and tropical studies, and the review found no significant difference in soil-loss reduction between silvopastoral and other agroforestry systems [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_1]. The runoff units from Central America are earlier studies cited in a CATIE edited volume and a Spanish-language review, entering as components of erosion, and the Costa Rica and Nicaragua figures span high- and lower-middle-income settings [ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1, ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__water_quali.mechanism: Trees and shrubs in grazed pasture hold back nutrients that would otherwise leave the field. A global review of plot and field studies found that silvopastoral systems reduced nutrient losses from leaching, runoff and sediment by 45%, 47% and 42% on average against single pastures [ev_nutrient_removal_zhu19_1].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__water_quali.conditionality: The strong class rests on one review with no second independent source to test agreement against. Its percentages are averages of compiled study reductions rather than weighted meta-analytic effects, from temperate and tropical sites rather than low-income settings, and they measure nutrient loss at the field, a component of water-quality risk, not water quality downstream [ev_nutrient_removal_zhu19_1].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__water_stres.mechanism: In a New Zealand silvopasture, summer water use and end-of-summer soil moisture were no different from open pasture once the trees reached four growing seasons old, as the maturing tree roots came to occupy the profile at depth and dominate water use across every system [ev_soil_moisture_pollock08_1].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__water_stres.conditionality: After a drier-than-normal winter, the same trial measured deeper (1-2 m) soil moisture lower under a silvopasture than under open lucerne pasture, attributing it to the trees' higher winter water use drawing down deep soil water that the below-normal winter rain did not replace [ev_soil_moisture_pollock08_2]. Both readings come from the same single New Zealand silvopasture experiment, high-income temperate evidence well outside the LIC/LMIC target; neither names a drought, describing instead an ordinary below-normal-rainfall winter. With only one independent source behind two readings that point one to no difference and one to a measured drying, agreement here is read as low.

agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk.mechanism: A sub-Saharan meta-analysis found agroforestry five and ten times better than controls for runoff and soil loss respectively [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1]. A pantropical meta-analysis found agroforestry trees reduced soil erosion by 50% against crop monocultures, and stated mechanisms include greater soil cover and structure protecting against raindrop impact, roots aiding infiltration and reducing surface runoff, and live fences lowering runoff velocity; runoff reduction is used as a component [ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_santos25_2, ev_runoff_reduction_watts22_2, ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_5]. A review compiling published field studies of agroforestry against its controls found average soil-loss reductions of 68% for silvopastoral systems, 66% for silvoarable agroforestry and 55% for linear tree plantings, with no significant difference among the system types, and average water-loss reductions of 73% for silvopastoral and 43% for silvoarable systems [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_3, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_1, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_2]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT compiler adds that, due to less wind and water erosion, the siltation of ponds and water pans is reduced [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. In Lower Nyando, Kenya, farmers reported that tree roots prevented extensive soil erosion and soil fertility loss during the floods [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1]. During Hurricane Mitch in October 1998, Honduran farmers practising the Quesungual system suffered less landslide damage than those using traditional slash-and-burn [ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1]. In Costa Rica and Nicaragua, runoff equalled 28-48% of rainfall on pastures without trees against less than 10% in silvopastoral systems [ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1]. Runoff was higher on grass pasture than in tree-dominated fodder banks, so tree cover attenuates runoff and the soil erosion it causes [ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1]. Within single sub-practices, live fences of Gliricidia sepium are used to prevent erosion, shade trees attenuate runoff and erosion by close to a factor of two against full-sun plots, and in Colombia's Coffee Ecoregion erosion under silvopasture was 35.3 percent lower than on degraded pasture soils [ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_2, ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1]. In shaded perennial systems, a study on a Costa Rican coffee farm found shade trees reduced sheet erosion by a factor of 2 against full-sun plots [ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1], and after Hurricane Stan in Chiapas, Mexico, coffee farms with more complex vegetation suffered less landslide damage [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_10]. Along field boundaries, on Saskatchewan prairie fields with old shelterbelts planted to reduce wind erosion, erosion midway between the belts has generally been much less than in unsheltered fields, judged from depth to carbonates and 137Cs, and the authors expect soil productivity there to be higher than in open fields [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5]. In Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual system report that soil erosion has been nearly stopped, and estimate nutrient loss through erosion at more than 10 times lower than under slash-and-burn [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4]. A meta-analysis of seven African erosion-control studies (Kenya, Nigeria, Zimbabwe) found agroforestry outperformed controls by a response ratio of 5 for runoff and by 7.2 to 8 for soil loss depending on agro-ecological zone (humid vs semi-arid) [ev_runoff_reduction_kuyah19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_2, ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_3]. A separate meta-analysis found infiltration rates 75% higher and runoff 57% lower under agroforestry than crop monoculture (an overall 50% reduction in soil erosion), and separated the erosion-rate response ratio by tree type: 0.29 for non-nitrogen-fixing trees against 0.41 for nitrogen-fixing trees (lower is less erosion), a difference the authors found was not statistically significant [ev_runoff_reduction_muchane20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_2, ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_3]. Agroforestry farmland is reported to be more resilient to heavy rainfall through a 20-50% decrease in runoff and an increase in soil-water infiltration [ev_runoff_reduction_dobhal24_2]. In Argentina, soil erosion and soil exhaustion under yerba mate grown as a monoculture were much lower when the crop was grown with trees in an agroforestry system [ev_erosion_hazard_montagnini15_1]. In Costa Rica, shade trees are described as protecting soil from sheet erosion and conserving fertility through organic-matter inputs [ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11]. In Kenya, a farmer in Isiolo County explained that planting trees in a line prevents soil from being swept away by water [ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6]. IPCC assessments state in general terms that agroforestry limits soil erosion and helps stabilise soils against desertification, over an estimated extent of about 10 million km2 of land with more than 10% tree cover [ev_erosion_hazard_ipccar6ch5_5, ev_erosion_hazard_ipccsrccl6_2, ev_erosion_hazard_ipccsrccl6_5]. In Mexican coffee, the area affected by landslides significantly increased as vegetation complexity was reduced from forest to shaded monoculture [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_2]. The same Nigerian alley-cropping model also projects soil loss directly: over a 20-year horizon on a sloping field, 2 m-spaced Leucaena alley cropping gives the lowest predicted cumulative soil loss of the systems compared (2.5 t/ha), against 17.8 t/ha for the traditional short-cycle bush fallow it is compared with; 4 m spacing follows at 9.9 t/ha, still below the no-till (14 t/ha) and bush-fallow controls [ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_1, ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_2, ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_3]. On a steep hillslope in Laguna, the Philippines, a randomised trial of contour hedgerows (Desmanthus virgatus) on maize-mungbean alleys found annual soil loss fell step-wise with each added practice: from 124 t/ha/yr under the farmer's up-and-down-slope tillage, to 40 t/ha/yr once contour hedgerows and contour tillage were added, to 3 t/ha/yr once the hedgerow trimmings and crop residues were also spread as mulch, to 0.2 t/ha/yr once zero tillage was added on top of hedgerows and mulch; the hedgerow-plus-contour-tillage treatment alone also produced only about half as much annual runoff as the farmer's practice [ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_1, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_2, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_3, ev_runoff_reduction_paningbatan95_4]. In Jiangxi Province, China, a randomised trial intercropping peanut with Choerospondias axillaris trees on a sloping field found mean soil loss per rainfall event fell by 25.3% with younger trees and by 32.0% with older trees compared with mono-cropped peanut [ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_1, ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_2]. In Brazilian coffee, accumulated soil loss under shade was 26% of the loss measured in the unshaded area, and accumulated water loss was 44% of the unshaded area's, over the same rainy season [ev_erosion_hazard_decarvalho21_1, ev_runoff_reduction_decarvalho21_2]. In Niger, farmers and reviewers describe trees in the regenerated fields protecting against wind, reducing erosion and evaporation, and enriching the soil through litter decomposition and nutrients from livestock sheltering in their shade [ev_erosion_hazard_boton10_6].
agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk.conditionality: The class is moderate because it is set by a vote across sub-practices: the cross-family, planted silvoarable and silvopastoral cells read as strong reductions, linear boundary plantings as moderate, and regeneration-based farmland and shaded perennial systems as slight. The cross-practice syntheses agree on large reductions: the sub-Saharan and pantropical meta-analyses and the review of compiled field studies, whose averages hold across silvopastoral, silvoarable and linear plantings alike [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_3]. Single-practice field evidence is often weaker than those averages, so the size a project can expect depends on site and practice [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. The compiled-review percentages are simple averages of study reductions, not weighted meta-analytic effects, and they mix temperate and tropical studies [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1]. The shade-tree effect represents little at catchment scale on the andisols studied [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3]. Site matters within a practice: erosion fell 35.3 percent in Colombia's Coffee Ecoregion but only 5.4 percent in the Cesar River Valley [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. The sub-Saharan authors warn the very large effect sizes could reflect publication bias and expect more modest effects with more studies [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1]. Regreening Africa observed no large overall change in erosion prevalence and found no link between more trees on farm and lower erosion, the FMNR result is participants' reported erosion, and the Nicaraguan hurricane result bundles trees with terraces and contour planting [ev_erosion_hazard_rgaf23_3, ev_erosion_hazard_rgaf23_5, ev_erosion_hazard_wvfmnr19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_9]. The WOCAT unit is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet, not an erosion measurement, and the siltation rating enters as a component [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. The Lower Nyando erosion finding is farmer-reported, not measured [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1]. The landslide and runoff results are earlier studies cited in a working paper, a CATIE edited volume and a Spanish-language review; the runoff units enter as components of erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1, ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1, ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1]. The Chiapas landslide results are crop-specific coffee evidence from a single hurricane, with the landslide-volume and landslide-size trends only marginal (P = 0.062) and no effect of nearby forest cover [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_5, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_4]. The Honduran erosion claim is a narrative from a promoter-written grey-literature article with no measured erosion rate, and the effect belongs to the whole bundle of trees, mulch cover, zero tillage and no burning [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4]. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt unit is high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target; it infers past erosion from soil markers and states no erosion rate [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5]. In China, a field study of windbreak patches found windbreaks reduced average wind-erosion soil loss by 20% compared with open farmland [ev_erosion_hazard_chang21_1]. The Kenya/Nigeria/Zimbabwe meta-analysis breaks its result down by agro-ecological zone rather than giving one pooled number, and both erosion response ratios in it are large enough that, alongside the sub-Saharan meta-analysis already in this row, the same publication-bias caution applies [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_2, ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_3]. Most of these newer units are review or assessment statements rather than site measurements: the IPCC and farmland-resilience statements give no size or site, and the Argentine, Costa Rican and Kenyan farmer statements are a review citation, a Spanish-language case description and a single farmer's perception, not a measured erosion rate [ev_erosion_hazard_ipccar6ch5_5, ev_runoff_reduction_dobhal24_2, ev_erosion_hazard_montagnini15_1, ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11, ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6]. The Chinese windbreak study and the Kenya/Nigeria/Zimbabwe meta-analysis add upper-middle-income and LIC/LMIC evidence respectively, broadly consistent with the row's existing transfer. The Nigerian erosion figures are modelled, not measured, running a simplified USLE-based erosion model calibrated to plot-level erosion rates from the same research station, and the model's own ranking shows erosion as time-dependent: initial erosion rates are lower under no-till than under the 4 m alley, with the alley only overtaking by the end of the 20-year horizon. The Philippines result is bundled: each successive treatment adds a co-practice (contour tillage, then mulch from the hedgerow trimmings and crop residues, then zero tillage) on top of the hedgerows, so the hedgerow-alone share of the reduction cannot be separated from the tillage and mulch changes that go with it, and even the hedgerow-plus-contour-tillage treatment is still called 'considerable' soil loss by the authors, not yet a tolerable rate. Both the Philippines and Nigeria results sit inside the LIC/LMIC target; the Chinese trial is upper-middle-income evidence. The same Chinese trial found a reversal on runoff: mean runoff per event was higher in both tree-intercropped treatments than in mono-cropped peanut, even though soil loss was lower — the authors attribute the higher runoff to surface seals and crusts forming on the untilled soil under and between the tree rows, while tillage of the peanut area itself raised infiltration there; the engine counts this as measured harm for some adopters [ev_runoff_reduction_wei07_3]. Absolute losses were small in both the shaded and unshaded plots on this farm, so the shaded advantage sits on a very low base, and the comparison is a single-farm case study with no replication or significance test, upper-middle-income Brazilian evidence [ev_erosion_hazard_decarvalho21_1].

agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__farming.mechanism: Two studies on rainfed cropland point to less erosion with trees. In Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system report that soil erosion has been nearly stopped, and estimate nutrient loss through erosion at more than 10 times lower than under slash-and-burn [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4]. On Saskatchewan prairie fields with old shelterbelts planted to reduce wind erosion, erosion midway between the belts has generally been much less than in unsheltered fields, judged from depth to carbonates and 137Cs, and the authors expect soil productivity there to be higher than in open fields [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5]. Neither unit gives an erosion rate, so the engine reads a slight reduction.
agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__farming.conditionality: The evidence is thin and sits outside the target context. The Honduran claim is a narrative from a promoter-written grey-literature article with no measured erosion rate, and the effect belongs to the whole bundle of trees, mulch cover, zero tillage and no burning, so it cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4]. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt unit is high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target; it infers past erosion from soil markers and states no erosion rate [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5]. The two units describe different practices (a slash-and-mulch field system and field shelterbelts) and different erosion processes. Missing: measured erosion rates from rainfed cropland with and without trees in low- or lower-middle-income settings.

agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__farming.mechanism: In Isiolo County, Kenya, households said that planting trees in a line prevents the soil from being swept away by water [ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6]. In Lower Nyando, Kenya, farmers reported that tree roots prevented extensive soil erosion and soil fertility loss during the floods [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1].
agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__farming.conditionality: Both units are farmer statements from Kenyan mixed crop-livestock households, gathered in interviews and focus groups during or after floods, with no measured soil loss or effect size [ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6, ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1].

agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__farming.mechanism: In shaded coffee, a study on a Costa Rican farm found shade trees reduced sheet erosion by a factor of 2 against full-sun plots [ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1], with runoff and erosion attenuated by close to a factor of two [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3]; reviews state that shade trees protect soil from erosion through the leaves and branches they add, and that reduced erosion and enhanced infiltration are commonly documented under coffee agroforestry [ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11, ev_erosion_hazard_patil25_6]. After Hurricane Stan in Chiapas, Mexico, coffee farms with more complex vegetation suffered less landslide damage, and the farm area hit by landslides rose as vegetation complexity fell [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_10, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_2, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3]. In Brazilian coffee, accumulated soil loss under shade was 26% of the loss measured in the unshaded area, and accumulated water loss was 44% of the unshaded area's, over the same rainy season [ev_erosion_hazard_decarvalho21_1, ev_runoff_reduction_decarvalho21_2].
agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__farming.conditionality: The Costa Rican runoff source notes the plot-scale benefit represents little at catchment scale on its soils, and that evidence is high-income [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1]. The Chiapas landslide results come from a single hurricane: the landslide-volume and landslide-size trends were only marginal (P = 0.062), and nearby forest cover did not influence landslide frequency or extent [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_5, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_4]. The review statements give no size [ev_erosion_hazard_patil25_6, ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11]. The evidence is crop-specific and from upper-middle- and high-income countries, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target. Absolute losses were small in both the shaded and unshaded plots on this farm, so the shaded advantage sits on a very low base, and the comparison is a single-farm case study with no replication or significance test, upper-middle-income Brazilian evidence [ev_erosion_hazard_decarvalho21_1].

agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__income_.mechanism: In Costa Rican coffee, a study on a large farm found shade trees reduced sheet erosion by a factor of 2 against full-sun plots [ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1], shade trees attenuated runoff and erosion by close to a factor of two [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3], and a review states that shade trees protect soil from erosion and conserve fertility through the leaves and branches they add [ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11]. On Saskatchewan prairie fields with old shelterbelts planted to reduce wind erosion, erosion midway between the belts has generally been much less than in unsheltered fields, judged from depth to carbonates and 137Cs, and the authors expect soil productivity there to be higher than in open fields [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5].
agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__income_.conditionality: No unit states a size against the counterfactual (full-sun plots for coffee, unsheltered fields for shelterbelts), so the engine reads a slight reduction. The runoff source notes the plot-scale benefit represents little at catchment scale on these soils [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3]. All units are from high-income settings, outside the LIC/LMIC target: the Costa Rican units are crop-specific coffee evidence, much of it from a single farm, and the Canadian unit is temperate shelterbelt evidence [ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1, ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11, ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5]. The Canadian unit infers past erosion from soil markers and states no erosion rate [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5]. This evidence should not be transferred to LIC/LMIC systems without local evidence.

agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__income_.mechanism: In China, windbreak patches reduced average wind-erosion soil loss by 20% compared with open farmland by slowing wind speed [ev_erosion_hazard_chang21_1]. In Colombia's Coffee Ecoregion, a World Bank project evaluation found soils under silvopastoral systems eroded 35.3% less than degraded pasture soils (12.3 vs 19 t/ha/yr), though in the flatter Cesar River Valley the reduction was only 5.4% (17.5 vs 18.5 t/ha/yr), which the evaluation attributes to less scope for improvement on flatter ground [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. In Argentina, soil erosion and exhaustion under yerba mate were much lower grown with trees than as a monoculture [ev_erosion_hazard_montagnini15_1]. In Brazil, agroforestry is described as increasing soil cover and structure, protecting against raindrop impact and reducing wind speed and runoff [ev_erosion_hazard_santos25_2]. In a Colombian review, runoff was reported higher on grass pasture than on tree-dominated fodder banks [ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1]. In Chiapas, Mexico, after Hurricane Stan, coffee farms with higher vegetation complexity suffered less landslide damage at farm and landscape scale, landslide frequency rose significantly as vegetation complexity fell, and landslide size showed the same tendency, though only marginally (P = 0.062) [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_10, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_2, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_5]. On a steep hillslope in Laguna, the Philippines, a randomised trial of contour hedgerows on maize-mungbean alleys found annual soil loss fell step-wise as practices were added: from 124 t/ha/yr under the farmer's up-and-down-slope tillage, to 40 t/ha/yr once contour hedgerows and contour tillage were added, to 3 t/ha/yr once the hedgerow trimmings and crop residues were also spread as mulch, to 0.2 t/ha/yr once zero tillage was added on top of hedgerows and mulch; the hedgerow-plus-contour-tillage treatment alone also produced only about half as much annual runoff as the farmer's practice [ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_1, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_2, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_3, ev_runoff_reduction_paningbatan95_4]. In Jiangxi Province, China, a randomised trial intercropping peanut with Choerospondias axillaris trees on a sloping field found mean soil loss per rainfall event fell by 25.3% with younger trees and by 32.0% with older trees compared with mono-cropped peanut [ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_1, ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_2]. In Brazilian coffee, accumulated soil loss under shade during the rainy season was 26% of the loss measured in the unshaded area, and accumulated water loss was 44% of the unshaded area's [ev_erosion_hazard_decarvalho21_1, ev_runoff_reduction_decarvalho21_2].
agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__income_.conditionality: The Philippines trial is bundled: each successive treatment adds a co-practice (contour tillage, then mulch from the hedgerow trimmings and crop residues, then zero tillage) on top of the hedgerows, so the hedgerow-alone share of the reduction cannot be separated from the tillage and mulch changes that go with it, and even the hedgerow-plus-contour-tillage treatment alone is still called 'considerable' soil loss by the authors, not yet a tolerable rate. The same Chinese peanut-tree trial found a reversal on runoff even though soil loss was lower: mean runoff per event was higher in both tree-intercropped treatments than in mono-cropped peanut, which the authors attribute to surface seals and crusts forming on the untilled soil under and between the tree rows, while tillage of the peanut area itself raised infiltration there — the source of this row's measured harm [ev_runoff_reduction_wei07_3]. The Brazilian coffee comparison is a single-farm case study with no replication or significance test, and absolute losses were small in both the shaded and unshaded plots, so the shaded advantage sits on a very low base [ev_erosion_hazard_decarvalho21_1]. The Chiapas landslide findings are crop-specific coffee evidence from a single hurricane event, with the landslide-size trend only marginal and, separately, neither forest proximity nor the proportion of surrounding forest cover found to significantly affect landslide frequency or extent [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_4]. The Colombian evaluation shows the benefit is site-dependent: a strong reduction on the more erodible Coffee Ecoregion slopes against a small reduction on flatter Cesar Valley ground [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. The Argentine and Brazilian statements are review citations rather than measured erosion rates [ev_erosion_hazard_montagnini15_1, ev_erosion_hazard_santos25_2]. All units in this scope row are upper-middle income (China, Colombia, Argentina, Brazil, Mexico, the Philippines), which is why the row transfers in_context to its own scope but not automatically to the LIC/LMIC target as a whole.

agroforestry__water_quality_risk.mechanism: Trees on farms reduce the nutrients and sediment that reach water. A global review of plot and field studies found that silvopastoral systems reduced nutrient losses from leaching, runoff and sediment by 45%, 47% and 42% on average against single pastures, and that linear tree plantings decreased average nutrient loss from leaching and runoff by 16% and 33% [ev_nutrient_removal_zhu19_1, ev_nutrient_removal_zhu19_2]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet rates downstream siltation as decreased, its compiler noting that less wind and water erosion reduces the siltation of ponds and water pans [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation].
agroforestry__water_quality_risk.conditionality: The size rests on a single review, whose percentages are averages of compiled study reductions rather than weighted meta-analytic effects, drawn from temperate and tropical sites rather than low-income settings [ev_nutrient_removal_zhu19_1]. Nutrient and sediment losses are components of water-quality risk measured at the field edge; no unit measures water quality in streams or reservoirs. Linear plantings vary widely: the same review reports their effect on nitrogen loss ranging from an increase to a large decrease [ev_nutrient_removal_zhu19_2]. The Kenyan FMNR siltation unit is a compiler judgement on a technology sheet, not a measurement [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation].

agroforestry__water_stress.mechanism: The measured evidence splits on whether trees add water the system can use or compete with crops for it, and the separator is usually which water measure is used — system water-use efficiency (biomass per unit of water used, which counts the tree's own biomass) versus the crop's own soil moisture. In Niger, Ziziphus mauritiana trees raised millet's rainwater-use efficiency by 17 to 47% depending on fertiliser treatment, and raised the millet/cowpea intercrop's water-use efficiency by 11 to 17% [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_2]. In Malawi, a long-running gliricidia agroforestry trial found system water-use efficiency (total above-ground biomass, including the tree, per unit of seasonal water use) strongly and significantly higher in every season for gliricidia-based systems than for sole maize or maize-pigeonpea, by a wide margin (for example 1.43-1.97 g/kg for gliricidia+maize against 0.15-0.54 g/kg for sole maize) [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_5]. In Honduras, the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system retained 15% more soil water in the driest month than slash-and-burn (23% against 8% humidity), equivalent to about 20 mm of extra rainfall and 20 more days a crop could survive without rain, attributed to better infiltration through soil cover and higher organic matter [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1]. A sub-Saharan meta-analysis found agroforestry improved both infiltration and soil moisture content compared with controls [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1]. A continental-scale model finds rainfall dependent on upwind tree cover by 10 to 20%, rising with more tree cover and falling with upwind deforestation [ev_water_regulation_vannoordwijk21_4]. A WOCAT compiler for Kenyan FMNR rates water availability increased, attributing it to greater water retention raising groundwater levels [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. A second Malawi reading confirms the recharge-season pattern: available soil water tended to be greater in the gliricidia+maize+pigeonpea system at the peak of the recharge phase across two further seasons, attributed to increased infiltration and reduced soil evaporation [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10], and further seasonal readings of system water-use efficiency confirm gliricidia-based systems using water more efficiently than sole maize or maize-pigeonpea [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_6]. In Jiangxi Province, China, a peanut-tree alley-cropping trial found the profile-mean (0-150 cm) soil water potential drier in both tree-intercropped treatments than in mono-cropped peanut or either tree monoculture, consistent with tree-crop competition for water, with the difference larger in the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_wei07_4]. In Malaysian oil palm, alley-cropping with black pepper or cacao measured significantly wetter topsoil than the monocultures, which the authors attribute to greater leaf area, lower light penetration and reduced wind cutting evaporation from exposed soil [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_1].
agroforestry__water_stress.conditionality: Set against this, when the same Malawi trial measures the crop's own soil moisture rather than system water-use efficiency, the sign often reverses: available soil water at the start of the cropping season was generally lower in the tree-based systems, consistent with trees depleting moisture through the dry season, and the decline from March to August was most pronounced in the gliricidia-based treatments; volumetric moisture was significantly lower under the gliricidia+maize+pigeonpea system at depth in one season reading and slightly lower in another, though a later-season reading found it significantly greater at depth, and the authors' overall conclusion is that pruned gliricidia does not create undue water competition under Malawi's rainfall, several season-level contrasts showing no significant difference [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_1, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_6, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_7, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_9]. In Ghana and across a ten-country cocoa meta-analysis, shaded cocoa and cocoa agroforestry measured significantly lower soil water than full-sun or monoculture systems, attributed to combined shade-tree and crop transpiration raising water uptake [ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]. In Ethiopia, subsoil moisture was lowest for wheat grown with Faidherbia albida, intermediate for sole tree and highest in the open field, though topsoil moisture showed no difference [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_2]. On the Canadian prairies, soil water near an old shelterbelt dropped noticeably in one year, tentatively attributed to uptake by the trees and grasses in the preceding fallow year [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. In Mexican coffee, high-shade sites showed smaller day-to-day swings in soil water from evaporation than low-shade sites, a buffering benefit rather than a higher measured moisture level, since shaded sites also gained less water after rain through canopy interception [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]; a German alley-cropping trial in a drought year found soil water lower on the open field than under trees, though not significant at every position [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. The class is set from this balance of measured gains and reversals rather than a pooled sign: the sub-practice rows themselves disagree (regeneration-based farmland reads conflicting on its own, shaded perennial and linear boundary read a slight increase in water stress, while cross-family and planted silvoarable read a benefit), so the roll-up states conflicting evidence. Most of the evidence (Niger, Malawi, Ethiopia, Ghana) sits inside the LIC/LMIC target; the Canadian and German units are high-income temperate evidence outside it [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. A French walnut-alley trial adds a further example of the plough-layer-versus-depth split already seen in this row: soil water in the plough layer was drier under the walnut alleys than in the full-sun control through spring, while at depth (50 cm or more) soil water dynamics were very similar between the two systems, consistent with the trees competing for moisture near the surface while deeper water use is comparable [ev_soil_moisture_blan22_4, ev_soil_moisture_blan22_5]. This is high-income French evidence, from a single season and site, outside the LIC/LMIC target. This Chinese result is upper-middle-income evidence and adds to the depth-dependent drying pattern already described for the African and French trials rather than changing it. Set against this, the same Malaysian trial found alley-cropping with bamboo measured significantly drier topsoil than the monocultures, attributed to bamboo's sparse canopy and gaps leaving the ground exposed to radiation — the wrong alley crop can dry the soil rather than conserve it [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_2]. In Brazilian coffee, soil moisture under shade was measured lower than under the unshaded area at every depth and throughout the monitored period, with the drying most pronounced soon after rain in drier periods, which the authors attribute to canopy interception lowering the rainfall reaching the soil and tree root uptake depleting the deeper layers — a clear case of shade drying the soil rather than conserving its moisture, even though the authors separately argue tree-coffee water-use complementarity kept available water sufficient for the coffee through the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_5, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_6, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_7]. In a New Zealand silvopasture, summer water use and end-of-summer soil moisture were no different from open pasture once the trees were four growing seasons old, as the maturing tree roots came to dominate water use across every system; and after a drier-than-normal winter, deep soil moisture under silvopasture was measured lower than under open lucerne, because the trees' higher winter water use had drawn down deep soil water the low winter rain did not replace — a further measured instance of trees competing with the crop or pasture for water under reduced rainfall [ev_soil_moisture_pollock08_1, ev_soil_moisture_pollock08_2]. None of this new evidence names a drought: the Brazilian site describes a below-average-rainfall month and the New Zealand site a below-normal-rainfall winter, not an extreme event. Malaysia and Brazil are upper-middle income and New Zealand high income, extending the pattern of measured splits in this conflicting-evidence row rather than resolving it.

agroforestry__water_stress__farming_syst.mechanism: In rainfed cropping the measured evidence points both ways. Trees draw down deeper and dry-season soil water: under Faidherbia albida parkland with wheat in Ethiopia, soil moisture in the sub-soil was the least for wheat with tree, intermediate for sole tree and the highest for open field [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]; in a Gliricidia + maize trial at Makoka, Malawi, the lower available soil water at the beginning of the cropping season in the tree-based systems suggests that the trees continued to deplete moisture during the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2], the March-to-August decline was most pronounced in the tree-based systems [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3], water content was slightly lower under gliricidia + maize in the dry season when the trees were left unpruned [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5], and in the first season's May water content under gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea was lower than in all other treatments below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4]. Beside Saskatchewan field shelterbelts, spring soil water content in 1990 dropped noticeably from 0.1 to 0.05 relative distance from the belt, which the authors put down, tentatively, to uptake by the trees and grasses in the previous fallow year; in 1989 the pattern differed, with a slight trend of decreasing available water from the field edge to the centre [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. Against this, at Makoka available water content tended to be greater in the gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea system at the peak of the recharge phase, which the authors attribute to increased infiltration and reduced soil evaporation [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10]; in the second season's May that system held much more water than all other treatments below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8]; and water use efficiency was higher in the tree systems in every season, for example 1.43 against 0.52 g of biomass per kg of water for gliricidia + maize against sole maize in 1997/98 [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_6]. At Sadore in the Nigerien Sahel, Ziziphus mauritiana trees in millet fields raised the rainwater use efficiency of millet by 17 and 47 % with farmyard manure and without fertilizer, and that of a millet/cowpea intercrop by 11 to 17 % [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_2]. A German alley-cropping trial in a drought year found soil water content remained lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. Several measurements found no difference: topsoil moisture under Faidherbia [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_2]; and at Makoka the generally comparable distribution of water in the profile [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_1], and no significant treatment effects in the second season, the second season's October, or December and January of the third season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_6, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_7, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_9]. The Makoka authors conclude that gliricidia pruned before and during the cropping season does not provoke undue competition for water with associated crops [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11]. In Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual system report 23% soil humidity in the driest month (April) against 8% in a traditional slash-and-burn field, a difference equivalent to 20mm of rainfall, or 20 more days that crops can be sustained without rain; they explain it by better infiltration through the soil cover and more soil organic matter [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1]. In France, a walnut-alley trial found a similar depth split: soil water in the plough layer was drier under the trees than the full-sun control through spring, while deep soil-water dynamics were very similar between the two systems [ev_soil_moisture_blan22_4, ev_soil_moisture_blan22_5]. In Jiangxi Province, China, a peanut-tree alley-cropping trial found the profile-mean (0-150 cm) soil water potential drier in both tree-intercropped treatments than in mono-cropped peanut or either tree monoculture, consistent with tree-crop competition for water, with the difference larger in the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_wei07_4].
agroforestry__water_stress__farming_syst.conditionality: What separates the sides is timing and depth: the trees deplete dry-season and subsoil water, so the crop may start the season with less, while recharge-season soil water and whole-system water productivity favour the tree plots [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10]. The African studies all involve pruned trees: heavily pruned Faidherbia on farmers' fields, gliricidia pruned before and during the crop season, and Ziziphus pruned before sowing; denser or unpruned canopies are not covered [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1]. The water use efficiency figures are total above-ground biomass of trees and crops together per unit of seasonal water use, not grain per unit of water, so the tree biomass lifts the tree-system values [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1]; the Niger figures, by contrast, count crop biomass only per mm of rainfall, so they show the crop itself using rain more efficiently with trees nearby [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1]; the authors caution that soil evaporation and water-table uptake were not measured and the gap is probably overstated, and these units count for water stress only, held out of the production gap because they do not measure crop yield. The German trial counts little: it is a temperate high-income site, its differences were not significant at all positions, and it measured surface soil only [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt unit is high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target; it measures soil water close to the belt rather than crop water stress, the drop appeared in 1990, not in 1989, and the authors hedge its cause [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. No study in this cell measures crop water stress itself; soil moisture and water productivity are read as components of it. The Honduran soil-humidity figures come from a grey-literature article by the project's own promoters, report no replication or significance, and compare a bundle (trees with mulch, zero tillage and no burning) against slash-and-burn, so the trees cannot be credited alone [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1]. The French result is high-income temperate evidence from a single season and site, outside the LIC/LMIC target, and it echoes the same depth-dependent pattern already described for the African trials: near-surface drying under the trees but little difference at depth [ev_soil_moisture_blan22_4, ev_soil_moisture_blan22_5]. This Chinese result is upper-middle-income evidence, adding a further harm reading to the depth-dependent drying pattern already in this row rather than changing it.

agroforestry__water_stress__farming_syst.mechanism: In tree-crop systems, shade and tree water use change soil moisture in opposing ways. A multi-country meta-analysis of cocoa agroforestry across Ghana, Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire, Indonesia, Malaysia, Costa Rica, Panama, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia found soils under agroforestry have a significantly lower volumetric water content than under monocultures [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]. In Ghana, the combined transpiration of shade trees and cocoa plants raised water uptake, with a consequent reduction in soil water compared with full-sun cocoa [ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]. Against this, in a Mexican coffee lysimeter study, soil water losses and gains fluctuated far more at the low-shade site than at the medium- and high-shade sites, showing that shade can buffer soil moisture loss through evaporation [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. In Malaysian oil palm, alley-cropping with black pepper or cacao measured significantly wetter topsoil than the monocultures, attributed to greater leaf area, lower light penetration and reduced wind cutting evaporation from exposed soil — the one unit in this row's newer evidence that reads as a soil-moisture benefit [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_1].
agroforestry__water_stress__farming_syst.conditionality: This row rolls up all tree-perennial farming-system evidence regardless of sub-practice family; in practice all three units come from shaded perennial-crop systems (cocoa, coffee). Most of the units measure less soil water under shade — the multi-country cocoa meta-analysis and the Ghana study — so the class is a slight increase in water stress rather than a benefit, and the Mexican coffee buffering result is the one offsetting signal, which keeps agreement at high rather than a stronger reading [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. None of the three states a size for the difference, and none measures a drought or other named water-stress hazard — all describe ordinary dry-season soil moisture [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. The Mexican result is a slower rate of loss and smaller swings under shade, not a higher measured moisture level, and the same site gained less water after rain through canopy interception [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. The cocoa evidence sits in lower- and upper-middle-income countries across Latin America, West Africa and Southeast Asia, in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. Every other new unit adds to the drying side already dominant in this row: the same Malaysian trial found bamboo alleys measured significantly drier topsoil than the monocultures, attributed to bamboo's sparse canopy leaving the ground exposed [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_2]; and in Brazilian coffee, soil moisture under shade was measured lower than under the unshaded area at every depth throughout the monitoring period, with the drying most pronounced soon after rain in drier periods — shade drying the soil rather than conserving it, even though the authors separately argue tree-coffee water-use complementarity kept available water sufficient for the coffee through the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_5, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_6, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_7]. None of the new units states a size or names a drought, and all are upper-middle-income evidence (Malaysia, Brazil), consistent with this row's existing transfer.

agroforestry__water_stress__income_group.mechanism: Only two temperate field studies sit in this high-income row, and they point in opposite directions. In a German alley-cropping trial in a drought year, soil water content remained lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though differences were not significant for all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. Beside Saskatchewan field shelterbelts, spring soil water content in 1990 dropped noticeably from 0.1 to 0.05 relative distance from the belt, which the authors put down, tentatively, to uptake by the trees and grasses in the previous fallow year; in 1989 the pattern differed, with a slight trend of decreasing available water from the field edge to the centre [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. The first reads as less water stress with trees, the second as more water stress next to them. A French walnut-alley trial adds a third pattern: soil water in the plough layer was drier under the trees than in the full-sun control through spring, while at depth (50 cm or more) soil water dynamics were very similar between the two systems [ev_soil_moisture_blan22_4, ev_soil_moisture_blan22_5]. In a New Zealand silvopasture, summer water use and end-of-summer soil moisture were no different from open pasture once the trees reached four growing seasons old, as the maturing tree roots came to dominate water use across every system [ev_soil_moisture_pollock08_1].
agroforestry__water_stress__income_group.conditionality: The two units differ in practice, year and position, so they do not contradict each other directly: the German comparison is alley cropping against an open field in a drought year, while the Canadian study compares soil close to a shelterbelt with soil further into the same field [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. Neither measures crop water stress itself; both measure soil water as a component of it. The German differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1], and the Canadian drop appeared in 1990, not in 1989, and its cause is hedged [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. Both are high-income temperate sites (Germany, Canada), outside the LIC/LMIC target. Missing: further studies of each practice, and any measure of crop water stress. The French result narrows to depth: the drier reading is specific to the plough layer near the surface, and does not extend to deeper soil water, unlike the all-depth German and Canadian comparisons already in this row. It is a single season and site, with the two conditions not randomised within the parcel, and is high-income temperate evidence (France), outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_soil_moisture_blan22_4, ev_soil_moisture_blan22_5]. After a drier-than-normal winter, deep soil moisture under silvopasture was measured lower than under open lucerne pasture, attributed to the trees' higher winter water use drawing down deep soil water that the low winter rain did not replace [ev_soil_moisture_pollock08_2]. Both readings are from the same single New Zealand silvopasture trial as the German and Canadian evidence already in this row, adding a further high-income temperate measurement rather than a new country or practice; neither names a drought, describing instead an ordinary below-normal-rainfall winter.

agroforestry__water_stress__income_group.mechanism: The measured soil-water evidence points both ways, and timing and soil depth separate the sides. On the side of more soil water, a sub-Saharan meta-analysis finds that agroforestry improved infiltration and soil moisture content compared to the control (RR 1.6 for soil moisture, with 70% of soil-moisture observations above RR 1) [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1]. In a Gliricidia + maize trial at Makoka, Malawi, available water content tended to be greater in the gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea system at the peak of the recharge phase, which the authors attribute to increased infiltration and reduced soil evaporation under greater ground cover [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10], and in the second season's May water content in that system was much greater than in all other treatments at depths below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8]. Water use efficiency was also higher in the tree systems in every season, for example 1.97 against 0.15 g of biomass per kg of water for gliricidia + maize against sole maize in 1998/99 [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_6]. In Niger, Ziziphus mauritiana trees in the cropped block increased the rainwater use efficiency of millet by 17 and 47 % with farmyard manure and in the unfertilised control, and that of the millet/cowpea intercrop by 11 to 17 % [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_2]. On the side of less soil water, under Faidherbia albida parkland in Ethiopia soil moisture in the sub-soil was the least for wheat with tree, intermediate for sole tree and the highest for open field [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]; in cocoa, a pan-tropical meta-analysis found soils under agroforestry significantly lower in volumetric water content than under full-sun monocultures [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]; in a Ghanaian cocoa field, the combined transpiration of shade trees and cocoa resulted in higher water uptake and less soil water than under full sun [ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]; at Makoka the lower available soil water at the beginning of the cropping season in the tree-based systems suggests that the trees continued to deplete moisture during the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2], the March-to-August decline was most pronounced in the tree-based systems [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3], water content was slightly lower under gliricidia + maize in the dry season when the trees were left unpruned [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5], and in the first season's May water content under gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea was lower than in all other treatments below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4]. Trees therefore draw down dry-season and subsoil water, while recharge-season soil water and whole-system water productivity favour them. Several measurements found no difference: topsoil moisture did not vary under Faidherbia [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_2], and at Makoka the distribution of water in the profile was generally comparable in all cropping systems [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_1], with no significant treatment effects in the second season, in the second season's October, or in December and January of the third season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_6, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_7, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_9]; the authors conclude that gliricidia pruned before and during the cropping season does not provoke undue competition for water with associated crops [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet adds increased water availability, its compiler crediting an increase in water retention which increases the ground water levels [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. In Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual system report 23% soil humidity in the driest month (April) against 8% in a traditional slash-and-burn field, a difference equivalent to 20mm of rainfall, or 20 more days that crops can be sustained without rain; they explain it by better infiltration through the soil cover and more soil organic matter [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1].
agroforestry__water_stress__income_group.conditionality: Within low- and lower-middle-income evidence the sides still disagree: the sub-Saharan meta-analysis, the Malawi Gliricidia trial and the Niger Ziziphus trial point to less water stress, while the Faidherbia subsoil depletion in Ethiopia and the cocoa soil-water deficits in the meta-analysis and in Ghana point to more [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]. The separator is timing and depth: trees deplete soil water through the dry season and below the topsoil, so less may be available when the crop is sown, while recharge-season water and system water productivity favour the tree plots [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10]. Management matters: the Malawi conclusion holds for gliricidia pruned before and during the cropping season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11], and the Ethiopian parkland trees were heavily pruned on farmers' fields [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]. The Makoka water use efficiency figures are total above-ground biomass of the whole system, trees and crops together, per unit of seasonal water use, not grain per unit of water [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1]; the tree biomass inflates the tree-system figures, and the authors caution that soil evaporation and water-table uptake were not measured, so the gap is probably overstated. The Niger figures are crop biomass per unit of rainfall, from a trial with the trees in a single block and the tree-free comparison in a separate block, so tree presence was not randomised and the contrast carries block effects [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_2]. The Makoka units therefore count here, for water stress, and are held out of the production gap because they say nothing about crop yield. The WOCAT unit is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet, not a soil-moisture measurement, and stays on water access rather than soil moisture [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. Infiltration and groundwater-recharge findings for catchments are carried in the agroforestry catchment water yield rows. The cocoa units are crop-specific and do not measure crop water stress directly; the Ghanaian study is a single farm with shade trees of Albizia ferruginea and Antiaris toxicaria [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]. The Honduran soil-humidity figures come from a grey-literature article by the project's own promoters, report no replication or significance, and compare a bundle (trees with mulch, zero tillage and no burning) against slash-and-burn, so the trees cannot be credited alone [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1].

agroforestry__water_stress__income_group.mechanism: This upper-middle-income scope row rests on two measured results that point opposite ways. In Chiapas, Mexico, a study of shaded coffee farms found soil water in weighing lysimeters fluctuated far less day-to-day under high and medium shade than under low shade, which the author reads as shade buffering soil-moisture loss through evaporation — though the same shaded sites also gain less water after rain, through canopy interception, so the benefit is a steadier moisture level rather than a wetter one [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. In Jiangxi Province, China, a peanut-tree alley-cropping trial found the profile-mean soil water potential drier in the tree-intercropped treatments than in mono-cropped peanut, which the authors attribute to tree-crop competition for water, worse in the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_wei07_4]. In Malaysian oil palm, alley-cropping with black pepper or cacao measured significantly wetter topsoil than the monocultures, attributed to greater leaf area, lower light penetration and reduced wind cutting evaporation from exposed soil [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_1].
agroforestry__water_stress__income_group.conditionality: The two results are not directly comparable — one measures the day-to-day swing in soil water under shade-grown coffee, the other the profile-mean water potential under peanut-tree alley cropping — but they sit on opposite sides of the benefit/harm split, which is why this scope row states conflicting evidence rather than a direction. Neither unit states a size for its effect, both are upper-middle-income evidence (Mexico and China), and neither names a drought: both describe an ordinary dry season or dry-season months, not an extreme event. The same Malaysian trial found the opposite for bamboo alleys, which measured significantly drier topsoil than the monocultures, attributed to bamboo's sparse canopy and gaps leaving the ground exposed [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_2]. In Brazilian coffee, soil moisture under shade was measured lower than under the unshaded area at every depth throughout the monitoring period, with depletion after rain much more intense in drier periods, attributed to canopy interception and deeper tree root uptake [ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_5, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_6, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_7]. These five new units split in both directions within the same upper-middle-income tier as the existing Mexican and Chinese evidence, which is why this scope row states conflicting evidence rather than a direction; none names a drought.

agroforestry__waterlogging__all.mechanism: Trees take excess water out of waterlogged soil. A review reports, second-hand, that under waterlogging in Punjab, India, agroforestry systems had higher evapotranspiration than sole crops, indicating greater removal of excess water from the soil and a better soil environment for plant growth [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9]. A biodrainage field study planted parallel strip plantations of Eucalyptus tereticornis along canal-irrigated, waterlogged fields in Haryana, India; over three years these strips lowered the groundwater table beneath them by an average of 0.85 m compared with control wells in adjacent unplanted fields, mainly through the trees' heavy water use [ev_waterlogging_hazard_ram11_1]. With that lower water table letting rainwater percolate and relieving oxygen deficiency in the wheat root zone, overall wheat grain yield in the research plot was 2.2 t/ha, 3.4 times the 0.6 t/ha measured in adjacent fields without the plantation [ev_crop_yield_ram11_2].
agroforestry__waterlogging__all.conditionality: The Punjab evapotranspiration finding is still a second-hand reading in a review, from lower-middle-income India within the LIC/LMIC target, and on its own it does not report a yield or livelihood outcome [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9]. The Haryana biodrainage findings now come from the original field study rather than a review's second-hand summary: the water-table drawdown was measured under the strips themselves against unplanted fields, and how far it reaches into the cropped space between strips is not stated [ev_waterlogging_hazard_ram11_1]. The wheat-yield gain compares a single research plot with adjacent fields, not a randomised or replicated trial, and the study does not say how severe the waterlogging was in either case [ev_crop_yield_ram11_2]. The Haryana case is a canal-irrigated system, and nothing in the evidence covers severe or extreme waterlogging.

agroforestry__wind_cyclone__agro_pastora.mechanism: Windbreaks reduce wind speed over a zone that typically extends 10 to 20 tree heights downwind, and live fences in India are used as windbreaks [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15, ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4]. In the other direction, a Latin American adaptation review lists planting shade trees that damage existing infrastructure in storms as a case of increased vulnerability [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].
agroforestry__wind_cyclone__agro_pastora.conditionality: The evidence splits between wind sheltering and storm damage, and the wind units concern wind erosion and sheltering rather than cyclone impacts [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15, ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5]. All three are reviews citing other work; only the Indian unit names a country (lower-middle income) [ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4]. No unit is from an agro-pastoral system; the evidence is applied to agro-pastoral systems by default [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5, ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15, ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4].

agroforestry__wind_cyclone__all.mechanism: Windbreaks and shelterbelts work mechanically, by slowing the wind reaching the sheltered crop. A review on windbreak airflow states that a major effect of a windbreak is to reduce the incidence of low-frequency, high-magnitude damage events such as sandblasting or lodging [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_cleugh98_3]. The zone of reduced wind speed behind a windbreak typically extends 10 to 20 tree heights downwind, so large fields often need multiple barriers [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15]. In China, farmland shelterbelts cut wind speed by 35.8% compared with unsheltered farmland [ev_windbreak_protection_hao26_1]. In Senegal, windbreak hedges are described as having a major impact on wind and playing an important role in protecting sandy, degraded soils from wind erosion [ev_windbreak_protection_faosen24_12]. In India, live fences are used as windbreaks and to raise soil-moisture retention through litter accumulation [ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4]. More generally, on-farm trees serving as windbreaks and shelterbelts are also used to supply material for rebuilding storm-damaged property [ev_windbreak_protection_lasco14_1]. In Mexican shaded coffee, vegetation management had a significant effect on landslide risk but not on coffee harvest lost [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6].
agroforestry__wind_cyclone__all.conditionality: Against this, a Spanish-language climate-risk review lists an explicit maladaptation example: planting shade trees that increases storm vulnerability by damaging existing infrastructure when the trees come down in high winds [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5] — the measured harm behind this row's class. The roll-up states conflicting evidence because the family vote splits: linear-boundary windbreak evidence reads as a benefit, the shaded perennial-crop family (the Mexican coffee study, which found no relationship between management and harvest loss) reads as no effect, and the cross-family pool lands on conflicting evidence. Only the Chinese shelterbelt study states a size for the wind-speed reduction; the rest describe mechanism or role without a magnitude, which caps the class at moderate. None of the units measures a severe or extreme wind or cyclone event — the evidence covers routine wind and erosion control, not storm or cyclone damage. The Chinese and Mexican units are upper-middle income, the Senegalese and Indian units lower-middle income, so the row sits adjacent to, not squarely inside, the LIC/LMIC target.
